div.p: voetvg:

THE WOLF OUTWITTED. A hungry wolf in search of food, One chilly autumn day, In passing through a grassy field, Saw there a foal at play. The young foal's mother some way off Was grazing in the field; She saw the wolf, and from his jaws Thought how her foal to shield. The wolf walked gently to the daughter; He hoped her health was good, Just mentioned tba he was a doctor, And thought, "I've here found food." When up the wise old mother trotted. And said, "I'm in such pain, I've hurt my foot; if you are a doctor, Pray give me ease again. "Put on your glasses; worthy sir, A thorn I'm sure you'll find Run deep into my tender foot— • It is the foot behind." The wolf stooped down behind the mother, And then there was a crash; First one good kick and then another, Into his face went smash.

THE SUNSET'S GATE. In they came, racing and tumbling, With faces and voices forlorn, With hair all toss'd and dishevelled. And garments all streaming and torn. "For, oh," said the weary children, "We have rambled afar to-night. Along the path by the river, Where the meadow-sweet dowers are white. "And we've climbed the hill of the fairies, they say, If you only wait, Where, You will see, on a summer's evening, The opening of sunset's gate; "And the wondrous magic castles, With turrets of jewels and gold, And knights in their glittering armour, Like the stories of days of old. "But the way was hot and dusty, And the hill was so hard to climb, With tangle of briars and brushwood, We took such a weary time, "That when we had reached the summit All was dreary and chill and gray; No vestige of gold or crimson— The castles had faded away." Then a voice came from little Amy, With a happy secret confessed: "I am not strong, like the others, So I could not climb with the rest. "I sat down beside the river, To wait, on a mossy stone. I could not help grieving a little. As I found myself all alone; "When, oh, such a radiance, mother, Came flooding all through the air Everything around grew golden— Gold above, beyond, everywhere; "And far away in the distance, As I shaded my eyes with my hand, Not castles we children speak of, But the gates of the Better Land. " For I saw bright bands of angels, With their wings all radiant white. And I think I heard their singing; „ They will come in my dreams to-night." The mother smiled as. she listened, While she comforted and caressed, And saw each tired wanderer . Gathered safe in the household nest. She sat in the fading twilight, As the murmur of day grew still, And thought how life !Inds an emblem In the children's climbing the hill. Ah, the dreary ways we traverse Through the storm and tempest and heat! Ah, the briars which clog our footsteps, And the stones which bruise our feet! As we pant and toil and struggle For the long-cherished hopes of years— As vain, alas as the castles The children bemoaned in their tears— We find but the chill of failure Disappointment, and sorrow's blight, While the evening's creeping shadows Tell of death's approaching night. But, thank God, there comes so often, . To the patient hearts who wait, The gleam of God's blessed angels Through the opening of Heaven's Gate. J. C. A., in Good Words for July.

A schoolboy on being asked what made the Tower of Pa leas. replied, "Because of the famine hi the land." There is no necessary sacrifice of self in kind words, nor in energetic action, nor in schemes of benevolence, nor in the busiest pursuit of works of charity. Miss Bernhardt is reported as saying that she "can't see how the men resist tumbling head and ears in love with the handsome &merican girls." Perhaps they don't resist. Teacher : "Suppose that you have two sticks of candy, and your big brother gives you two more; how rflany have you got then ?" Little Boy (shaking his head) : Yon don't know him. He ain't that kind of boy." The physicians of Nashville, Tennessee, have petitioned the Common Council to prohibit the tolling of bells for the dead, on the ground that the sound has a depressing effect on such of their patients as have not succumbed. Self may stand out prominently from amidst charitable designs and efforts, even from a life spent in such Sims. The charitabie design, or the absorbing interest of benevo- lent energy, may even feed the self which they envelop.— Carter. An enterprising American shipped some wheelbarrows to Rio Janeiro, and the natives filled them with stones, and carried them on their heads. They said it was a capital contrivance, and wondered how they managed so many years without it "But a man must live," says someone. How often one hears that made the excuse for all sorts of meanness, dis- honesty, grasping tyranny. "A man must live t " Who told you that? Not the example of great and good men. It is better to die like a man than to live like a slave, and a wretch, and a sinner —Klngsiev. REPENTANCE.—Teacher, who is trying to explain the meanirg of repentance: "Suppose a had boy were to steal an orange, and his good mother should catch him with it, and take him by the band gently' and tell him how wicked it is, and how very, very grieved she was; don't you think now that the little boy ought to feel sorry?" Sunday Scholar: " Yessurn." Teacher: "And why, Marmadnke I" S.S.: "'Cause—" Teacher: "Because what, Marmy?" S.S.: "'Cause he hadn't et the or'nge befo' his ma notch him and tuck it away film him !" The little village of Abilene, Kansas, is noted for having six churches. It has only one newspaper, and that is a weekly; but Abilene is nevertheless ahead of all other towns in this season's competition in the matter of warm weather stories. A farmer living near Riley Center—so it is printed—started for Garrison with a load of hogs; but the sun was warm, and the bogs were fat, and when the farmer arrived in Garrison, his eighty-five dollars' worth of pork had melted, and leaked through the bottom of the waggon box.

A QUAINT CONCEIT.—AO Old preacher used to say that reading the Bible was like eating fish. When he cams to a hard place he left it and called it a bone. The older he grew the fewer bones he found, until when he came to be an old man the book that he used to find as full of bones as a herring was like a halibut, with only one big bone in it of God's incomprehensibility, and that was in such plain sight that no one could stumble over it, and grandly served its Ttirpose as strong framework to keep the sweet, white, nutritious meat in its place. Children are unfortunately addicted to telling the truth, and there are times when the truth is about the only thing that shouldn't he told. When a fashionable young lady was in full dress for a ball it seemed to her, unsophisticated little brother that if her dress should be drawn up towards the neck about six inches it would be a great improvement. He went to the wardrobe, and, bringing a shawl, presented it to her. "What's that for ? " she asked. "Why, its for you to put on," said the enfant terrible. ." For a.nli to pnt on? Why, I'm all dressed. Don't I look pretty ? ' "Oh, yes," blurted out the little observer, as he looked at her bare shoulder, "but you had better put on the shawl, for, sister, somebody might see you, you know." DR. CHALMERS'S EIOME-MISSION WORK IN EDINBURGH. —He had selected one of the worst and most degraded localities in Edinburgh for putting in practice the principles which he so long advocated for territorial work, bringing education, social influence, and the Gospe! of Christ to bear within a definite area. He condemned all promiscuous charity, free education, and similar methods tending to panperise rather than elevate the people. Something, how- ever little, must be paid by the poorest for the education of their children, believing that if the education imparted was really valuable, the poor would not only appreciate the benefit, but be morally elevated in being called on to con- tribute to its support. . . . It is interesting to remem- ber that Chalmers's theory was magnificently successful when practically applied. School and church, and wise personal influences went hand in hand. The West Port population, from being perhaps the most degraded in the city, manifested the symptoms of an extraordinary change. When the work began, the number attending all places of worship did not exceed one-eighth of the population—of chlalren capable of education, three-fourths were not at school—and the district was on Saturday nights and Sun- days a scene of drunkenness and riot. In two years after Chalmers began his work, "three hundred sittings in the new church were taken, one hundred persons from the district partook of communion, of whom there were eighty (many advanced in years) who had never communicated in their lives before, or so long ago that they had long for- gotten the nature of the ordinance." As regards education, "the ratio was reversed, three-fourths were now at school. In five years afterwards there was not a child in the district who was krown not to he at school." The very outward ?l3l,earance of the locality was changed, as witnessed to by increased cleanliness and the comparative quiet which reigned on Saturdays and Sundays." Ninety-four lamps, encicsed in safety lanterns, were used ; the results were considered satisfactory and may be regarded as an important step in the progress of electric lighting. We learn from the Scotsman that stones have recently been erected on the battlefield of Culloden, inscribed with the names of the several Highland clans which tradition associ- ates with the graves still* be traced there. The clans thus cominemorated are M‘Gillivray, M`Lean, and M'Lanchlan on one stone ; and Stuart of Appin, Cameron, and Mackintosh. An Inscription has also been placed on the great cairn, which is a conspicuous object on Culloden Moor. A portion of the stone used in constructing the new High School building in Leadville, Colorado, was taken from a neighbouring mountain on which several rich gold mines have since been opened. When the building was in course ot erection, the stone-cutters found in one of the blocks a vein of natural gold, which is described as being "about the size of a knife blade," and it is said that the entire facings of the structure are cut out of gold-bearing rock. THE 'index-Hamm. MULTICHARGE GUN.—Work has been begun, in the pattern room of .the Reading Ironworks, on the first Lyman-Haskell accelerating or multicharge can- non. The gun will be 25ft. long and have a bore 6in, in eFameter. Along the bore four pockets will be located, in each of which a charge of powder will be placed, with the view of accelerating the speed of the ball after it leaves the chamber of the gun and during its progress through the. bare. The charge of powder will be 130 pounds, and the weight of shot 150 pounds. It is calculated that a shot from the gan will penetrate through 2ft. of solid wrought iron. The expected range of the gun is ten to twelve miles. A DACIAN }intro.—The Transylvanian paper the Hermann- et alter Zietung, gives a short account of a large white marble slab, nearly 40 inches square, which was lately dug up near Va,hely, the site of the old Ulpia Trajana, bearing a Latin inscription. The inscription indicates that some wealthy Cacian had erected a temple to certain *divinities of his race, whose names are see out, and had "added a kitchen" (colinam subiunzit). This is accounted by local archaeo- logists a valuable discovery inasmuch as it mentions several Dacian divinities by name, whereas hitherto nothing was known on this subject. It appears also that the Dacians worshipped their ancestral divinities in preference to those of their Roman conquerors, and that offerings of cooked food enteredinto the worship, otherwise the addition of a kitchen to the temple could not be readily explained. AN IMPORTANT SIGNALLING INVENTION.—Germany is to contribute to the Electro-technical Exhibition, at Paris, the model of a new and important signalling apparatus, the invention of a railway official at Elberfeld, which is intended to dispense with intermediate block stations, and to allow trains to follow each other at closer distances than hitherto. The device, which has been tried and found to work excel- lently, is called an electro-autornatic block station telegraph, and is so constructed as to register simultaneously by wheel. pressure at two stations the passage of a train at a point equidistant from them. The invention promises to be of great importance and will at any rate deeply interest all railway engineers who visit Paris in July.

_ PREPARING PAPER AND WOOD FOR PAINTING.—A new method of preparing paper tissues, wooden tablets, Sze., for the purposes of painting, has been patented in Germany by M. Dupays, of Nancy, the advantages being that in use of crayon or chalk the colours adhere better to the surface; in water-colour work the moisture is long retained, so that the colour tones retain unchanged during work, and in oil painting the colours easily mix, greatly facilitating the work of beginners. The process is essentially as follows:— One or two coats of size are first applied to remove porosity, then a thin layer of a paste of whitelead (200 gr. and boiled oil (50gr.) is put on. After drying for half an hour, fine cotton dust is sprinkled on the surface from a sieve, and by striking the piece on the back, the fine cotton fibres are caused to rise, forming a velvet-like surface. The material is let dry two or three days, and brushed with a woollen brush so as to depress the cotton somewhat; then a mixture of whitelead (Bpts.), gold lac (lot.), spirit of turpentine (lpt.), and starch (lpt.) is applied. This is equally dis- tributed by passage between rollers, with caoutchouc sur- face. The cotton particles are raised again with a fine brush of couchgrass, and after two or three days' drying, the material is put in a bath of alcohol and water (half of either). • • - -

, SIBERIAN ExPuntartort.—lt appears probable that there will be a good deal of activity this season on the north.west coast of Siberia. especially in the Obi and Yenisei Gulfs. M. Sibiriakoff is fitting out three sledge expeditions to take supplies to the Oscar Dickson and Nordland, which have been frozen up during the past winter in the Gulf of Obi, and of which no intelligence has been received since he left them in September last. The steamer Nordenskiold is also being fitted out at Gothenburg for another voyage to the month of the Yenisei. The objects of the aboveimentioned expeditions are chiefly commercial, but science will not be umepresented in the same region, for we learn that a Rus- elan hydrographic expedition started from the Obi on May 27th. The party is under the command of Col. Moisseieff, of the pilot service, who is accompanied by Capt. Abramqff and Lieuts. Philippoff and Mikheieff. -M. Fuchs will act as astronomer, and two students skilled in surgery and natural history are also attached to the expedition. Two steam cutters for their use have been sent on by rail to Rybinsk, whence they will proceed by the Volga and the Kama to Perm. It is intended that their crews should be instructed in hvdography and the navigation of the Gulf of Obi and the Kara Sea, which as yet is very imperfectly understood, as W 35 shown by the difficulty experienced by M. Sibirla- koff's expedition last summer.

TEE CAPACTIT or THE DF.AF FOR SPERM—The deaf are possessed of the organs of speech, but they are ignorant of their use, for the sense is absent which would have made them subject to the will. But another sense can take its place, and do part of its service. Touch has to be made sensitive to the action of the voice and the difference of its tones. Hence the business of the teacher is to cultivate touch by suitable exercises till the will is able to act upon the muscles of the larynx, and regulate the glottis to every vowel-sound. The voice in deaf and dumb children differs much. Some can utter a few sounds clearly and softly. It is a valuable foundation, and little more has to be done for them than lead them on to all the remaining sounds, main• taming, if possible, the same softness. Others, again, can utter a few sounds, but very imperfectly. More effort is required to correct their voices and guide them to their full control. But a third class either utter no sounds, or only such wild and discordant ones as are out of place in speech. These have to be reduced till the right tone is secured. This is the most trying class for the teacher, for not unfrequently they seem indisposed to attempt any utterance. But patience, firmness, and gentleness will triumph. Never despair. The rough can be made smooth, and the harsh sweet. Some of these may turn out the best speakers.—A Method of Teach ing the Deaf and Dumb Speech, Lipreading, and Language. Bu Thomas Arnold. MRS. CARLYLE.—The Athenaum says—ln an article that is to appear in the July number of the British Quarterly will be found some clever letters of Mrs. Carlyle—so clever. indeed, as to make the reader long for the volumes other letters which rumour says are preparing. The writer helped Mr. Carlyle in many ways, more especially by preparing in- dexes and maps to the Life of Frederick the Great,. At length he was so worried by the petulances of the sage that when the work was done he wrote to Carlyle, expressing "a bit of. his mind," and after that he had the courage to go to Cheyne-row When I entered his study he met me very much as usual, but I could both see and feel that he was greatly hurt; and when I looked in at the drawing-room Mrs. Carlyle received me with wide-open eyes of astonish- i ment, which might have meant, 'Et tu brute?' or might I only have meant, 'Are my forebodings at last fulfilled?'" Mr. Carlyle did not encourage those who volunteered help in a spirit of hero worship. She remarked to Mr. Larkin, "It was mostly mad people who came running after Car- lyle." But she made use of them. For instance, she writes after an illness :—"Set out I must, however, as early as is consistent with ordinary prudence; for the idea Of Mr. Car- lyle going about at home, seeking things like a madman, and never finding them; and of his depending on the tender mercies of Charlotte for his diet, leaves me no rest—partly on Charlotte's account, I confess, as well as his own! div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 9, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 9, 1881.
NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &c.

THE Cum.—The crops of grass which have been cut as yet have been exceedingly light in character, and in some places they have been badly taken as well, owing to the frequent storms of the past fortnight, which seem to have proved extremely partial, in some districts not yielding any- thing like enough rain for requirements, but in others ca using quite a deluge of downfall. Probably the late crops Of meadow grass will yield heayier cuts than have yet been realised. Accounts vary considerably respecting the wheat cr”p, which is not only short in the straw in many districts, t characterised by remarkably short ears likewise. Ac- cording to general experiences, heavy yields seldom are ex- pr dewed when the heads are thus diminutive, but a great deal will, of course, depend on the nature of the kern. The al.pearance of the barley crops is far more favourable, and, according to present prospects, the experience of last year is likely to be repeated in barley proving a far better crop thin wheat. But it is Much to be hoped that we shall not have a repetition of the July of 1880, which turned out so ruinous to the latter. The turnip crops in Scotland have /roved thus far a failure, and our northern neighbours will have to depend very much on the later sowings. Thus far the root prospects in England are much better than in Scot- lend, but it is much too early yet to predicate what the turnip crop in England will be.—Farmer's Chronicle. TEE DECLINE OF PEASANT PROPRIETORS IN WESTMOR- LINIL—Mr. Coleman, sub-commissioner, has presented a report to the Royal Commission on the state of agriculture in Cumberland and Westmorland. It contains the following int-resting passage on the dying out of the yeomanry or " estatesmen ' in the county of Westmorland :—" When Pringle wrote his report of Westmorland, in 1797, a large p-oportion of the land in both counties was occupied by est ttemen, i.e., men who owned the land. The holdings were mostly small, ranging, principally from £lO to £5O, o^casionally rising to £lOO a year of annual value. There was a time when theme men were a flourishing part of the co-nmunity ; and reared in habits of thrift and industry, their offshoots went out into the world, and in not a few ewes built TM large fortunes in trade, frequently returning to their native county, there to found families which be- c trite famous. This much-respected class has gradually dis- appeared, until at the present time they are nearly extinct; a few only remain, principally in the mountain dales. However we may regret the change, it appears to have been inevitable. Land is an expensive luxury, and not a profit- able investment. As civilisation progressed, and the cost of living increased, returns were not proportionately advanced. The land became gradually burdened with charges, and, often suffering in condition, was eventually parted with, going, as a rule, to swell the larger estates. Nor, as regards the public advantage, need such a result be lamented, for it is quite certain that a flourishing tenantry, under a liberal and wealthy owner, are far more productive than owners whose means are too straitened to allow of the proper appli- cation of capital. Probably the most complete illustration of this change is seen in the Earl of Bectives fine property at Underley which comprises about 25,000 acres, of which a considerable portion is hill land. A large part of this property was formerly owned by small proprietors, mostly estatesmen. These men held on as long as possible, and when eaten up with debts and charges, and the soil wretchedly impoverished, the trustees of the late Alderman Thompson, who himself, if I mistake not, sprang from a statesman family, bought up the farms by degrees, and there is still money waiting similar investment. In no case did the investment pay more than n per cent. on the pur- chase money. In many instances the former owners con- tinued as the tenants, and when the land was drained and limed and proper buildings erected, these men, who were formerly hard up, became well-to-do farmers. A better example could not be found of the truth which I have to frequently insisted on that the influence of large estates when well worked is decidedly good for the public weal. The Underley estate probably yields more than double the produce of which the land was capable when divided and ill-managed. The number of farms under 50 acres has slightly declined in Cumberland, and somewhat increased in Westmorland. In much the same proportion the next class, i.e., farms ranging from 50 to 100 acres have increased in Cumberland, whilst in Westmorland they are nearly sta- tionary. Farms from 100 to 300 acres have increased in both counties, and the larger farms were much the same at
, both periods. That out of a total of 7.999 farms returned 19 Cumberland over 6,000 should be under 100 acres proves that small farms are still very much in the ascendant."

CRUELTY TO ANIMALS —Benjamin Brighty, Eaton, shep- herd, was charged with driving a sheep, minus one of its fore feet, and one of the legs completely gone below the knee joint, so that every step the animal took it dropped on to the stump and left a bloody track behind. Defendant said the animal had lost his foot about a year ago by being worried by a dog. This had been dressed and bound up, and the wound had healed. The magistrate told him that he must have known the state of the animal, and he would be fined 5s and 265. 6d. hosts, in default 14 days hard labour. —Charles Porter, summoned by the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, was fined 20s. and Costs at the Marlborough-street Police-office, for riding a I horse in Rotten Row and spurring it unmercifully. Mr. W. Sharp, of Albert Gate, said he saw the blood running down its side. Never having seen greater cruelty in his life, he told the defendant that he should summon him. The wit- ness said he had been used to horses all his life, and gene- rally kept four or five. THE COMMERCIAL PRINCIPLE.—If, by adapting the com- mercial principle to farming, is meant that the farmer shall abandon the present method of buying and selling "by favour and guess," and shall endeavour to establish open markets, at which by telegraph all England may compete, tben the adoption is highly desirable. But in order that markets for fat cattle may be open. a method of selling must be in practice which will enahle all the by-standers to com- prehend what is going on, and to communicate accurately what they see to others. In America the tidings, "full mar- ket, good beeves going at 4c. to sc. per 1b.," would be tele- graphed to twenty other centres besides the town in which the market is held, and bids would come in speedily from distant, buyers. In England nothing of the kind can be done, except in most general terms, because the terms on which the -lots are being sold Cannot be expressed with pre- cision. There can be no public notice to distant places of a glut, because nobody really knows what a pound of beef or mutton is really going for. Sales by weight are impera- tively called for in the cattle markets in the interest of the producer.—D. S. L., in Agricultural Gazette.

div.head: HAYMAKING.
div.p: HAYMAKING.

A short article on haymaking, or what might perhaps now-a-days be headed " grass-spoiling" :—No doubt a great deal may be written upon this subject, especially during ' showery weather, when we cannot be actually engaged in its practine. During the last few years an immense deal 1 of grass has been spoiled, and but very little hay has been ' made, worthy of the name. Most text books on agriculture (my own among the number) give glowing descriptions of haymaking. The grass is to be cut when the majority of the plants composing it are in flower. This is the easiest , part of the process, and the only direction which we may I reckon on being able to follow implicitly. Aocording to the Middlesex method, which you have yourself described, the grass cat to-day is tedded, twice turned, and cocked to- morrow; thrown out into staddles, turned, and cocked again the third day, and thrown out and carted on the fourth day. This is the method first described by Mr. Middleton, but we have never yet seen it done in practice. Our own experi- ence is more as follows. First we experience a dry April and May, resulting in a thin and poor crop of grass. This we proceed to mow, or cut down with a machine, and as , soon as this is accomplished, so far as our experience extends, the weather changes and it begins raining. This does the grass no great harm 80 long as it remains un- touched, for nature has furnished every blade of grass with a waterproof mantle which protects it from the rude approach of external moisture. To let our grass alone appears then to be the best course for some time at least. The longer grass is cut the more injury is it liable to incur from rain. The soluble matter is washed out in the form I of what is known under more auspicious circumstances as "hay-tea." This infusion of hay which is to an invalid cow what " beef-tea" is to a convalescent countess, is thus I formed at the wrong time, and soaks into the land. The remnant is left rich in indigestible fibre, bleached in ap- pearance, and dusty from the rapid development of fungi. It lies about for weeks, and whenever the weather clears up it is turned, only to get wet again. We have known it never carried home at all. On one occasion it lay out until the second or after-crop was ready to mow, and then it and the later-mown grass were carried home together. In making bay, it is sound policy to cure in "cock." In our +own immediate neighbourhood they have an abominable practice of letting the grass lie a,broad in swathe until it is fit to cart. If the weather should prove fine, it is soon dry, although it is apt to get over-made, and it must lose its colour and much of its flavour. No doubt the right course is to get it into cock as soon as possible. A well-made hay- cock will stand a lot of rain without taking in wet. It should be narrower at the bottom than the middle, and be well filled up on the top and combed down, so as to cause the water to run off it. As the hay approaches fitness two cocks may be thrown into one. Each fine morning these cocks should be opened out, and they should be formed up again towards evening, or when rain is expected. IV this means the colour, virtue,and aroma of the hay is preserved, and it may, under favourable circumstances, be carried to the rick, literally as green as grass. Hay should be carried when it is fit—not before and not after. The rick is all the better of a good sweating, but we must avoid over- heating. Few farming opera ions require so much patience, etautly prearadcyticta e l piece of u wp a experience, faith, hope, and charity as haymaking. It is a trial of every virtue and all our energy. It is an unmis- takably ork.parTtyliefmorastteedrdmust tbuernincong: cocking, or carting, the moment 'a favourable change of wind or weather will allow of it. Equally must he be ready to turn the hands and horses to other tasks should the hay- making be interrupted. Meteorologists should take note that about the time when grass is down the barometer falls for rain.—Agricultural Gazette.

By order of the Postmaster-General a number of female clerkships will shortly be filled up by open com- petition. The Lord Chancellor has appointed Mr. W. H. Bagshawe, Q.C., to be County Court Judge of Circuit No. 35, in succes- si,m to the late Mr. Edmond Beales, The Prince and Princess of %Vales went on Saturday after- neon to King's College, where his Royal Highness distri- buted the prizes to the successful students. Sixty thousand emigrants landed at New York during the month of June, making 242,000 for the half year, 65,000 more than during the same period last year On Monday, Bernard Jesse], a young man, was brought up at the Manchester City Police Court, and sentenced to sia months' imprisonment with hard labour for assaulting a police constable and attempting to stab his own fattier on S. a urday night. The Brighton Railway Company propose to introduce with their new tuliman train another important innovation. They will try with the Service the American system of checking luggage, which if found to answer, will be ex- t( tided to all their trains.

Wm. Boothman, assistant overseer and collector of taxes and inhabited house duty, was charged at Accrington on Monday, with embezzling various sums of money belonging ta the lownship. Formal evidence having been given, the p, iaoner was remanded. JEAN LIGE AGAIN.—At the Westminster Police Court, on Monday, Jean Luie, whose name will be remembered in connection with the. Tichborne case, applied for an. order

to compel the delivery to him of some papers in the hands of the police. The magistrate referred him to the Treasury. The Royal Commission on Mines will not be able to report this session, though it has completed the work of taking evidence. This will be laid before Parliament in the course of a week or ten days, with a preface in the form of a sum- mary, but the commission will not this year offer any recom- mendations.—Observer.

TyNwetn Des IN THE ISLE or MAN.—The annual and I ancient custom of promulgating the laws which have been passed by the Isle of Man legislature, tool place on Tuesday , at Tynwald Mount. The procession of officials, clergy, I members of the legislature, and others, was witnessed by an I immense number of visitors' from all parts of the kingdom. The local budget was passed. At Wednesbury, on Tuesday, a youth named Mark Hol- land was charged with committing a brutal outrage on his father. The prisoner and his father lived in a °elpsies' tent, and on Monday complainant remonstrated with the prisoner for haying dons something wrong, upon which the prisoner commenced a brutal attack upon his father. The prisoner was sentenced to Six months imprisonment. WHAT FIGURES PROVE.—The Hon. Charles Francis Adams, jun., in his book about railway accidents, says : " If any given person were born upon a railway car and re- mained upon it travelling 500 miles a day all his life, be would with average good fortune, be somewhat over eighty years of age before he would be involved in any . accident resulting in his personal injury, while he would attain the highly respectable age of 930 years before being killed." John Elias and Richard Walters, militiamen, were charged before the Swansea magistaates, on Tuesday, with causing tho death of Eliza Lee by striking bar in the eye. Walters was charged upon the coroner's warrant with man- slaughter. In a conVersatien between the prisoners, over- heard by the police, Waltets admitted having struck the girl The Bench committed Walters for trial for wilful murder, and acquitted John Elias. A somewhat serious accident took place on the Lanca- shire and Yorkshire Railway, near Wakefield, on Saturday. A passenger train from Wakefield to Manchester was moving Out of the Kirkgate Station when it was run into by a train consisting. chiefly of horse-boxes, coming from the opposite direction. The engine of the passenger train was thrown off the metals, and twenty-fire of the passengers received sl Erin injuries about the head and face. Two of the rail- way officials were also hurt. ALLEGED Cirstn MURDER —A coroner's inquiry at Ply- mouth has resulted in the committal of Emma Stapleton for trial on the charge of wilful murder. She was a single _ _ . .
woman, and had hal three children, each of whom had died

under the age of one month. In the last instance she alleged originally that death was from natural causes, but ultimately stated that she had give it spirits of salts in mis- take for borax. Mn. BRADLAUGH RESOLVES TO PRESENT HIMSELF AT ST STEPHEN'S AGAIN.—Mr. Bradlaugh has written to the Speaker of the House of Commons respectf oily giving notice that he will, in the manner and at the time provided by the Standing Orders of the House, again present himself at the table of the House, to complete the fulfilment of the duty imposed on him by law, and in the course of the performance of which duty he has been most improperly and illegally interrupted and hindered. RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT ACCRINGTON. —On Tuesday afternoon an accident occurred to the Manchester express due at Accrington at three o'clock. The train was approach- ing the platform, when a train of empty carriages was being backed up the line across the points. The engine caught the end carriage and telescoped it, the top of the carriage covering the engine like a van cover, and the two sides of the carriage dropping on each sided the engine. The fu,nnel of the en2ine was broken. Mr. Stott, German harm dealer, was hurt in the back. The up-line was blocked for several henrs, tho engine being off the metals. JUMPING ON A WIFE.-011 Saturday, at Newark, a man who works at the plaster pits quarrelled with his wife in the roadway, and, seizing her by the throat, threw her violently to the ground. lie then deliberately jumped upon her chest and stomach with his hobnailed heavy labourer's boots. The poor woman, who was enceinte, groaned, and then appeared to become insensible. The ruffian was secured by some militiamen, and a surgeon who attended the injured woman pronounced her to be in a dangerous condition. Patrick Staunton, one of the actors in the Penge mystery, has just died at the Knaphill convict prison. It will be remembered that Patrick, his wife, his broth'er, and Alice Rhodes were in September, 1877, sentenced to death for the murder of Harriet Staunton, wife of Louis Staunton. One of the convicts, Rhodes, was subsequently pardoned, and the capital sentence on the other prisoners was commuted'to penal servitude for life. Since his incarceration, Patrick Staunton has been in a week and dejected state, and he died last week of consumption. A BISHOP ON THE SALVATION ARMY—Speaking at the opening of a diocesan conference at Rochester, the Bishop of Rochester referred to the Salvation Army, and said that if it adopted methods which offended the tastes, and eccen- tricities which distressed the soberness of some, yet it aimed at results and reached classes which at present the Church could only pray for. No one who knew how difficult it was to get ot the lowest stratum of the London poor would rashly forbid or severely condemn any who, though imper- fectly, still sincerely, were reaching them with the message I of Jesus Christ. MR. GLADSTONE AND THE SUGAR Borwrrus.—The fol- lowing letter from Mr. Gladstone respecting the sugar bounties was read at a general meeting of the Workingmen's National Executive Commitee, held at the Central Rooms: "Sir—Mr. Gladstone has received the further communica- tion which has been addressed to him by the Workman's National Executive Committee for the Abolition of the Foreign Sugar Bounties, and he desires me to express his regret that his receat reply should have caused such disap- pointment to the Committee. He will only add that he endeavoured to base that reply upon fact and reasoning, with which, of course, the Committee will deal as they think fit.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, E. W. nanrwroN!' THREAT TO BLOW tlr RAWARDEN CASTLE AND EATON HALL.—The Liverpool Daily Post says :—For the past few days the city and county police autharities have been much exercised by letters received at Eaton Hall, the residence of the Duke of Westminster, and Hawarden Castle, stating that it was the intention of the Fenians to blow up those buildings. Copies of these letters have been received by the city and county authorities as well as the chief con- stable of Flintshire. Considering the attempt at Liverpool and other places, the authorities attach much importance to the threats, and consequently every precaution has been taken with a view to prevent any such attempt being made. DEATH OF MR. WILLIAM INMAN.—Mr. Inman, the founder of tile Inman line of Atlantic steamers, died on Sun- day forenoon, at his residence, Upton Manor, near Birken- head. Mr. Inman has been ailing for some months, and his death at the comparatively early age of 56 was not alto- gether expected. The deceased was born at Leicester, and, after serving an apprenticeship with a Liverpool firm of ; provision merchants, he became a partner in the firm of ;1 Messrs. Richardson Brothers and Co., and managed their , sailing ship department. In 1850 he established the Liver- pool. New York, and Philadelphia Steamship Company, and ; I was the first to send a screw-propelled steamer across the , Atlantic. Mr. Inman, who was a justice of the peace for , Cheshire, leaves a family of eight sons and two daughters. BLICkrOSe 5 Petty Sessions, at Norton, on Saturday, .Charles Brignall, Fhepherd, and Robert Grayson, waggoner, in the employ of ! Mr. Byass, Settrington, were charged with having assaulted a son of Mr. Byass, aged ten years. The boy's father had 3 sent him with a message to the servants, and he began playing with a little dog, and teasing the men with it. In , return for this Brignall went to the little boy, seized him by 5 his trousers behind with his teeth, and shook him as a dog • might a rat, biting into the flesh till the blood ran down. ' As soon as he could the lad got away, and ran a short di,- lance, screaming. Grayson then went after him, seized him, • threw him into a bed of nettles, and then " worried" him in , the same way as the other had done, biting through his clothes into the flesh till the blood came. The defendants were each fined 30s and 14s ed costs.

div.head: HER MAJESTY'S PRIME MINISTERS. THE RIGHT HON. W. E. GLADSTONE.
div.p: HER MAJESTY'S PRIME MINISTERS. THE RIGHT HON. W. E. GLADSTONE.

Circumstances over which we have no control will pre- vent us describing at length the various achievements accomplished by Mr. Gladstone's Ministry from 1868 to 1374. Certainly that Ministry did as much good work and more than any of its predecessors, and inscribed its name in the highest place on that historical roll on which are writ- ten the triumphs of legislative genius and industry. It disestablished the Irish Church, and removed most of the grievances inflicted upon Irish husbandry by the system of land tenure which there obtained. It constructed a vast machinery for the education of the people. It abolished purchase in the army, and restored that service from pri- vate to public control. It adopted the Ballot, and thus give to the Electors the power to be independent if they chose. It constituted a High Court of Judicature, in which the common law and equitable jurisdiction were to be blended. It effected financial retrenchment during the most critical European conjuncture. These great measures it had succeeded in placing upon the Statute Book. There was one other measure upon which Mr. Gladstone had set his heart, and to which we must briefly refer, as it brought about the downfall of his Ministry. This measure, which was known as "The Irish Univer- sity Bill," was introduced by the Prime Minister in the March of 1873. and was intended by its author to have complemented that policy of conciliation whereby it was hoped the peace and contentment of the Irish people would have been eventually ensured. But that measure—the leading measure of the Session, and one in which Mr. Glad- stone's generous ambition attempted to reconcile what was irreconcilable—pleased very few; not even the Irish people themselves. Unable to apply to Ireland the favourite policy of Rome, viz., that of the State finding the funds and handing them over to the Church for professedly secular services, leaving her uncontrolled power in religions mat- ters, he invented or accepted a Bill which did the secular service by professed State agency, but provided means for securing in time the full control to the Church. Mr. Glad- stone's own exposition of what he intended, in a speech of extraordinary length and eloquence, was almost unexcep- tional, but' of the two principles he set up, that of the ad- vancement of learning, and that of equal respect for the con- sciences of all, both were completely overturned by the tor- tuous details of his Bill. Worst of all, some of the most objec- tionable of these details came only in supplemental pro- visions. The discovery of this damaged the measure, and raised a very formidable opposition against it. Fro secure the successful passing of its second reading, its author pro- posed to abandon all its distinctive provisions, just as a mariner proposes to throw cargo overboard to ensure the safety of the endangered ship. But what the ship is without its cargo the Bill appeared when the "gagging clauses," the mutilated curriculum, the nominated council, the indefinite affiliation of diocesan schools, and other odd, queer, mis- chievous provisions were abandoned. It was in vain that Mr. Gladstone closed the debate on the second reading in a peroration of thrilling pathos and signal power : . . . "Arid if the labours Of 1869 and 1870 are to be forgotten in Ireland—iGwhere we have earnestly sought for peace we find only contention—if our tenders of relief are thrust aside with scorn—let us still remember that there is a voice which is not heard in the crackling of the fire, or in the roaring of the whirlwind or the storm, but which will and most be heard when they have passed away—the still small voice of justice. To mete out justice to Ireland according to the best view that with human infirmity we could form, has been the work. I will almost say the sacred work, of this Parliament. Having put our hand to the plough,let us not turn back. Let not what we think the fault and perverse- ness of those whom we are attempting to assist have the slightest effect in turning us, even by a hair's breadth, from the path on which we have entered. As we have begun so let us persevere even to the end, and with firm and resolute hand, let us efface from the law and the practice of the country the last—for I believe it is the last—of the religions and social grievances of Ireland." The House of Commons, though it did not entirely endorse the extravagant condem- nation which Mr. Disraeli launched against the measure when he said that "the Government proposal was monstrous in its general principles, pernicious in many of its details, and utterly futile as a measure of practical legislation," yet by 287 votes against 284, it put its seal of condemnation upon the Bill. The next day Mr. Gladstone waited upon her Majesty and' tendered his resignation. The Queen, as became a Constitutional Sovereign, accepted in the first instance the proposal of her Ministers to surrender into her hands the power with which she had entrusted them. Thereupon Mr. Disraeli was sent for and graciously requested to assume the responsibility of forming an Administration. The right hon. gentleman, after a brief interval for reflection and for consultation with his political friends, intimated to her Majesty his inability to carry on a Conservative Govern- ment in the face of the present House of Commons. The Queen accordingly requested Mr. Gladstone to resume office, and in compliance with this request the Liberal Ministry resumed the position they held before. There are not a few who have censured Mr. Gladstone for the part he thus played. There are not a few who thought he might have been content to have dropped the measure— notwithstanding that it was a leading measure and had been honoured with a paragraph to itself in the speech from the Throne—which the House by a majority of three only had condemned. But Mr. Gladstone, if he erred at all in meet- ing the event by resignation, erred on the right side. It is pleasing to witnese a display of that traditional high spirit of British Satesmanship which perhaps more than anything else has tended to confirm in the public mind its reverence for constitutional principles and modes of procedure. At any rate no one can charge him with trifling either with his own conviction or with the dignity of Parliament by retaining place after losing the power necessary to render it effective in the service of the State. The year 1874 opened without any sign of the great poli- tical change which was pending over the United Kingdom. On all hands there were signs of wealth. The public reve- nue was increasing, as the Prime Minister said, by "leaps and bounds." The exports of the United Kingdom, which had amounted in 1868 to £179,677,812, had risen in 1873 to £255,164,000, the highest aggregate ever yet reached in the commercial history of England. Immense reductions of tax- ation had been made, but the revenue had increased from £69,600,219 in '6B to £76,608,770 in '73. Expenditure in the meanwhile had been reduced. The outlay, which in '6B had amounted to £71,236,242, had fallen in '73 to. £70,714,448. Mr. Cardwell, speaking to the Oxford Druids on New Year's Day, said that "the autumnal fog" had lifted a little, and "would entirely disappear when Parlia- ment met." The Edinburgh Review, in the number issued in the middle of January, expressed the universal feeling among the Liberal party, by saying of the Opposition:— "When they have a programme; when they have a leader with whom they can actin perfect sympathy; and when the front bench of the Liberal party have done something really to forfeit the confidence of the country, the present Oppo- sition may hope for a term of office; but so long as they can confine themselves to carping at Liberal measures which they dare not propose to repeal, and exulting over Liberal disagreements which, if they exist, are only partial and temporary matters of procedure rather than of principle, so long they may calculate on acting simply as the brake and not as the driving wheel in the great machine of politics." Speaking at Huddersfield in the first week in January, Mr. Leathern ridiculed the idea of a Conservative reaction. "The nation," he said, "is keeping a kind of political Sab- bath. It looks hack on eix Liberal years and it rests on the seventh, and with one unfortunate exception sees that its work is good." He concluded his speech by saying, "On every side of late has been heard the cry, 'The Philistines be upon thee Samson.' Well, then, let Samsongo and shake himself as at other times." The official announcement that the Parliamentary session would commence on the sth of February gave some support to the statements that had been made by members when addressing their constituencies. But a Cabinet Council was held on the 19th of January,at which all the Ministers were present except the Prime Minister. The subject that engaged their attention was soon made known, for late in the evening of the 23rd of January Mr. Gladstone's address announcing a Dissolution was sent to the newspapers, and on the following morning (Saturday) the readers of the daily papers were surprised to learn that the Parliament of 1868 had ceased to be. The address which Mr. Gladstone issued was of portent- oas length. In the Daily News it occupies three columns of the type in which the leading articles are printed. It was described by Mr. Disraeli as a "prolix narrative," while the Daily Telegraph spoke of it as "an admirable record of success." Certain it is that no former Prime Minister had ever been able to present to his country such an account of his stewardship as was presented in this review of five years' Liberal legislation. After reviewing the labours of the late Parliament, Mr. Gladstone gave a sketch Budget and a promise to repeal the Income-tax. This part of the address was shrewdly described by Mr. Chamberlain as being " an appeal to the selfishness of the middle-classes and in this view of it the Opposition was justified in speak- ing of it as "a huge bribe.' But, though Mr. Gladstone descended upon the country amid "a shower of gold," he did not prove as irresistible as the "father of the gods." It soon became evident that Mr. Gladstone had not carried all the country with him in his beneficent legislation, and that the progress be had made was too rapid, not for the interests of the country, but for the popularity and permanence of the Government. Out of 652 members the Conservatives returned 349, and the Liberals 303, thus giving the former a majority of 46 votes. The Liberals lost 95 seats and gained 39, so that their net loss was 56 seats, being equivalent to 112 votes on a divi- sion.

Thus the Minister who six years before had been brought into power and endowed, amid much enthusiasm, with over- whelming strength, was dismissed with an emphasis of dis- approval as distipct as the applause with which he had been installed, while Mr. Disraeli found himself once more in Downing-street, that "happy spot, where they draw up constitutions for Syria and treaties for China with the same self-complacency and the same success." However, in stepping down from his high iy)sition—over. shadowed but not disgraced—we can find no words more appropriate in which to describe him than those once used by Lord Beaconsfield concerning Sir Robert Peel :—" Placed in an age of rapid civilisation and rapid transition, he had adapted the practical character of his meat tree to the con- dition of the times. •He had never employed his influence for factious purposes, and had never been stimulated in his exertions by a disordered desire of obtaining office ; above all he had never carried himself to the opposite benches by 'making propositions by which he was not ready to abide,"

div.head: DEATHS FROK SUNSTROKE,
div.p: DEATHS FROK SUNSTROKE,

The Aldershot- police have received information that four soldiers died from sunstroke after the sham fight on Monday. The first to succumb as James Lindress, gunner, Royal Artillery, who expired at three o'clock on Monday afternoon. About 40 others are in hospital from. the same cause, some not being expected to recover. A later communication says the number of casualties resulting from tge great heat at the -Aldershot sham fight, on Monday, was increasing. One of the men of the militia regiment was found dead and conveyed to the mortuary, and altogether, six men are reported as having succumbed to sunstroke.

A well-known amateur cricketer, named Wilson, has died at Betchworth, near Reigate, Surrey, where he was staying with some friends, from the effect of sunstroke. He was playing cricket when he had the stroke. A man in the same village was struck while haymaking. He is under treatment, but not expected to recover. Two other slight cases were reported on Tuesday in the same loeality. The heat was most intense.

THE NATURAL BRIDGE.—MISs RANDOLPH AND THE CEDAR.—Reaching this dizzy brink, the party of young ladies and gentlemen gazed below, when one of the gallants Pointing to the broken stump of a huge cedar which had once towered aloft upon a jagged abutment, separated by an intervening cleft from the main structure, expressed his conviction that no human being lived sufficiently daring to stand erect upon it. A gay laugh echoed the words, a silken scarf brushed by him and the whole party uttered a cry of terror—Miss Randolph, at one bound, had reached and now stood erect upon the dizzy pinnacle. Tradition relates that her companions looked at her, white and speechless, as so many corpses. Her death seemed certain. A wild spirit of bravado had given her courage for this terrible proceeding; but, perched thus on her slight footing above the frightful abyss, she must lose her nerve, grow dizzy, and be hurled upon the rocks beneath—the beautiful being of a moment since—a mass of mangled and unrecognisable flesh and bones. For an instant, the daring young lady stood erect, riding-whip in band, her scarf floating, her eyes sparkling with triumph; then, at a single bound, she regained her former position, and, with a gay laugh, asked if any gentle- man could do as much. Tradition declares that, desPi” their gallantry, the youthful cavaliers exhibited their Foot' judgment by declining.—Froan" Picturesque Anlerzca for July. BARROW, MONDAY.—A better trade has been noticeable all round in the hematite irpn trade during the pig we'.3l" Makers are very fairly employed, although in several in: stances theyhave reduced the output of metal. The darnel?' this morning is rather stronger' and buyers are more rear/ to speculate. Prices although not quotably changed/ a" „a trifle firmer, both with Bessemer and ordinary for irt' Stocks are still heavy, but they are not so bulky as 04; have been. A fair weight of iron and steel is being shil from local to foreign ports. Steel makers are experieno, a very good demand, and their mills are well employed, prices remain at a low figure. The shipbuilding trade , fully employed, and a large number of contracts are in Pr° gress. Iron ore rather firmer. Coal and coke unchanged. LANSASHIRE, WEDNESDAY.—EXtreMe dulness continue! to characterise the coal trade of this district, and the reCen!, hot weather has tended to still further restrict the reclu",e_ ments of consumers. In the house-fire coal trifle espectal,s business during the past week has been of the most lion proportions, and both for iron making and mill 1 there has been a lessened consumption owing to the In many of the large colliery districts the pits' on an a, age, are not working more than half time, and in the chester district, Where the collieries are still kept fill hag, stocks are rapidly accumulating all round. -, nominally are without alteration, and, with the probat of a renewed agitation for an advance of wages toward: close of the year, colliery proprietors do not care to co themselves to extended engagements. The market at sent, however, is decidedly weak, and to secure porary business special quotations are made, low being taken for sales in bulk for anything like delivery, and the Manchester. firms who maintain ~,,0 rates are being undersold from outside districts. ~ ."8,1 average prices at ae pit mouth remain at about for best coals, 6s. 3d. to 69. 9d. for seconds, and ss. 3d. for common round coals. The usual season's coot for gas-making coals are being given out, and of these e number have recently been placed. Burgy at the Pit averages about 4s. to 4s, 9d., and good average slack . to 4s. 3d. per ton. BELGIUM. Bnussar.s, JULY 5.—A great popular demonstration in favour of universal suffrage took place this evening. A 'procession, consisting of several thousand people, paraded ' the principal streets, and as the cortege defiled before the official residence of the Ministers shouts for the extension of the suffrage were raised. ATTEMPTED MURDER OF PRESI- DENT GARFIELD. WASHINGTON, Saturday Evening. At half-past nine o'clock this morning a mad kind of rumour suddenly ran through the city. "The President has been shot; the President is.dead." The wild declaration went from lip to lip until it became a cry. As it spread people hurried from all points towards the White House. It was a strange crowd. It ranand pushed from street to street Impelled with its earnest mission of inquiry. Some went to the Baltimore and Potomac railway station. Theile and at the White House they were eventually met by treops and; police. The city was in a wild commotion. The President' and Secretary Blaine left the White House a few minutes after nine o'clock in the carriage of the former, driven by the Ball2e faithful colouredemachman who has continuously had charge of the President's carriage since the inauguration lof President Grant. The President reached the Sixth-street I entrance to the station at shoat twenty minutes past nine, when the carriage stopped. He said to the officer Kearney, "How much time have we, officer ?" To which Kearney replied, "About ten minutes, sir." The President lingered in the carriage for a Yew minutes, as if to finish a nonver- sation with Secretary Blaine. Then he alighted, and, fol- lowed by the secretary, proceeded to the ladies' entrance of the station. They passed leisurely through the ladies' wait- ing-room arm in arm, the President on the left of Mr. Blaine. Thence the President and Mr. Blaine went to the general passengers' room, and had hardly entered the doorway when two pistol shots were fired in rapid succession from the rear, and to the right of Secretary Blaine. The first shot passed 'through the right coat sleeve of the President; inflicting no injury; but thesecond shot entered his body above the third rib. When the 'President was struck he turned sharply to the right, butimfore he could take a step and make another motion he fell heavily to the floor, the blood spurting pro- fusely from a jagged wound caused by a ball. Atter the suf- ferer had been cared for as far as possible, it was resolved to remove him to White House. While be was tenderly lifted from the vehicle with the pallor of death stamped upon his countenance, glancing upwards to the windows he saw some familiar faces, land, with a smile which those who saw it will never forget, he raised his right hand and gave the military salute, which seemed to my," Long live the Republic.". The President was carefully lifted from the ambulance and car- ried to a sleeping chamber in the' south-east corner of the building. He was soon surrounded by the most eminent physicians in Washington. Owing to the nervous prostra- tion which followed the shock, the surgeons did not deem it advisible to probe for the bullet while the President was at the depot. Upon reaching the White House this nervous- prostration seemed to pass away. The President assumed his his mud composed manner, greeting the members of the Cabinet and other intimate friends with a warm pressure of the hand and cheerful words. Before leaving the station the President manifested some anxiety about the effect of the intelligence upon Mrs. Garfield, and, turning to Colonel Rockwell, dictated to him a Jespatch which be requested might be sent to Mrs. Garfield at Long Branch. The cheer- ful manner of the President for so4e time excited hopes that he was not mortally injured. These hopes fluctuated, and daring the evening unfavourable symptoms are said to have I set in. At one time, while Secretary Blaine was sitting at the bed- side, the President said, "Blame, what motive do you think that man could have had in trying to assassinate me ?" To which Mr. Blaine replied, "-I don't know. He says he had no motive. He must be insane." The President smilingly answered, " I suppose he thought it would be a glorious thing to emulate the pirate chief." At another time, when one of his sons was sobbing at his bedside, the President said, " Don't be alarmed, Jemmy; the upper story is all right it is only the hull that is a little damaged." When Colonel Rockwell announced to him that Mrs. Garfield had started I on a special train from Long Branch he said with evident feeling, " God bless the little woman. I hope the shock won't break herdown." There was in the prisoner's possession a letter addressed to Vice-President Arthur, in which Guiteau informs him of the assassination of President Garfield, and says that he (Arthur) by this act is made Pusident. During the afternoon the President informed the medical attendant, Dr. Bliss, that be desired to be kept ac- curately informed about his condition. "Conceal nothing from me, doctor," raid he "for remember that lam not afraid to die." Towards four o'clock, when the evidence of internal hemorrhage became unmistakable, and all indica- tions Ayr "Your readynt rh ee condition onrd bad,tith eoDnwo Doctor? or Bert:: gone pointed to dissolution, the President asked Dr. Bliss tpybherewceasrpi critical President," ioaecbsinadept;ef eedwp,moepl were. neeoodicrttoaptnHrhrk..ielnßyskal. ua‘ can live many hours." 'God'st‘pwr ohMmnar'te" I'm ready to go if my time has come," firmly responded thb wounded man.
Telegrams from all parts of the country and Europe kept pouring in at the White House all the afternoon.

CLEv-Itawn, Sunday Evening.—Since becoming Presi- dent, Garfield has on several occasions lately referred to the death of President Lincoln. A singular coincidence occurred here in regard to a presentiment of harm to Garfield that troubled his aged mother. Immediately on receipt of the news that he had been shot, Mrs. Larabee, the President's sister, with whom Mrs. Garfield, Ben. had been staying, sent her mother over to the house of Mrs. M. Trowbridge, another sister. liVing a quarter of a mile away, so as to be out of hearing of the dreadful news. Mrs. Garfield, sen. bad been prostrated some days in consequence of the death of her brother-in-law, Thomas Garfield. Yesterday morn- ing she was informed of the death of Mrs. Arnold, the Presi- dent's cousin, who died yesterday, and it was deemed certain that should the President die the blow would be fatal to her. This morning she said to Mrs. Larabee, "I expect something is going to happen to James." "Don't worry," Mrs. I Larabee said, " I think the trouble in James's family is ' passed," alluding to Mrs. Garfield's illness. "No. I fear something is going to happen to him," his mother replied. She afterwards reiterated her presentiment to Mrs. Trow- bridge, adding" Accidents never come singly. I feel some- thing is going to happen to James." According to a statement made by the would-be assassin's brother, who lives at Boston, the prisoner's name is Charles Julius Guiteau, and he was born at heeport, Illinois. His 'brother also states that the prisoner is insane, and a letter, written by his father in 18T3, mentions the fact of his in- sanity. Vice-President Arthur reached Washington this morning, and desired to see President Garfield to express to , hint his sympathy, but did not press the wish as the physi- , dans ordered quiet. It is said that the prisoner has been placed on board a gun-boat moored in the river, as fears are entertained of his being lynched. The news agencies have never closes since the attempt, and all the papers through- out the country have been issuing special editions through- out the day, which were eagerly purchased by the excited people. Meetings were held in many towns to express abhor- retce of Saturday's event. The greater portion of these meetings were held in the south, where the feeling of horror is very manifest. All day long despatches have arrived from prominent men of all parties, anxiously inquiring after the state of the patient, and expressing the hope that God will save the President's life. General Hancock has requested General Sherman to express to the President his heartfelt wishes for his recovery. Prayers have been offered in the churches everywhere to•day for President Girfield's safe recovery. The sports and pastimes arranged .for the 4th of July have been countermanded in consequence of the President's condition.

div.p: PRESIDENT GARFIELD'S ASSAILANT. FULL DETAILS.

The assassin's full name is Charles Jules Guiteau. He freely gave his pistol and papers lo the police when arrested. Answering questions, he said :—" lam a native- born American, born in Illinois. I did this to save the Re- publican party. With Garfield out of the way, we can carry all the Northern States. With him in the way we cannot carry a single one." He further said to the officer: You stick to me; have me put in a third storey front of the gaol. General Sherman is coming down to take charge. Arthur and all these men are my friends. I'll have you made chief of police." Being- asked whether anybody else was with him in the matter' be said: "Not a living soul.l I have contemplated this thing for the last two weeks." On reaching the gaol, Guiteau said he bad been there last Saturday, and wanted them to let him look through. They declined, telling him to come on Monday. He wanted to S 5 e what kind of quarters he would have to occupy. Guiteau seems to be a person of disordered mind and restless habits. Nominally a lawyer, though without practice, he has a bad reputation wherever be has been. He was at times a re- ligious enthusiast. Last summer he turned hie attention to politics, apparently hopino• to gain preferment by making Republican speeches in New York. His brother, John Guiteau, residing at Boston, sar Charles was barn at Fceeport, 11l iaois, in 1841. He was a tractable boy. When a youth he ,4oit'aed the Oneida Com- munity at New York, living there several years, but left because he could not live up to the restrictions of the .com- munity. Being angered, he threatened to publish a state- ment about them, but their chief thwarted him. He left Oneida about ten years ago, and studied law in Chicago, but lost caste by collecting money, which he neglected to pay to his clients, and had te leave Chicago. Recently he had been travelling in New England. Guiteaa's brother further says he has seen little of him for the past twenty years, but has often heard from him. He had long considered him in- sane, and always expected that he would end his career in 8 lunatic asylum or meet a worse fate. lie does not believe he had any preconceived purpose to kill the President, but thinks that he took a sudden .notiento do ea. He had intense Republican views, but an politics he was too un- reliable in every way for anyone to have entrusted him with such an undertaking. Guiteau before !hooting the Presi- dent, prepared the following letter, which was taken fron his pocket by the police:—To the White. House,—Th• President's tragic death WM a sad necessity, but it wit unite the Republican party and save the Republic. Life a flimsy dream, and it matters little wlien one goes. A ]

humen life is of small value. During the war thousands of brave boys went down without a tear. I presume the Presi- dent was a Christian, and that he will be happier in Paradise than here. It will be no worse for Mrs. Garfield, dear soul, to part with her husband this way than by natural death. lie is liable to go at any time; anyway,l had no ill towards the President. His death WU a political necessity. I am a lawyer, theologian, politician; lam Stalwart of the Stalwarts; I was with General Grant and the rest of our men in New York daring the canvass. I am going to gaol. CHARLES Gorman. A similar letter was found in the street addressed to G'neral Sherman. It read as follows :—I have just shot the Presi- dent. I shot him several times, as I wished him to go as easily as possible. His death was a political necessity. lam a lawyer, theologian, politician; I am Stalwart of the Stal- warts. I was with General Grant and the rest of our men in New York during the canvas. lam going to goal. Please order out your troops and take possession of the gaol at once. CHARLES GIIITEALT.—The gaolers say that Guiteau during the past two weeks made visits to the gaol, but was not ad- mitted. The Press Association has been favoured with some particulars respecting Guiteau, the would-be assassin of President Garfield. Mr. Farnwell, a member of the Illinois Congress, who is at present staying in London, says that about five years ago Guiteau came into his office and demanded a loan of $200,000 to start a newspaper. He left SOON editorial opinions which seemed to be the effusions of a diseased brain. Subsequent interviews with him confirmed the belief that Guiteau was insane. The brother-in-law of Guitean asserts that the latter has been 'several times ex- amined by physician, who pronounced him to be insane. The same person states that his insanity took the form of imagining himself to be a great man. He was considered as harmless and a great coward, although he once threatened to kill his sister.

The reports on Tuesday night as to the condition of Pre- sident Garfield stated that the physicians regarded the case with feelings of encouragement. Mr. Secretary Blaine, in a communication addressed to the American press, acknow- ledges the very numerous messages of condolence and affection.which have been received since Saturday morning from almost every state in the union. From the south as bountifully as from the north, and from countries beyond the sea have, Mr. Blaine says, come messages of anxious inquiry and tender words of sympathy in such numbers that it has been foand impossible to answer them in detail. He, therefore, asks the newspapers to express for the President and Mrs. Garfield the deep gratitude which they feel for the devotion of their fellow countrymen and friends abroad in this hour of heavy affliction. The bulletins issued on Wednesday showed a marked im- provement in the condition of President Garfield; and, although the President was not out of danger, the chances of a complete recovery were happily brightening. CONSPIRACY TO LYNCH THE ASSASSIN.

The New York Everting Post says, referring to excited rumours of conspiracies and other troubles, that the laVest story is that the police have been advised as to the secret formation within the last two days of an organisation of coloured men, numbering MO, who have arranged to set in motion a scheme to lynch Gultean. NARROW ESCAPE OF MRS. GARFIELD.

It seems that Mrs. Garfield also narrowly escaped a serious and, perhaps, fatal accident, The train that brought her from Longbranch consisted of an engine and one Pullman car. When within two miles of Bowie Station, 16 miles from Washington, a parallel rod on the side of the engine broke while the wheels were making 250 revolutions a minute. The rod is a steel bar which connects the wheels. It is about twelve feet long, six inches wide, and our inches thick. As the ei. continued to thunder along, although the engineer imue twly reversed steam and put on the air brakes, the broke, 'ld plunged into the ballast with each revolution of the u i.e.;4. tore up the sleepers, and considerably damaged the engine. This continued for two miles before a stop could he effected. An eye-witness states that as the train flow by Bowie Station splinters of shattered sleepers filled the air. Rad the engine left the track the Pullman car must have been splintered into ,kindling wood, and the passengers all killed. Another engine was sent out from Washington. and Mrs. Garfield's car was brought to the city. .

MELANCHOLY DEATH OF GENERAL GARFIELD'S UNCLE. The death, under very melancholy circumstance& of Mr. Thomas Garfield, uncle of the President of the United States, is announced in a despatch from Cleveland, Ohio, dated the 22nd ult., and just received at Liverpool. Mr. Garfield, it appears, on the afternoon of the day in question, was returning to Isis home in Randall, in a carriage, accom- panied by a friend, Mrs. Alonzo Arnold. Mr. Garfield was driving, and just before arriving at the Warrensville cross. ing of the New York, Pennsylvania, and Ohio Railway, he saw a train approaching. Thinking that he could cross the line in safety before the train came up ,he whipped his ! horses and proceeded. But he had miscalculated the die- ' lance. Before he gained the other side of the railroad the train dashed into his carriage and broke it to pieces, throw- -1 . ing both occupants to the ground. They were picked up 1 ! immediately afterwards and conveyed to their homes, but' Mr. Garfield died an hour afterwards, not having uttered a I word. Mrs. Arnold received a fracture of the skull, but was expected to recover. Soon after the sad occurence President Garfield was informed of his uncle's death. ANXIETY TO SHOOT MR. BLAINE. WASIIINGTON, JULY 5.—A madman, named Daniel IVPNamara, called at the police headquarters expressing a , desire to shoot Mr. BlaMe. He was arrested and sent to the I lunatic asylum. He states that he is not clear whether his' mission was to kill the Secretary of State or Vice-President Arthur. He also declares he was inspired to take Genera) Garfield's life during hi 9 presidency, but was defeated.
