ROUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Chesre Lines Committee Bill was read a third time and passed. THE CONDITION OF PRESIDENT GARFIELD.—EarI GRAN- VILLE, in giving, in response to a question by the Marquis of Salisbury, the latest information up to that time as to the condition of President Garfield, said the expressions of sympathy on the part of the people of this country with the people of the ,United States increased every hour in intensity. PROCESS SERVING IN IRELAND—EarI CARLINGFORD, in reply to Lord Harlech, said that the discretion of permitting the custom of process-serving upon substitutes rested with the county court judges, but the Government would call the attention of the Lord Chancellor of Ireland to the subject. THE ROYAL UNIVERSITY OF IRELAND.— Lord CARLING- FORD, La reply to a question, said he would shortly lay I before the House a bill for the purpose of charging on the Irish Church fund such an annual sum as in view of the Government would be sufficient to enable the Royal University of Ireland to perform its work efficiently. ErnicaTrox.—Earl FORTESCUE presented petitions to have the limit of age for compulsory education lowered to below I fourteen years, and to have the passing of the third instead I of the fourth standard made the condition of children being I allowed to work for their living. Both the Duke of Rich- I mond and Earl Spencer having spoken against any such I alteration as that petitioned for being made the subject was allowed to drop. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MoNDAY.

PRESIDENT GrARFIELD.-Sir-g: NORTIICOTE, in enquiring whether the Government had any later information as to the attempted assassination of President Garfield, took the op- portunity of expressing the general feeling of anxiety with which the President's condition was watched and the honor and indignation excited by the event. Mr. Gladstone fully concurred in these sentiments.

THE COURSE OF BUSINESS.—Mr. CrLADSTONE proceeded, in fulfilment of his promise, to state the intentions of the Government with regard to the bills on the paper. The Corrupt Practices Bill they could not hope to make progress with, except by an expenditure of a great deal of time, and it had been decided, therefore, to abandon it for the present session. The bill for the amendment of the Ballot Act would also be withdrawn for the session, hut it would be necessary to introduce a Continuance Bill. With regard to the notice which the Attorney-General had given of a bill with respect to Parliamentary Oaths, there was no intention of taking any further step. The Government still hoped that they might be able to proceed with the Bankruptcy Bill in the margin of time left by the favourable progress of the Land Bill. If the future progress of .the Land Bill was to be judged from what occurred between two and seven o'clock on Friday, he should form a sanguine estimate upon the subject; but if it was to be judged by what was done at the night sitting, he should say that it was impossible to fix any limit to the discussion. The Alkali Works Bill stood for report, and he thought there would be no diffiulty, there- fore, in passing it this session. The Rivers Conservancy Bill they were also very anxious to pass, and considering the favourable manner in which it had gone through the Select Committees of both Houses, he trusted it might be pro- ceeded with. He would say the same with regard to the bill relating to educational endowments in Scotland. There were two bills which it was absolutely necessary to pass— the one with regard to naval discipline, and the other to the regulation of the forces; the former dealing with corporal punishment in the navy, and the latter being the legislative supplement of the scheme of the Secretary for War. Measures would be proposed with reference to the places in which corrupt practices had been reported to have extensively prevailed at the last election, the main purpose of these measures being the suspension of writs. The Government hoped also to be able to getthrough the Judica- ture Act Amendment Bill, which had been introduced in the other House, and the object of which was to redeem a pledge given in the early part of the session with regard to making provision for the distribution of the patronage which was in other days in the handa of the two chief judges. The County Government (Ireland) Bill, referred to in the Queen's speech, it was obvious could not, under existing circumstances, be proceeded with this session, nor could the two measures in charge of the President of the Board of Trade—namely, the Thames River Bill and the Merchant Shipping Bill. The Local Loans Bill and the National Debt Bill were matters af netessity, and :t would also be necessary to bring in a bill relating to the Irish University. —Sir S. NORTHCOTE, bearing in mind the large amount of Supply yet to be got through, thought the Government would act wisely in at once deciding to drop the Bank- ruptcy Bill.—Mr. LABOUCHERE anticipated the concurrence of the leader of the Opposition, in the suggestion that the Bankruptcy Bill should be abandoned, and that in its place should be taken the bill which he had introduced on the subject of the Parliamentary oaths. THE limn LAND BILL—The House again went into committee on this bill, resuming at sub-section 8 of clause 7, which enables the court to disallow any application to fix a judicial rent where the court is satisfied that the holding , has heretofore been maintained and improved by the land- lord. At the suggestion of Mr. Plunket and Sir S. North- cote the clause was amended so as to run that the improve- ments must have been made and substantially maintained by the landlord and not by the tenant. At Mr. Parnell's suggestion it was further amended, so as to require that the improvements should have been made during the tenancy of the occupier or his predecessor in. title.—Mr. A. BALFourt raised the question of perpetuity of tenure by moving that, after the expiration of two statutory terms, a tenant shall be deemed a future tenant —After discussion, Mr. CHAPLIN moved to report progress, in order to complain of the con- tinued reticence of the !Government on various points.— An animated scene followed, in the course of which Mr. Gladstone was accused by Lord R. Churchill of having "jockeyed " the committee, and Mr. C. Bentinck exhorted him to deal with the Opposition in a more straightforward manner.—The committee adjourned until Tuesday at two o'clock.

idebate the Government would withdraw all obstacles to Lord Sandmen's motion. Lord Sandon thanked the Prime Minister for his "handsome" conduct, and the motion for adjournment was ultimately withdrawn. MR. BRADLAUGH AND THE SPEAKER.—The SPEAKER read a letter, which Mr Bradlaugh had sent him, giving notice that he should disregard the order of the House of the 10th of May. because of its illegality. The Speaker added that he had given such directions to the Sergeant-at-Arnms as might be necessary to enforce the order of the House, which directed that functionary to remove Mr. Bradlaugh Irons the House until he should engage no further to obstruct the proceedings.—Lord R. CHURCHILL desired to treat the communication as a breach of privilege with the view of moving that the letter be not printed on the journals of the House.—The SPEAKER at once dm cideil that the question could not be treated as one of privilege; and Sir S. Northcote suggested, amidst cheers, that it would be more respectful to the Speaker if the matter were left with the chair.—Lord RANDOLPH persisted, however, that he would bring forward a motion of the kind he had indicated. A THREAT IN THE Lonsar.—Mr. MACIVER complained that Mr. Lyulph Stanley, the member for Oldham, had "threatened" him in the lobby for going beyond what he described as the forms of the house. He admitted that be did use language that was out of order, but contended that he had not said anything beyond what was stated in the petition which he presented. He therefore wished to ask the Speaker, under a motion for adjournment, whether the honourable member for Oldham had a conversation with the Speaker, and that in that conversation the Speaker had spoken of his conduct in bringing a petition before the house.—The SPEAKER declared that this was not a matter of order, and Mr. LYULPH STANLEY explained what had taken place in time lobby. Having looked at the petition presented by Mr. Maclver, he had come to the conclusion, after consulting with Mr. Dillwyn—that the honourable member was not justified in going so far as he had done. Meeting Mr. Maclver in the lobby, he told him on the spur of the moment that he had abused the forms of the house, and that if he did so again he should call attention to it. That was, he said, all that had taken place.—The member fur Birkenhead attempted to reply, but the Speaker, inter- rupting him, ordered the clerk to proceed with the orders of the . day -

THE IRISH LAND BILL.—The House afterwards resumed Committee on the Land Bill. The question whether Clause 7 should stand part of the bill drew a short speech from Mr. Gladstone, who spoke of the vital importance of the clause and upon the importance of the division which was about to he taken.—Mr. CHAPLIN afterwards attacked Mr. Glad- stone for what he was pleased to call his "levity and in the absence of the Prime Minister was sharply rebuked by Mr. Forster.—Upon a division the clause was carried by a majority of 132 votes, the numbers being received with pro- longed cheerfbg from the Liberal side. Clause 8 was after- wards to the bill, and the sitting was suspended at ten minutes to seven. The evening sitting was occupied with the Land Bill, commencing with Clause 9. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

LOCAL Parinoxs.—A petition in favour of Sunday closing was presented by Colonel Blackburne from Prescot. . ANOTHER "REMARKABLE" PETITION-Mr. • STEVENSON presented a petition in favour of his Sunday Closing Bill, which he etated was 1,100 yards long, and signed by 84,283 women, a large majorityof whom weae the wivesof working men, while the signatures included the names of many pub- licans' wives. THE LAND BILL.—The House again went into committee on the Land Law (Ireland) Bill.—During the debate on one of the amendments proposed, Mr. FORSTER explained the proposals which the Government intend to make with re- gard to arrears. The Government desired to give a fair , start, if possible, to tenants in arrears, and for that purpose they thought Parliament might holdout temptations to both landlord and tenant. The Government proposed that in re- gard to all holdings where the tenants had settled with their landlords for the rents due since the last crop the commis- sion shall have power to advance to the landlord '5O per cent of any arrears thtt might be due for the two previous years, on condition that the landlord and tenant should i I agree n the application, that the landlord should undertake to repay the advance in 15 years, that the tenant should , allow such payments to be added to his rent for the 15 years, and that in consideration of this advance the landlord should give a release in full to the tenant in respect of all arrears. These advances are to be made on the security of the Church Funds, and the proposal will be submitted as a separate clause of the bill.—Sir M. HICKS-BEACH said he had reason to know that in many parts of Ireland the dis- tress of landlords and tenants would far less justify Or re- quire such a relief than the condition of many.patts of the south of England ; to which Mr. Foresymt replied that in such parts of the country as Sir Michael had indicated advances would not be required, as the rents were well paid up. He added that the offer would be limited to tenancies of a valuation at or under £3O. The committee had reached clause 14 when progress was reported.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: STATE OF IRELAND.

Twenty-eight persons were brought before the magistrates at Semll,in West Cork, on Saturday, charged•with taking part in the recent disturbances there. One of them was , committed to prison for six months and most of the remainder were sentenced to a month's imprisonment. A Daily News New York telegram of Monday says : Mr. Secretary BlaMe, in response to an inquiry, telegraphed from Washington :—"You have my full authority for the statement that the visit of the President's private secretary to London has not the remotest connection with any phase of the Irish question." At the weekly meeting of the Land League, held in Dublin, on Tuesday, Mr. Healy, M.P., presiding, it was an- nounced that £1,487 had been received since the last meet- ing, including about £1,200 from America.—Mr. Sexton, M.P., said the GrOvernment being unable or unwilling to keep the peace in Ulster during the Orange anniversaries, the Land League had taken up the task and effectively per- formed it.—The deputation from the Dem2cratic Federation of Great Britain. which had gone over tallinquire into the state of the land question, was present, and several members of it addressed the meeting. Mr. P. J. Murphy, a member of the Cork Town Council and a prominent Land Leaguer, was arrested on Wednesday under the Protection Act. The warrant charges him with treasonable practices. Mr. Murphy formerly belonged to a class of politicians, now happily defunct, who believed the regeneration of Ireland was only to be gained by the sword. He was reputed to be a member of the Fenian organisation. Since the establishment of the Land League in Cork he hag allied himself with the extreme section of that party. His arrest is believed to be due to a speech he recettly made urging the constabulary to break their allegiance and emigrate. A process server named Durkan, who was procbeding from Callow on Wednesday form Swinford quarter sessions, was attacked by two men and severely beaten. The horse be was riding took to flight, and Darkan, not having succeeded in extracting his foot from the stirrup,s was dragged along the road for some distance, and he now lies in a precarious condition. At Westmeath assizes, on Wednesday, Patrick Daly pleaded guilty to the manslaughter of Michael Curran, near Mul'ings-, on the 29th ult., and was sentenced to 25 years' penal servitude. STATE OF AGRICULTURE IN IRELAND.

The preliminary report of the Assistant Commissioners forlreland kßoyal Commission of Agriculture) was issued on Tuesday. They comment upon the heavy indebtedness of small farmers to usurers, the excessive subdivision of holdings, the wretched condition of the dwellings, and the evil effects of the practice of the people going to England for harvesting. They state that there are large tracts of waete land which might be productively cultivated, and they suggest buying up portions of these lands and placing upon them the surplus population of overcrowded districts. As regards peasant proprietary, the Commissioners con- sider that the indiscriminate sale of holdings to tenants on such, conditions as those offered by the Irish Church COlll.. mission cannot realise the hopes of the advocates of the sys- tem, and unless provision be made for the execution of im- provements it would only aggravate existing evils. Re- specting bad cultivation, the Commissioners state that the conviction appeared to be deeply impressed upon small farmers that if they improved farms their rent would be raised. The return also shows that during the last thirty years 14,811,000 was advanced by the Public Works Loan Commissioners for public purposes in Ireland, of which £1,479,000 had been repaid;" and £11,788,000 was ad- advanced from the Excheeper, of which £8,907,000 had been repaid.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TCESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TCESDAY.

• NEW PEER—Baron Ampthill, hitherto known as Lord Odo Russell, took the oath and his seat on his elevation to the peerage. DEATHS FROM EXPOSL-RE AT ALDERSHOT.—The Earl of MortLEY, who was questioned respecting the report that some of our soldiers had died from exposure to the great' heat on 'Monday, during a review at Aldershot, stated that a number of men who took part in the review had been ad- mitted to the hospital suffering from the effects of the I extreme heat. Of these four had since died. The Secretary ' of State for War at once telegraphed to the General com- manding at Aldershot for information as to the "sad occur- rence," but full information had not yet been received.— The Duke of CAMBRIDGE, who bad been present at Alder- shot, had "no idea that such a thing had taken place, and it was to him "most unaccountable." The opinion of His Royal Highness is that Monday was "warm, but not not unpleasantly so," and he assured their Lordships that he had been out on " fifty times hotter days." He added that. It was not a review but a simple field day, and "the whole affair was overin a short time." Tums AND TRIPOLI—EarI GRANVILLE, in reply to a question as to the intentions of France and Turkey in re- gard to Tripoli, said that all the Government had beard on the subject was that on the 28th of last month a Turkish ship of war arrived there having on board a Turkish general lof division and two battalions of infantry. JUDICATURE ACTS AMENDMENT BILL.—The LORD CHAN- , CELLOR introduced a bill to amend the Supreme Court Of Adjudicature Acts, one of the amendments being the making of the Master of the Rolls a judge of appeal only. THE CENSUS.—Lord CARRINGTON laid on the table the preliminary report of the census of England and Wales. The total population of England and Wales is now 125,968,286, being an increase since 1871 of 3,258,020. The rate of increase was higher than any decennium since 1831-41.

div.head: HOUSE 'OF COMMONS.—TuEsDay.
div.p: HOUSE 'OF COMMONS.—TuEsDay.

A REMARKABLE PETITION.— Mr. MecIYER, gave some trouble at the commencement of business by his persistent attempts to deliver a speech on presenting what lie termed "a remarkable petition." It was 250 yards long, was signed by 21,000 people in Bradford and neighbourhood who wished for work and wages which were denied them by the pressure of unfair foreign competition with the industries on which the prosperity of Yorkshire depends. After being called to order several times, Mr. Maclver contented himself by requesting that the petition should be read at the table, and this was accordingly done.

THE REVENIJE.—In reply to a question from Mr. Laing as to the revenue, Mr. GLADSTONE said: With regard to the particular point which my hon. friend has raised, I think I can give him satisfactory information. On examining the year's returns of the revenue, members could not but be struck with the ominous fact, as it would naturally appear, that there was a decrease of £420,000 upon the excise. The reason for that &crease, which is tke one distinctly and strongly unfavourable feature in the revenue, is the different distribution of the malt duty and beer duty over the four quarters of the year. The beer duty is distributed in very nearly four equal portions' but the malt duty varies as much in the four quarters as 14 per cent, in one quarter and 40 per cent, in another. There is no such inequality in the present case, or else the deficiency in the excise would have been much gteater, but the difference is this, that 30 per cent. of the malt duty was received in the three months ended 2nd June, and only 24 per eent. of the beer duty. When I mention that 1 per cent. of the duty means £87,000, and consequently that 6 per cent, means £512,000, it will be obvious at once that this disposes of the whole of the apparent decrease. (Cheers.) THE FRENCLI TARIFF—Lord SANDON moved an adjourn- ment in order to complain of tbe action of Mr. Chamber- lain in offering formal opposition to his motion for a trans- lation of the French tariff. Lord Sandon regarded the course taken by the President of the Board of Trade as a personal affront, and ascribed it to the right hon. gentleman's in- experience. The noble lord insisted upon the interest taken e by the working classes in the French tariff, and charged the Government with pursuing a policy of concealment.—Mr: GLADSTONE, in a very happy and caustic reply, successfully vindicated Mr. Chamberlain from the charge of inexperience, remarking that before he entered the House the President ot the Board of Trade had had such an experience in public business as probably no other member could boast. The Prime Minister ridiculed Lord Sandon's accusation that the Government had been trying to pursue a poliey of conceal. ment behind the impenetrable mysteries of the French language ;" and sarcastically congratulated the Opposition on this demonstration of their sense of the monstrosity ot excessive foreign bounties. Finally Mr, Gladstone intimated that rather than that there should be a prolongation of the

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THURSDXY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THURSDXY.

1 THR GREEK FRONTIER—EarI Granville reported that' on Wednesday the Turks retired from Dina:trio, the left Turkish frontier, and that the Greeks crossed and took possession, that all was done in good order., THE FISCAL ACTION OF FOREIGN PONVERS.—The marquis of Salisbury, after presenting a petition from merchants, planters, and others connected with the island of Barbadoes complaining that their interests were injuriously affected by the fiscal action of foreign Powers, proceeded to dilate at length on the "remarkable change of feeling that has taken place in many centres of industry." He said he should be sorry to say what might be interpreted to be at variance with those principles of commercial policy which this country had deliberately adopted. The noble Marquis then complained of the way in which Austria had dealt with sugar and the adverse manner in which she had acted towards this country . and our Colonies, and the West India planters in particular, and urged that the matter ought to be dealt with by the Government before it became Magnified into a very great grievance. The argument of the Conservative leader then : took this form: that we are not bound by the principles of I Free Trade to look on calmly and coldly while we witness the destruction of British commerce, for if we did the prin- ciple would be extended and industry after industry would be destroyed by the unfair com- petition of foreigners. There was, he said, a cry for remedies which it might puzzle and perplex states- men to apply, and while he did net wish for any action in- consistent with Free Trade he could not join the Chancellor 1 of the Duchy in applying the term "lunatic" to everyone 1 who advocated reciprocal or retaliatory action, because that would amount to an admission that there were more : lunatics in the world than sane people.—The Earl :of KIMBERLEY complained that the greater part of the speech of the noble Marquis had been directed to the encouragement of a policy of retaliation. If the noble Marquis had made up his mind that the Con- servative party would join in the cry raised in some quarters for a reversal of the Free Trade policy he hope.l he would give a fair notice of it in order that there might be a full , discussion on the subject.—The Earl of CARNARTON urged that the case of the West Indian planters was a hard one, and said with reference to the negotiations with Franco that if we could not get an equally good treaty to that of 1860 but a superior treaty, it was better to have no treaty all.— Earl GRANVILLE joined in the protest of Lord Kimberley, , and the subject thert dropped. '

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THtiRSDAY. r 'IIIEFRENCH TREATY.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said that a circular had been addressqd to 20 chambers of commerce for their opinions as to an English translation of the new French tariff. Out of 20 replies, seven were in favour and 13 against —The PRIME MINISTER afterwards remarked that the country would make a great mistake if it supposed that this tariff was the final and practicable arrangement under which the commerce of the two countries was to be conducted. The French Government Objected to the publication of the proposals upon which the present nego- tiations were based. I THE BRIGHTON TRAGEDY.—The HOME SECRETARY stated that the police constables who had to do with the escape of Lefroy after the railway murder were in the employ of the railway company, though they were nominally members of the Metropolitan police force. The right hon. gentleman could not admit that what had happened affected the con- duct of the police generally. THE DEATII OF SOLDIERS FROM SIINSTROKE.-Mr. CHIL- DERS gave the facts in connection with the melancholy deaths at Aldershot on Monday. The official statement amounts to this—that after the manceuvres were over the heat greatly increased, and the anxiety to get to their lines causing the regiments to hurry the pace a good many men fell out, and 19 were sent into the hospital. Three died of sunstroke and a fourth from heart disease. From the brigade which went over most of the ground and did the hardest work the smallest number of men fell out and none went into the hospital, and the distressing and lamentable results of the day occurred under exceptional circumstances. The light hon. gentleman also gave an outline of the arrangements made by the authorities for the comfort of the men who will take part in the Volunteer Review on Satur- day. THE hum LAND BlLL.—Rapid progress was made in Committee with this Bill. An i-npertant discussion took place upon Clause 19, which authorises the Land Commis- sion to assist tenants in purchasing their holdings groin landlords willing to sell by advancing any sum not exceed- ing three-fourths of the principal.—Mr. ',mot; moved an amendment authorising the Land Commission to provide the whole of the principal sum, or not less than four-fifths in cases where the tenant could not give sufficient security. —The PRIME MINISTER explained in a conciliatory speech that the Government could not possibly go beyond their present proposal. To advance three-fourths of the purchase Imoney was a thing totally unknown in private transactions, and the Government had made the most liberal proposals possible, consistently with public prudence.—ln the course of the discussion which ensued, Sir S. NORTHOOTE protested against any alteration in the direction desired by Mr. Litton, and Mr. H. HENRY blamed Irish members for looking a gift horse in the mouth.—After a speech by Mr. Bright, Mr. Litton's amendment was rejected by 247 votes to 78.

Replying to a memorial signed by over 200 clergymen of York diocese, praying for the release of the Rev. F. Green. of Miles Platting, M. Gladstone intimates that he has no power to act in the matter, and cannot therefore interfere. A Paris correspondent of the Times states that a Legitimist Committee, headed by M. de la Rochefoucauld-Bisaccia, has been formed in Paris, for collecting subscription tow.] rth he expenses of Legitimist candidates in Paris in the pro. vinces at the general electi3n. The committee professes. however, to renounce all control over the choice of sod. candidates.

WED:casnax.—Before G. Artingstall, Esq. (chairman), P. Stubs, Esq., and S. Rigby, Esq.

HIGHWAY OFFBN'ats.‘—. Thomas Lythgoe was summoned for allowing his cow to stray on the highway at Poulton, on the 30th June. P. C. Stead proved the case, and defendant was fined is. and costs.—Noah Oldfield, for allowing a horse to stray on the highway at Croft, on the 30th June, was fined is. and costs. BEING IN POSSESSION or GAME NETS.—Tbomas Dutton, a young man, residing in Egerton-street, Warrington, was charged with having in his possession nets for the killing and taking of game, in Padgate:road, and with unlawfully using the same.—P. C. McFarlane said that at twelve minutes past twelve on Friday morning, the 17th ult., he was on duty at the Cemetery, Padgate-road, when he saw tbe defendant. He noticed his pockets were bulky, and he ran after and stopped the defendant After some conversa- tion witness looked into defendaat's pockets and found the nets produced and a !emit, and he saw defendant throw the othernet produced over a hedge when he called out to him to stop.—The defendant had been previously fined for an assault on the officer on the date named, and the bench now discharged him, but ordered the nets Lobe destroyed. ASSAULT ON A FELLOW WORKMAN AT SANKEY.— Thomas Locker was summoned for having assaulted Thomas Spenceley, at Sankey Bridges, on the 27th June.— Complainant said on the 27th ult., he was at Sankey Bridges about half-past one o'clock. He was returning to his work at Messrs. Houghton's wire mills, where both of them were employed, together with William Massey, when Locker came up to them and caused a disturbance by striking Massey. He went between them, and defendant struck at him, and caught him by the throat and knockerl him down. While on the floor defendant continued striking him. He, however, managed to get to his feet, but defendant again knocked him to the ground. He also "knocked one eye up," and injured the ether. Owing to the abuse he had been subject to he had not been at work for a week. Defendant contended "they were drunk in a ruck and were fighting together."—He was fined 102. and costs, or fourteen days' imprisonment. PIROBBERY OF FOWLS AT PADGATIL—ThOMAS MelOr and Thomas Cawley were charged with stealing four hens from the hen-cote of Sarah Potter, farmer, Padgate, on the 13th ult. At the last petty sessions the prisoners were brought before the bench on this charge, but were remanded until the following Saturday, when they were again remanded to be dealt with that day. On the night of the 13th June, Mrs. Potter saw the fowls in the ben-cote, but on the morning of the 14th found the hen-cote had been entered and found four hens stolen. The police were informed of the robbery, and they, on examining the place, traced footprints and feathers from the hen-cote to a brickfield close by,,where the prisoners worked, and in the hut fire, found a quantity of feathers, legs, and entrails of fowls which had evidently been killed, and cooked there. The prisoners were at the Dog and Partridge Inn, at a quarter to 11 o'clock on the night of the 13th ult. They were apprehended oti the morning of the 14th ult. and on their coats were found blood and feathers. On comparing the clogs produced with the footprints, they were found to correspond.—Mr. Moore, who appeared for the prisoners, said the case was one of strong suspicion, but beyond that be did not see how the prosecution could go. The evidence was decidely circumstantial and such as no jury would convict upon. He called Michael Melior, Lather of the first named prisoner, who said he remembered the prisoners, who lodged with him, coming home on the night of ths 13th ult. about 11 o'clock, and saw them go to bed. Next morning they all left the house together about a quarter past six, and they did not leave the premises dur- ing the night.—The bench, however, considered the case proved, and sentenced them to two calendar month's hard labour.

div.head: HEAVY THUNDERSTORMS.
div.p: HEAVY THUNDERSTORMS.

On Tuesday 'evening, one of the most terrific thunder- storms within living remembrance, buret over this district. The storm appears N have visited nearly every part of Eng- land except the Midlands, and is described as the most tremendous atmospheric disturbance that has occurred for years. Nor is this surprising when we reflect that the heat which preceded it was tropical in its intensity. The damage done by the storm is of an exceptionally severe kind, though had it not been for the tremendous downpour of rain, the loss of life which resulted would probably have been greater. In one town in Flintahire the lightning entered a house where a family were sitting, and instantaneously killed one child, besides severely injuring another, and the father. At Dublin, a woman working in a field was struck dead. Two boys met their deaths in the same sudden and terrible fashion at Ormskirk, while the tale of cattle either killed by the lightning or washed away down the flooded streams already reaches a dis- tressingly high figure. From Bolton we hear of solid mills being partially swept away, of workmen being thrown out of employment, and of w fl.ten and children being rescued from • drowning in villages where the water bad. risen to the depth of a a couple of yards In the public streets. Three persons were known to haye been drowned when the storm built in all its fury over the Rossendale Valley, and it is estimated that damage to the extent of fifty thousand pounds was inflicted on tne crops and house property in that district alone. Pres- ton, Leeds, Blackburn, Burnley, Durham, and Liverpool all suffered more or less severely, and from towns further north, as well as all along the southern coast, and from many places in the eastern counties, come reports of a simi- lar kind, showing that the elements spent their fury with more than ordinarily michieyous result. At Eagley a sub- stantial iron bridge was swept away. At Croston, near Preston, two boys were struck by lightning, and one of them was killed. From several other places there are ac- counts of loss of life. Extensive damage was done by flood in the valleys of Todmorden and Halifax. The chimneys of two houses in Morley-street were some- what damaged, several tiles being hurled into the street, and a portion of the road between the Bird in Hand and the Old Toll Bar was torn up.

div.head: CANARY SHOW AT PRESCOT.
div.p: CANARY SHOW AT PRESCOT.

The second annual first feather show of Ecligan, Lizard, and Norwich canaries in connection with the Prescot Canary Society was held on Saturday, at the King's Arms Hotel, Warrington•road, Prescot. The main object of the society in holding these first feather shows is to encourage the pure breeding of birds of the several vareties mentioned. The prizes were awarded for purity of race, beauty of plumage, quality and high condition, and the regulations expressly stated that "Specimens entered in a wrong class, or clipped, drawn, or artificially coloured, be excluded from taking prizes and the entrance money forfeited." There were ten classes, all of which were represented excepting the Belgian classes (2.) The number of enteries was about the same as last year, and a similar amount in prizes was given. All the birds exhibited were of a fair description, the variety most worthy of mention being those of the Norwich class which were characterized as being first.class. The cages and birds were excellently, arranged on tables in the large room of the hotel. The judges were Messrs. Weldon, of St. Anna, Eccleston, and Jump, of Wigan, and generally speaking, their awards , gave satisfaction. The attendance was very meagre, and the majority of those who paid a visit to the show were bird fanciers from Liverpool. The president of the society is Mr. W. Evans; vice-president, Mr. J. Beesley; treasurer, Mr. R. Rigby; hon. secretaries Messrs, S. Taylor, and J. Lucas. The flowing is a list of the awards:—

I NOTES, QUESTIONS, AND ANSWERS ON THE CHURCH CATECHISM AND CONFIRMATION (London: Simpkin, Marshall and Co.)—This is a revised and enlarged edition of a little work by John Bowes (Hon. Ph.D.) F.R.G.B, Master of the Warrington Blue Coat School, designed to open up the religious knowledge contained in the Catechism of the Church of England. A careful perusal of the work shows that Dr. Bowes has been at great pains to accomplish the task he set himself, and we congratulate him upon the success which he has attained, for he displays throughout the work the tact of an experienced and accomplished teacher highly deserving of praise. The notes, questions, and answers have been carefully and well written, rendering it a very useful and practical work for those for whom it has been written. The Rev. Gilley H. Cary, M.A., of Christ Church, Oxford, formerly head master of Warrington Grammar School, speaking of it says it is "A really excel- lent little manual. Though not bulky it is full of really useful suggestions; and I should think that anybody would be glad to use it when preparing for continuation and al other times also. I like your method very much;' it is orderlyand clear ; the exegesis is lucid without being re. &indent, and when you have found it necessary to para- phrase certain awkward passages you have done it yen neatly." We are not surprised to learn that the tirst editior rapidly sold out, and have no doubt that this edition will also command a ready:sale.

At the Present Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. F. W. Earle and J. Bibby, a respectably-dressed young man named William Preston, was charged with having at Whis- ton, on the previous Friday. unlawfully wounded ltobert Sparkes, by stabbing him.—Mr. T. Swift, of St. Helens, de- fended.—lnspector Barnett said the prisoner and the injured man were colliers, and about a fortnight previous to the occurrence the prisoner had some difference with his parents and left home, and went to reside in the immediate neigh- bourhood. On Friday night he went home for some cloth- ing, and had a disturbance with his parents, and smashed the window. His mother took refuge in a neigh- bour's house. A men named Peter Ludrick and his ledger, bearing the disturbance got out of Lea and came downstairs ' and into the street to quieten the prisoner. Eventually Sparkes came up and endeavoured to get him to go home. ' A quarrel ensued, in the course of which the men fell to the ground, and on the prosecutor getting up he called out that ; be was ststhed, and the prisoner, who was present, made no anewsr.—Robert Sparkes said he was a collier, and resided at No. 1, Cook-street, Whiston. About eleven o'clock on Friday night prisoner's Mother came into his house, and in consequence of what she said, he got up and looked through ' the bedroom window and saw the prisoner in the street. He was calling his mother "a old witch," and asked him to turn her out. Witness dressed and went downstairs and into the etreet, and asked the prisoner if he was not ashamed of himself for running his mother about at that time of the night. Prisoner asked witness what he had to do with it, and he said to him, "Be shifting." Witness got hold of a bundle, which was lying on the ground, and put it into his hand and said, "Come on, I will take thee down the road to thy lodgings." Prisoner asked a man named Ludrick to hold his bundle while he fought witness. Ludrick refused to do so, and witness told the prisoner that if he wanted to beat him he could put the bundle on the ground. Prisoner then rushed at witness and seized him by the shoulders, but wit- ness threw him down at once, and said. "I don't want to touch thee. What could Idoif I liked?" He took hold of the prisoner's arms, and held him on the ground for some time. Witness eventually got up with the intention of going away, when the prisoner jumped up and made a second rush at him, and witness felt something like a blow on the left shoulder, which entered his flesh and took away the use of his arm. He also felts similar sensation on the right arm. Witness said to Ludrick, "He has stabbed me," and the latter seized the prisoner's right hand as he was putting it. into his pocket. Witness put his hand into the prisoner's pocket, and pulled out a knife. The knife produced was the same. Prisoner never replied when he said he was stabbed. Witness tried to strike the prisoner, but found be had no use in either arm. Witness lost a great deal of blood, and had been unable to follow any employment• since. When he left the scene the prisoner was in the custody of P.C. Bell.—Cross-examined: When witness felt he was stabbed he kicked prisoner. He thought he had another knife, and would stop him, and he therefote went into him any way.—Mr. Swift: That was not the first time you had kicked him? Witness: I have kicked him when he has kicked me.—Mr. Swift: Have you net kicked him three or four times previous to that night? Witness : I have kicked him when he has kicked me. I can't tell whether I have kicked him a dozen times or not.—Mr. Swift: May it have happened twenty times previously? Witness: I have kicked him when he has kicked me.—The question was repeated and the same answer was received.— Mr. Swift: The man's more knave than fool. Well, I will have the question answered if I keep the court waiting. Now, have you kicked him twenty times previous to the night? Witness: We have not been together so many times.—Mr. Swift: May it have been fifteen times? Wit- ness: I can't say. I have kicked him when he has kicked rne.—Mr. Bibby to Mr. Swift): He tells you he never kicked him only in return, but could not say how often. You are keeping the court waiting, Mr. Swift.—Mr. Swift: He says he can't tell whether it was Mom, andl am en- deavouring to get it down, and I shall have it down, too.— Witness stated that he did not think they had been together fifteen timei.—Mr. Swift: I suppose you can see he has got a black eye? Witness: Yes, but it was done before I went to him.—Mr. Swift: Oh, I know you will say anything. When Mrs. Preston came into your house did not your wife say to you "Oh, never mind, it is only the old man and old woman having a word or two ?" Witness: Yes, she did.— Mr. Swift: Did you not say "I know who it is. I can quieten him in about five minutes?" Witness: No I did not. I said to Mrs. Preston, "Is it your William" and she replied that it was, and I said " I think I can get him home!' Mrs. Preston told me to mind as her husband had gone for a policeman. Mrs. Preston asked my wife to let her out by the back door.—Mr. Swift: And did you not want to go cut at the same time? Witness: I was going.—Mr. Swift: Answer the triestion, yea or no. Witness: I was going.—Mr. Bibby intimated that he considered Mr. Swift was not conducting the case as he should do. He asked the witness a question, and would not let him give an answer.— Mr. Swift: Nobody says so, but you, sir.—Mr. Bibby: I must be a very strange person then.—Mr. Swift: I don't want to have any altercation with the bench; I have had enough of it in my time, and I will try to conduct my case, properly. I will have answers to my questions if I have to wait all day. Witness stated, on further cross-examination, that when be went out of the house be put on a pair of clogs. tie did not 'hove tee prisoner up and down. He kicked the orbs ,ner three times, because witness thought he had another knife. Hs did no; want to hurt him; in fact he wanted them to let him go after he was stabbed.—Peter Ludrick. collier, residing at 22, Cook-street, Whis:on, stated that on Friday night, whilst he was in bed, some one knocked at the door. He got up and went into the front room, and saw his lodger, Humphrey Dyson, looking through the window. Witness dressed and went to Preston's house. Dyson was there before him. Witness saw the prisoner standing near the back door. He asked prisoner what he was doing there, and he replied that he had come for his clothes. Witness went with him a short dis- tance on the way home. On getting into Shaw-lane. Sparkes came up and said, "What's to do with you, Bill," and the prisoner replied, "What's that to do with thee." Sparkes then got hold of prisoner by the collar. Prisoner said to witness, "Take my bundle," but he refused to do so, and remarked that there must be no fighting. Sparkes took hold of the bundle and pitched it to one side and 'said" Nobody will touch thy bundle." Prisoner then began to strip himself, taking eff his coat, waistcoat, hat, and handkerchief. Sparkes and the prisoner then began squaring, and witness said to prisoner, "H you don't stop it off I shall go bonne, and leave Sparkes to do what he likes." Sparkes then got hold of prisoner, and threw him down. No blows were struck at that time. While prisoner was down, Sparks said to him " Now, what can Ido for thee?" When Sparkes wall getting up he called out that prisoner had stabbed him. Vl'itness seized hold of prisoner's hand, hut there was no knife in it. Sparkes immediately put his hand into the prisoner's trousers pocket and pulled out a knife, which he handed to witness. Sparkes then com- menced to kick the prisoner about the head and body. Wit- ness got hold of him and said," Stop it, step it," and. Sparkes said," He's stabbed me, Peter." Witness shoved Sparkes away, and Dyson struck a match, and they ex- amined him and found he was bleeding severely. He an to bandage Sparkes's arm before he went to the doctor. He handed the knife (produced) to P.C. Bell the same night. —By Mr Swift: Sparkes appeared to have had drink, but was not drunk. He had never seen Sparkes kick the prisoner befere.—Humphrey Dyson gave correhoriaive evidence, and added that when the prisoner and Sparkes were upon the floor he heard something like the click of a knife, and Sparkes im- mediately afterward said" Pm done."—He had seen Sparkes kick the prisoner on several occasions before. Witness believed prisoner got his hlacx eye during the quarrel, and when Spark es kicked him on the head. Prosecutor after the quarrel appeared to be disabled.—Mr. R. F. Brindle, surgeon, said that Sparkes was brought to his surgery at Prescot between half-past twelve and one o'clock on Saturday morning. He examined him and found two incised wounds, one behind the left shoulder and the other on the inner side of the right elbow. Each wound was about one inch long and thtee- quarters of an inch deep. The wound in the elbow bled very freely. The wounds appeared to have been inflicted by a sharp instrument. The knife produced would eau.e such wounds as he had ex.mined.—Cros.-examined : Sparkee, as far as he could've, had not had any drink. Any sharp cutting instrument would cause such wounds as Sparkes received —P.C. Bell said he apprehended the priso- I ;ter in Shaw-lane, Whiston. Prisoner was laid down under the hedge when he found him. Witness told him he was going to take him to Prescot foraitabbing Robert Sparkes with a knife. Prisoner said "They never saw a knife." Witness charged him with wounding Robert Sparkes by stabbing him with a knife. The plsorter replied" lam not guilty." He received the knife produced from Ludrick. He noticed it and saw blood upon tit- blarle.—Cross-examined : Prisoner appeared to have had drink. When witness found him ' he appeared to be suffering from the effects of recent violence.—Mr. Swift, for the defence, submitted that it was not a case for committal. First of all their worships would be conscious that the first witness with whom he bad a very great deal of trouble, and who was not by any means a satisfactory witness, hod not in many respects told the truth. The witness was not wishful to I make a clear statement of the facts as they, occurred, and had been contradicted ins great wary material particu'ars by the testimony of the other witnesses called for the prose- cution' so that his evidence was not to be relied anon, Implicitly. He put it to their worships that even if they 'should think it was the prisoner who inflicted those wounds, it did not follow that it was a ease of unlawfully wound- ing, because it was quite possible that wounding might be lawfully done, and tees I wfully done in self-defence. It was quite clear that `4earkes went out with his clogs on, determined to have St fight with the prisoner, and be was the first tonee any vio,enee whatever. He contended that it was not by any means a CAse of unlaw• fully wounding or a case which ought to go for trial.—AL.f the magistrates had conferred together a few minutes, Mri Feria said they were of opinion that he cage ought to go for trial at the Sessions, but they woitl4 admit prisoner to bail, himself in £4O and two sureties •f £lll each.

Even x -,lv to jg,...llleAriaann is Resident Governess. For prospectu those 35,246,000 persona do not include all the ' Queen's subjects (exclusive of the people of British India and of the Colonies), who ought to be reckoned if they could be got at. Some thousands of civilian Englishmen are living in countries upon the Conti- nent of Europe, and in other parts of the world, whom the national census-takers do not reach. Their numbers, indeed, are partially balanced by those of foreign subjects domiciled in England and enumera- ted at the census. In the United States of America multitudes of people from these Islands are living who have not naturalized themselves there, but are still British subjects, and many of whom intend to re- main so. But even confining our view to the popu- lations which actually inhabit the Mother country, the growth of their numbers is something porten- tous, if regard be had: to the contracted territorial spaces in which they have to animist.. It is far more significant that there should be 35,246,000 souls in the United Kingdom, and 25,968,296-in the parts of it called England and Wales, that there are now 50,009,000 of people in the vast continent contained in the United States of America. It is perhaps the greatest wonder of the age how all these people can subsist, and in- so much general comfort and plenty, in a little country like ours. Still more sur- prising is it how the large increment of 3,401,000 souls within ten years has been absorbed into the industrisil system of the country without perceptibly intensifying the conditions of the general struggle for existence. England (with Wales) now con- tains close upon twenty-six millions of in- habitants; and the numbers exceed twenty-six millions if the population of the Channel Islands, which really is as much a part of England as the Isle of Wight, be added. The Isle of Man, with its 53,000 people, may hardly be claimed to belong more to England than to Scotland or Ire- land, being nearly equi-distant from each. The increase in ten years in the population of Eagland and Wales has been 3,256,020. Scotland, also, has made the goodly increase for the relative numbers of its total of 374,352; but against that has to be set the decrease of the popula- tion of Ireland by 252,538 since 1871. Had. Ireland been but able to hold its own i population, the total for the United Kingdom would have been thirty-five and a half millions, instead of thirty-five and a quarter. Yet it is not only in Ireland that the testi. sunny of the census is one of local displacement, as well as aggregate increase, of the population. There are eight English counties and six Welsh counties which have sustained a reduction of inhabitants in the decade. One English county, Cornwall, seems to be undergoing a depopulation as wholesale as that which has occurred in parts of Ireland. Cornivall has lost nearly 33,000 inhabitants since 1871. Little Rutland has nearly t,OOO fewer inhabitants than it had ten years ago. On the other side Lancashire maintains the front position in increase of all the counties. It has gained 634,730 inhabitants since 1871, ana now contains 3,483,989 souls. The neigh- bottring county of York, in area the largest, has increased by 449,954 persons. Of the four counties which embrace London, Middlesex has added 379,000 to its numbers of inhabitants, and Surrey 344,207. London, within the bounds of what is called the Metropolitan district, now supports a population of 3,814671, showing an increase in ten years of over 560,000, whish is about equal to the entire present population of Liverpool. London still distances enor- mously the greatest of foreign capitals, rapidly as same of them have increased in recent years. Paris, the next in magnitude, had a population on a recent return of 1,988,000, so that the English metropolis is almost twice as big as the French. Berlin contains 5,128,000 people, Ind is much less than one-third the size of London. Vienna has 731,000, and St. Peters- burg 669,000 inhabitants. These are the largest European cities. New York, which though not the capital of the United States, stands far ahead of all other American cities—population, contained in June, xBBo, 7,206,000 people, and if we add Brooklyn, divided by an arm of the bay from New York, which has 566,000 inhabitants, the two together make up a total very considerably below the half of the popula- tion of our English Babylon. Philadelphia is the second of American cities in point of size, with 846,000 souls. Thus London remains the most startling example of the concentration of people in immense urban communities, which has been the most conspicuous feature of the operation of the modern social system.

THE startling news irom Washington that rno at- tempt had been made to assassinate President Garfield has been received in this country with mixed feelings of indignation, horror, and sympathy. The dastardly crime that was committed has all the worst features of cowardly attrocity, and it was a matter for universal regret that the 4th of July, the anniversaii of the Declaration of Independence, which is always set apart as a general holiday in the United States, should this year have b: m darkened by such an out- rage. The perpetrator of the foul deed is fortunately in custody, and will be duly arraigned to answer for his crime. It is no doubt better that the trial should proceed with every regard for recognised legal forms, but there can be no doubt that if the criminal had fallen into the hands of the righteously exaspera- ted people of Washington, his crime would have been followed by an example of that swift justice which has a strikingly deter: ent isfluenoe on the criminal classes. President Garfield had been staying at Long- branch for the health of his wife, and his assailant Seems to have tracked him there, and tollowcd him back to Washington. At the railway depot at which he was assailed he was moving about with the confidence of a man who suspected no one and was quite unaware that any danger threatened him until he was shot down. The crime is appalling, and if suggests that even the freest of institutions do not shelter a nation's highest representatives from the operations of the misguided men who endeavour to accomplish their objects by resorting to violence and the instruments of the assassin. For the victim of this diabolical outrage the civilised world have showa the deepest sympathy which has been extended to the whole people of the States, who in the midst of their general rejoicing have been shocked by a deed which recalls one of the most terrible episodes in their history. We mbpeaetnhy. examined . can scarcely recall a publio event which elicited such During ttihht e tittilhaeS satisfactory of pe few thatd a days thesth etyo telegramswidespread have might convey good news, a learn that the latest intelligence received time of our writing leaves the Preaide.up to the ni.a condition which, if still giving cause for grave room to hope that the life which has been so suddenly sudideaves menaced may yet be spared. In a vicarial en enly it may be truly said that millions of people are sense lug by the bedside at Washington, and that every ermine favourable symptom is a source of g • - satis- faction.

last. As the Scotch express train was leaving 'St. Pancras terminus, an inspector saw a man sitting behind the end brake. The train was immediately Stopped, and the un- lucky sugar boiler found lying down under the brake van among the iron work. On the following day he was politely asked to clear himself from a charge of attempting to de- fraud the company of the fare from London to Edinburgh— £l 13s. As he was unable to pay that, I scarcely think he will be able to pay the fine of 20s. and costs imposed—rather dear for an uncomfortable ride of a mile or so at the tail-end of a train. The moral is don't attempt to find the "fourth class " until the railway authorities ehow it you.

A RUNCORN SCHOOL THEAT.—The Runoorn Primi- live Methodist Sunday school had their annual treat on Monday afternoon. The children and friends went in pro- cession to a field lent by Mr.i. Ashley, one of the superin- tendents, and the weather being of a most delightful char- acter, they had" a good time.' The youngsters were pro- vided with tea and other refreshments. ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN CARTER. On Monday, carter in the employ of Mr. T. Rigby, of Frodsham, was in charge of a lurry drawn by three horses, at Messrs. Occles- ton and Sons' tan-yard, Runcorn, when the animals were I frightened from some cause or other, and crushed the driver against a wall,- so that he received injuries of a somewhat serious nature. He was attended by Dr. Carruthers. ACCIDENT nv a WEsroN Qtramar.—On Thursday after- noon, as John Oldfield, Agri 19, of Ford Bank-terrace, was working at Messrs. J. and 'P. Handley's quarry, Weston, a piece of rock, which had been undermined, fell upon him, crushing him severely. Dr. Robinson was in the village at the time, and had the poor fellow taken home, where he rendered him every assistance. THE ASSAULT BY 'manta-Ex.—Yesterday, the two youn men, and the other brother, named Martin Grady, who had surrendered thet morning to P.C. Stott, were brought up on remand, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., charged with unlawfully and maliciously wounding Doyle. The evidence was similar to that given at Wednesday's court, with the addition df that of two young women, who corroborated complainant's statement. In answer to the charge, the prisoners Thomas and Martin Grady said they were not at the place when the assault was committed. No witnesses were called, and each of the prisoners was committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial. THE REV. JOSEPH MORTON, OP RUNCORN.—For two years Mr. Joseph Morton has occupied the post of superin- tendent minister of the Primitive Methodist Freston Brook circuit, and during a considerable portion of the time he haa suffered from ill health. Mr. Morton has been appointed to a similar position in the Warrington and Widnes station. We understand some of the members were not quite satisfied with the selection made by the Conference, as Mr. Morton is in indifferent health, has a large family, and is not fond of visiting, but they were told that they ought to have made their objection earlier, and it was too late to give it consi- deration. On Sunday evening, the reverend gentleman preached his valedictory sermon in Greenway-road Chapel; and in the afternoon gave a farewell address at the Sunday school.—Corn. •

A most disgraceful fracas is reported to have taken place between two colliers at Whiston on Friday last, in which it is alleged that one man stabbed the other. As the matter is still subjudice I will, of course, refrain from expressing any opinion upon the guilt or innocence of the prisoner, but I think that the evidence given before the magistrates dis- closed a very disreputable , state of affairs, which certainly reflected no credit on either of the parties. The injured man admitted that he put on a pair of clogs when he went out to the prisoner, and that he had frequently kicked the prisoner when that worthy had kicked him. 1 hope that these kicking matches will soon be numbered with things of the past, and that colliers, as well as other workingmen in this district, will learn to settle their disputes in a more manly fashion than by such means as that. A very amusing episode occurred the other day at a re- gistrar's office not a thousand miles from here'. A stalwart man who had seen about fifty-six winters, entered the regis- trar's office, and asked in a very confidential manner for a private interview with that official. This being granted, he disclosed the interesting fact that he was about to take unto himself a second wife in the person of a blooming young damsel of eighteen summers. As the sweet maiden occupied the humble position of a domestic servant, the in- tended bridegroom expressed his intention to spend as little cash about the ceremony as potible, seeing that he had promised to leave his farm and all his other property by will to his new wife, an he therefore spent considerable time in endeavouring to persuade the registrar to reduce his fees for tying the nuptial knot, but without avail. Having at length ascertained the lowest possible amount that the re- gistrar would consent to accept in fees, the farmer gave the necessary notices, fixed the day ter performing the cere- mony, and was about to retire. He had, however, only get as far as the door, when he suddenly turned back, and going up the registrar, he thus addressed him in a loud whisper :—" Oh, I forgot to tell you that when I was mar- ried before, the old parson shook hands with my wife in the vestry, and gave her back all the money as I gave him for marrying us. Now, I suppose you will have no objection to do the same, but I thought as I had better mention it to make sure." The registrar replied" Oh, no, I certainly never could think of doing that." Farmer: "Well, but the parson did it, and you ought to do the saute." Registrar: "I don't care what the parson did, I can't do it." Where- upon the farmer departed, grumbling loudly at the "stingi- ness," as he termed it, of the registrar. A friend of mine who has lately been rusticating, says that he saw the other day in the grounds of a florist and market gardener, the following terrifying announcement : 'Beware I Polypodittms and ' Scolorendriams set here." This is vastly superior to the comparatively tame warning, "that man-traps are set here." It has also the advantage of being true, which the latter since the practice of Bettina man-traps was prohibited by Parliament has not. I learn from an American source that there is another comet" scooting round creation." I hope not, especially if the celestial visitation that has recently been exercising our speculative faculties has anything to do with the almost tropical heat of the last few days. On Tuesday the temperature in England was no less than a degree and a half within that of the hottest day last year in Bombay. What it might be with two comets visible to the naked eye is too dreadful to contemplate.

11111 REPRESENTATION OF WIGAN AND CHESTER—Truth Says that the Government propose to move for a royal com- mission to inquire into the corrupt practices at the last Wigan election. There is no truth in the report that a writ will be issued for Chester shortly, and under no circum- stances would Mr. Raikes again contest that city. BOY DROWNED AT SOUTHPORT.—On Thursday morningo shortly after six o'clock, as two boys named Robinson were I attempting to bring ashore a •rowing boat, the property of their father, who lives at 98, Sussex-road, Southport, it cap- sized, throwing both lads into the *water. The eldest managed to swim ashore, but William Robinson, aged about thirteen, was unable to light against the heavy waves, and quickly saqk. His body was recovered about ten o'clock. The accident took place close to Southport Pier. Fon POISONING IN TER Mantic—More destruction of fish in the Ribble has been caused by the poisonous matters turned into the stream from the works in East Lancashire. Four fine salmon and one large eel, and several smaller ones were picked up on the bank of the liver below Frenchwood, Preston, on Wednesday, and there can be no doubt whatever that numbers of others and similar fish have been thus sacrificed, especially in the upper portions of the river in the neighbourhood of the works referred to. WARRINGTON TNFIRILLRY AND DlSPENSARE.—House- surgeon's report for the week ending Thursday, July 7. Patients admitted and discharged—Home patients, 8; out patients, 19; accidents, 10; total, 37. Cured, 12; dead, 3 ; discharged, 6; total, 21. Present number of home patients 20. In-patients: Admitted, 6; d;scharged, 1; remaining in hospital, 19. Hon. Treasurer, J. R. Backton, Esq. ; Hon. Secretary, Jos. Davies, Esq. ; House Surgeon, M. C. E. Rich- mond. The House Surgeon will feel obliged for contributions of old linen, Sm. Medical officer for the ensuing week Mr. Gornall.

Miss Marianne Farningham has had a deal to say about the girl of the period, about her masculine ideas and adoption tion of ways and customs of the sterner sex. I wonder what she would have to say about our girls as foot- ball players and cricketers. Only a week or two ago a foot- ball match was played at Liverpool by young ladies, and at one of our school treats in this district, not far from some lunatic asylum (!) the game of cricket was pursued with zest by some lovely girls I should not like to mention, and who were assisted in "Ye old Englishe game" by one the mention of whose name ought to leave no doubt as to the wisdom of the proceeding. I have no objection to young ladies imitating the sensitive, bashful, sentimental hero named Harley in Henry Mackenzie's 'Man of Feeling," but when the aims at being a "man "whose average weight is 1501b5., height 69 inches, and strength 4201b5., then I think it is time I stood in an attitude of self defence. Fran AT WARanciTrom—About eight o'clock on Tuesday morning a fire of a trivial character occurred at the house of Mr. George Walton, 45, Allen-street. Mr. Walton and his wife were away from home, and had left in charge of the house a servant girl who was not considered by the police to be fitted for such a trust. The girl it appears put a quantity of burning cinders into a basket which she placed in a pantry under the stairs. Soon after the pantry door and stairs were discovered to be on fire. An alarm was given, and a reel was sent to the spot from the Fire Engine Station, but the fire was soon extinguisned by water being poured on the burning timberefrom buckets.

CHOIR PIC-NIC FROM WIDNES.—The members of the Widnes United Methodist Free Church choir had their annual excursion on Wednesday, when about forty persons left West Bank Dock, on board the steamer Firefly, for a trip up the Weaver to Winsford. During the day the weather was very unsettled, and considerably interfered with the pleasure of the excursionists. Arrangements had been made for taking breakfast, dinner, and tea, in pie-nic style, on the banks of the Weaver, but the unfavourable weather rendered this impossible. Breakfast was served onboard the Firefly, and on the party arriving at Winsford at akout twel we o'clock they partook of dinner at the cocoa rooms. After- wards they proceeded to the Over United Methodist Chapel, where an hour was agreeably spent in singing. Returning to the boat the party steamed back to Northwich where they again disembarked. RUNCORN AMATEURS AND WANDERERS' BICYCLE HANDI- CAP RACE.—This race came off on Thursday evening, near Sutton Weaver, on the Aston course (goalies), in the presence of a large number of spectators. The weather was fine, though a rather strong wind was blowing. Fifteen earies had been made, and fourteen men put in an appearance at the starting post, all of whom seemed in good form. Tim- mins (scratch) was the favourite, though Thomas Bate, with 45sec. start, was mentioned as likely to make it warm work for him. Timmins (Amateur) landed 21sec. in front of Bate (Wanderers). The noble manner in which Bate stuck to his opponent along the straight to the winning post was highly praise. Temperley (Wanderers) made a good third, but was disqualified for riding on the footpath. E. Rhodes (Amateur) came in fourth, followed close by Norman (Amateur). There was a close race for the sixth place be- tween Stanway and F. Bate, the former pulling it off by a length only. The following are the times in which the distance was run :
