LASE OF SUNSTROKE AT ASTON GRANGIL,--0/ITheidayp a labourer named James Dean, of Aston, had a sunstroke while haymaking in a field at Aston Grange, near Preston Brook, belonging to Colonel Talbot. The sufferer was at once conveyed home. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSAM—On Sunday last, two sermons were preached in the above church by the Rev. W. J. Fennell, of Hindley Green, formerly resident in the Frodsham circuit, A choice selection of hymns were nicely rendered by the choir, and Master Harry Aston presided at the organ. The collections amounted tu £l2 103. The annual treat to the Sunday school scholars was given on Monday, when by the kind permission of Mr. Percival about 100 children and 60 teachers and friends were entertainedat Godscroft Farm, and it being a fine summer day a very pleasant afternoon was spent. The farm bearing the name of "Godscroft " is the place referred to- in Nixon's prophecy, when after foretelling troublesome times, one asked Vixon where he might be safe in those days? He answered "In God's croft, between the rivers Mersey and Dee." THE REV. PETER MACKENZIE AT FRODSHAM.

A sermon was preached in Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, on Tuesday, by the Rev. Peter Mackenzie, when a large dumber of friends from Warrington, Runcorn, Helsby, and Kingsley attended. The text was taken from Ezekiel 47 chapter, 9, 10 1 verses, the sermon being illustrated in a clear and highly descriptive manner. Tea was provided in the school room adjoining the chapel, and was pre- sided over by Mesdames Berrington, Challoner (Nethertora(, Pronde, Challoner (Kingsley), Kent, Sbaircross, Turner, Denby, Codinson, Walker, Booth, and Lowe. The lecture in the evening was well attended, the.chair being. taken by Mr. W. Collinson, and there were also present on the plat- form Revs. J. M. Bamford, J. F. Edmonds, Nowell, and Valentine* The Rev. Mr. Nowell haviag engaged in prayer, the Chairman introduced the lecturer to the meeting, who announced his subject as "Gideon, the mighty man of valour." The lecturer described in a most graphic manner the sad condition in which the Israelites were at the time that Gideon was selected by God as their deliverer. The coun- try, which was one of the most fertile, was untilled and neglected. It was mournful to see nettles and weeds grow- ing apace, where formerly'flowers bloomed. Yet this was the state of things that the blight and curse a war always produced.
Man's Inhumanity to ;Ilan Makes eoutless thousands mourn.

We had seen enough of war in our own time. We had had the Franco-Prussian, with all the destruction that followed in its train.' We ourselves were a warlike nation. Our war with Russia cost 40 millions. Then, in Abyssinia we had to pay very dear for our coffee. (Hear, hear.) Oh, that this curse of war were rooted out! How many chapels might be Guilt, how many colleges might be endowed, how much good might be done in the world with the money we had spent in war. (Cheers.) He for one looked forward to that day When the war drum throbs no longer, And the battle flags are furled, In the Parliament f man, The federation of the world When the conmon sense of most Shall hold & fretful realm in awe. And the kindly earth shall slumler, Wract in universal law— (Applause.) He looked for it, believing it would be a great boon and blessing to mankind. (Hear, hear.) He described the call of Gideon and said God found Gideon at Ophrah, engaged in what might seem the humble occupation of threshing by the winepress. God often chose men lowly birth for His greatest work. Moses was a foundling; Christ choose poor fishermen as His disciples. They knew the story of two members of Parliament, one of whom con- temptuously told the other that he had blacked his father's boots. "Yes," said the other, "and didn't I make them shine! " (Laughter.) It .was a lesson they must lay to heart, namely, not to despise GrOu'ii in- struments, however humble. (Hear, hear.) When the angel of the Lord first appeared to Gideon he was dis- trustful, and said "The Lord bath forsaken us and delivered us into the hands of the Michanites." But it was wrong of Gideon to say that the Lord had forsaken Israel. He bad tried them, it was true; but did He not always try His chosen people? It was the productive earth that was torn up by the keen edge of the plough, not the barren shingle on the sea shore; it was the fruitful vine that bled beneath the knife of the vinedresser, and not the unproductive thorn. As gold was tried by fire, so God's people were tested in the furnace of affliction. When the angel told Gideon that it would be his mission to deliver Israel, he at once replied, "Oh, my Lord, wherewith shall I save Israel ?" He spoke as all great men speak, for they were always diffident, and never forward. Gideon could not understand how he was to deliver Israel without men or means or the sinews of war. Nevertheless, he took courage, and we were told that the "spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon, and he blew a trumpet." There was something that stirred men's courage when the trumpet sounded loud and long. It was to the trumpet's note that the walls of Jericho fell down ; it was to the trumpet's note that Waterloo and Inkerman were won. When the trumpet's silver note was heard, who did not feel patriotic? He described how Gideon sought for a sigo, and a sign was given him in the miraculous fleece, from which the dewdrops hung like orient pearls when all the earth was dry besides, and which was dry when every blade of grass was wet with dew. The lecturer also spoke of Gideon's army, and of the cowardice of those who de- serted. They evidently believed That he who fights and runs away. May live to fight another day. And in the course of a lengthy and eloquent discourse, which was heartily applauded, he pointed out the many useful lessons which they should learn from Gideon's his-
tory. EtTbe usual votes of thanks to the Chairman and Lecturer brougbt the meeting to a close. The proceeds amounted to about £25.

SAVAGE ATTACK ON A BRICKMAKER AT WARRINGTON. Five young men, named William and Thomas Mellor, brothers, Robert, William, and Thomas Forbes, also brothers, I were brought up at the Borough Court on Thursday morning, I before Aldermen Thewlis and Burgess, and Councillors Milner and Litton, charged under a warrant, witih unlawfully assaulting and beating John Ward.—Mr. Moore appeared for the prisoners Forbes, and also consented to defend th Meliors. The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said the prosecutor was a brickmaker, and resided at 35, Bostock-street. The pri- soners Wm. and Thos. Melior and Wm. and Thos. Forbes were also brickmakers, and Robert Forbes was a glass bottle hand. About half-past seven o'clock on Tuesday night the prose- cutor was at work at the moulding bench in the brickyard in Bostock-street, when William and Thomas Melior walked up the street. On 'approaching where prosecutor was at work, William called out to him "Ah you knobstick, I'll knock your head off;" asking shortly afterwards "Who stole the watch ?" Much improper language was used, and fora long time presecutor returned no reply to the prisoners' insulting remarks, At last he said "I never stole a watch," when the prisoner William pulled off his coat and hastened up to prosecutor' got hold of him, knocked him on the ground, and beat him with his fist on the head very much. Whilst the prosecutor was thus being ill-used Thomas Forbes picked up half a brick and struck him with it on the head. Martin Ward then went to the assistance of his father, the prosecutor, and to better defend his father he picked up an iron spade, and struck one of the Meliors. The spade was, however, wrested from him, and used alternately to beat young Ward and his father. Thjs had lasted for sonm ten minutes, when the brothers Forbes went to lend "a helping hand," and threw various missies I at the prosecutor. The crowd which had collected rescued I the prosecutor, and Mm. Melior again used threatening lan- guage, saying" kaebstick you are working for Is. 3d. per thousand, where you ought only to work for Is. ed, same as I do." A‘policeman than appeared on the scene, and quietness was restored. Prosecutor, whose head was bandaged, confirmed the statement of the Chief Constable, and stated that when rescued by the crowd he was covered with blood. William Forbes struck him with a spade, Thomas struck him on the knee with a brick, and Robert on the face with his fist. Evidence was also given by Martin Scanlan, Martin Ward, Themes Owen Cliffe, Thomas Buckley, and Sarah Owen in support of the charge, though the Forbes had been seen to take little part in the assault. Buckley stated that when Thos. Mellor went up to the prosecutor's bench, he got hold of a wooden spade, and knocked Ward down "as he would a cow."

Mr. Moore, in defence, submitted there was no case agajnst the Forbes, and said they had taken no part in that most disgraceful disturbance. He contended that it was a "regular set-to fight" between Ward and Mellor, and that equal violence had been used. He called Martha Jones, who said Martin Ward caused the wound on prosecutor's head when attempting to strike Melior with the spade. The Forbes "did nothing," but she saw Mrs. Melior being carried home, having fainted through being struck with a brick sent by young Ward. Mrs. Forbes also denied that her eons had any part in the row. Mary Ann Donoghue, who gave her evidence very clearly, said the prosecutor first taunted the Meliors with stealing hens, and the Meliors retaliates by saying prosecutor's daughter had stolen a watch. Martin then challenged Wm. ' Melior to fight, and struck him on the forehead, the row then becoming general. It was only a drunken row. While Wm Melior and the prosecutor were entangled on the ground, Martin aimed a blow at the former with a spade, but struck the latter on the side of the head in mistake. Mrs. Melior, who was near her confinement, was struck with a brick. She fainted, and had to be carried away. Other evidence having been given, Alderman Thewlis said the Bench were of opinion that the prosecutor had been grossly Mused, and the prisoners William and Thomas Melior would be sent to prison for two months with bard labour. With regard to the Forbes, the Bench thought they Fere part and parcel of the scrimmage, and they would be bound over in their own recognizance of £5 each to keep the peace for six months. The costs in the case of the Forbes amounted to 16s. ed. each, and Mr. Moore applied for a reduction, which the Bench refused to grant. The prisoners appeared much surprised at the sentence passed upon them.
COLRIIAN'S MUSTARD FACTORY DESTROYED BY FIRE.— A fire broke out on Wednesday nigut at Coleman's mustard manufactory at Norwich. The damage -is. estimated at £30,000. •

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOAED.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOAED.
The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, the Rev. Canon Barclay presiding. There were also present—Messrs. Simpson, Lea, Briscoe, Norman, and Rigby (clerk).
TRINITY' SCHOOLMASTER AND, THE BOARD.

Mr. Bowyer, school attendance officer, presented his docu- ment as to monthly returns, which was as follows:—"The returns for the past month I have been unable to complete, owing to Mr. Annett, master of the Trinity Boys' School, refusing to supply the necessary figures. On the 16th of Tune last I called at his school, and asked him if he would supply the Board with the returns as usual. He declined to do so, and informed me that his books were at my service to copy from them what the Board might require. Since the last meeting of the Board, I have summoned be- foie the magistrates, the nine parents ordered to be dealt with for contravention of the bye-laws. Convictions were granted in each case, and the usual fine of 65., including costs, imposed. During the past month I have also served final notices upon 31 parents, for the irregular and non- attendance of their children at school, a list of which I lay before you, showing their attendance since the notices have • been served. Several of the parents, I find, have not corn- plied with their notices as well as they ought to have done, The principal reasons given foie non-attend..nce have been want of means, insufficiency of clothing, and being sent back for school fees. I may say it is now the rule at most of the schools, to send home again those who do not bring their fees in advance. Since this rule has been so strictly ' enforced, my duties have considerably increased, and I have much greater difficulty in getting children into school again, as. they are kept at home, and allowed to run about the streets until I am able to visit their parents, and force them into school again." The Clerk: Mr. Annett practically refuses to give what eleven other teachers have given.—Mr. Norman: Why should not he do what other teachers do 7—The Chairman: He is not compelled. If eleven other people choose to give £5 to a charity, I am not bound to do so.—Mr. Lea: It would take him half an hour each day.—The Chairman: And you know it is his own less.—Mr. Simpson: Mr. Kyonersley, the Government inspector, says that Mr. Annett will lose his certificate if be continues to refuse to give the returns.— The Clerk said the section dealing with the matter in the Education Act was as follows :—"ln any school district in which a bye-law under section 24 of the principal Act is in force, the School Board in such district may from time to time supply forms to any public elementary school, for the purpose of obtaining reasonable information with reference to the attendance of children in their district who attend such school; and the managers of such school if they fail to cause such forms to be truly filled up and returned in manner required by the School Bq,ard, or to cause such information to be given as to enable the School Board to ascertain whether a child resident in their district, and attending that school, attends the same in manner required by the said bye-laws, shall cause to be produced to such member or officer of the School Board, or other person as may be duly authorised in that behalf by the School Board, at any reasonable time when required by him the register and other books containing information with respect to the attendance of children at such school, and shall permit him to take copies of and extracts from the same. If any difference arises between the School Board and the managers of a public elementary school, as to whether the information given by the said forms is or is not reasonable, such difference shall be referred to the Education Department, whose decision shall be final."--Mr. Simpson: If the Board are to put up with what the managers of Trinity School and their master have decided upon—for according to this the managers can insist upon the master giving these returns— and if the managers and master do not choose to fill up these forms it will not be fair to the teachers and managers of other schools to ask them to fill up the forms. The consequence will be that we shall either fail in carrying out the Act, or we shall require another officer. One officer cannot get all these returns and attend to his other work.— Mr. Lea: The objection Mr. Annett raises is that it takes up time when he could be doing something else.—Mr. Simp- son: Yes, but the other teachers do the same —The Clerk: The question is whether there is a difference. If there is a difference, you can appeal to the Education Department.— The Chairman said that if they wrote to the Education De- partment, probably Mr. Annett would say that though he bad failed to furnish the returns, he had offered to produce his books and documents.—The Clerk said that if the Edu- cation I ,epartment said that what Mr. Annett had done was enough, the School Board would have to make the best of the matter, but if they did not, the Board would have won their case. The object of the section he had quoted was evidently to avoid any unseemly wrangling between a school authority and a master—The Chairman: It is absurd for Mr. Kynnersley to say that Mr. Annett will be put on the black books until he does so. You must always take' w hat an inspector says cum grano salis. They want to be masters themselves. (Laughter.)—Mr. Simpson said the Act plainly showed that every assistance ought to be given to the School Board in working the Education Act; and it was not in ac- cordance with the spirit of the measure that managers and teachers should refuse to fill up the returns but give the in- spectors and the visitors the trouble of doing this them- selves. If in a place like Runcorn one or two teachers were allowed to take such a stand, others might do the same. Where a teacher took a stand like that, and the managers of the school supported him, the Education Department would be justified in saying "You are not carrying out the Act in the spirit required by it."—The Clerk said they must not forget that the Board had a court of appeal. The action of the master of Trinity school unhinged the whole of the statistics—The Chairman : It is his own loss.—Mr. Simp- son: Yes; but if we permit such a course to be pursued, shall we be doing our duty as a Board ?—The Clerk con- sidered that under such a state of things the Board could arrive at no kind of resnit which would be of any value.— Mr. Simpson : How can we instruct our visitor to look after the children unless he gets their names? It is not Annett's ioB3.—Mr. Lea said that Mr. Annett looked at the matter in this light—that Mr. Bowyer was kept for the purpose of looking over the registers and finding out the absentees. (Laughter.)—The Chairman: The managers do not mind at all about it.—Mr. Simpson was of opinion that if the managers of Trinity school decided to stand by Mr. Armen in his refusal to fill up the forms they would be making a great mistake.—The Chairman: That is for them to con- sider. I think so too, but before we make a fees about it I want us to be sure that we are perfeLtly right.—The Clerk said that when writing to the Education Department it was generally found that they would not answer if a dry, legal question were put to them, but where there was an instruc- tion in the Act—as in this case—they could not get out of it.—Mr. Norman: I cannot for the life of me understand why he should refuse to give these returns when every other schoolmaster and schoolmistress gives them. There must be a reason for Mr. Annett's action somewhere, and I think that reason ought to be sought.—The Chairman: We all agree that it is a great mistake on his part not to do it ; but, at the same time, we have nothing to do with his motives.— Mr. Simpson: Mr. Norman asks the reason, and Mr. Lea professes to give it, but it is not the reason. Mr. Armen, I in the first place, says "Because Mr. Bowyer does so and so. I I will not fill up these returns." Now Mr. Lea says Mr, Annett's reason for not doing it, is because it takes up so much time.—Mr. Lea replied that Mr. Annett had expressed his willingness to give two of the matters required by the Act.—The Clerk : I believe that Mr. Annett has bad very considerable experience as a teacher at a Board school, and by way of showing that the returns we tave put before him are not of an arbitrary character, I may say that they are copied almost exactly from these supplied by all the teachers to the Liverpool Scheol Board.—Mr. Norman moved that the Hoard ask the Department.—Mr. Simpson seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—The I Chairman: The department will write to the school man- ;mere (Laughter), and then they will have a word with Mr. Annett. I .should like to be behind the door. (Laughter.) Mr. Norman : Had not Mr. Lea better get ready, Mr. Chair. man ? (Laughter.)—The Chairman : Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof I (Laughter.)—Mr. Norman: Mr. Lea bad better stop the commnnication as It passe through his hand as postmaster. (Loud laughter.)

THE STORM AT WA.REINGTON.--The excessive heat of Monday and Tuesday was followed by a storm on the evening of the last-mentioned day, which broke over Warrington about eight o'clock, and was the most terrific experienced for many years. As evening drew on the sky became overcast, and about eight o'clock a heavy downpour of rain and hail took place. This was followed by other showers of rain, and the thunder, which had been heard in the distance, came nearer, and crashed repeatedly over the town with deafening roar. Vivid flashes of fork and sheet lightning now occurred on all sides, and continued incessantly for about an hour, causing an illumination by which distant objects became as visible as at noon-day, and affording a most brilliant and effective sight. Rain still fell in torrents, and as the sewers were unable to carry away the water the streets were soon flooded. In Sankey-street, at the end of Parker-street, Vie road was flooded knee-deep, and many un- fortunate wayfarers rushing about in search of a place of shelter found themselves hi a sad plight, as the darkness was rendered the more intense through the street lamps not hay- ing been lighted. The storm raged until next day, when it abated, but the weather has since been very unsettled: So far as we have been able to gather, no serious damage has been cause 1 in this locality.

• It will be seen from our advertising columns.th it the L in- I cas hire Telephone Company is about to be merged into a new company, under the name of the Lancashire and Che-' shire Telephone Exchange Company, Limited. The opera- tions of the company will extend over Lancashire and Cheshire, the six northern counties of Wales, the Isle of Man, and a portion of Westmoreland. Exchanges have been opened at various towns, and it is reported that 890 subscribers have joined the Liverpool and Manchester centres. The Post Office have granted permission, subject to a royalty of ten per cent. on gross profits, to establish exchanges in the various towns of the district, under the company's management, with radii varying from two to seven miles from the respective centres. This does not allow of exchange communication between different towns, although private wires will not be interfered with. As the telephone has, undoubtedly, become a great public conve- nience—indeed, almost a necessity to business life, it is not likely that merchants will rest satisfied till they are as free to talk between one town and another as they are low free to commuieate by the telegraph.

He could not consent to omit the section.—lt was amended accordingly.—Mr. VILLIERS STUART moved an amendment to provide facilities being given latiourers to purchase their holdings.—Mr. GLADsroasE said clauses affecting labourers would be introduced in a few days. _ THE SURVEYOR AND HIS DUTIES. The CHAIRMAN, in accordance with the notice given, spoke of the action of the surveyor in accepting the office of guardian of the poor for Stream. He brought it forward as a matter of principle. He had na personal feeling in the matter. When Mr. Derbyshire was appointed surveyor to the Board in 1874, the resolution doing so was in these words—" That he devote the whole of his time to the office." Mr. Derbyshire accepted these terms, and entered into an agreement, in which these terms were embodied. He (the Chairman) held that he had broken his contract with the Board. It might be asked why the mattter vaas brought up now when the guardians were elected in March. At the end of March or the beginning of April, at the last meeting of the old waywardens, he called the surveyor on one side, . and in the presence of the vice-chairman and the clerk, told him that he took exception to the action he had taken in allowing himself to be nominated an a guardian, and that he intended to bring it that day to the notice of the Board. After considerable discussion, the clerk having informed Mr. Darbyshire that it was not too late to decline to serve as a guardian, inasmuch as the clerk had not sent in the nomination returns, Mr. Darbyshire, in the presence of two others distinctly told him that he would write that night and withdraw his appointment. On that assurance be said, "lam very glad indeed you have fallen into my views, and I shall have no trouble in bringing this before the Board." Mr. Derbyshire had not kept that promise; he had been acting as a guardian of the poor, and also on the Sanitary Committee. He (the Chairman) held these things. so strongly that he thought Mr. Darbyshire had done wrong; and he was quite sure that any man who had con- trol of 140 miles of road had quite sufficient to do without having these honorary offices. He thought it his duty as chairman to bring this matter before the notice of the Board. They had heard all the facts, and he could appeal to the vice-chairman if he had not stated them correctly; and it was for the Board to give their opinion on the matter.— Mr. CLIFFE (vice-chairman) said the Chairman had cor- rectly stated the facts. He certainly understood tMr. Derbyshire to say that he would write to Mr. Linaker, and withdraw his name from the nominatiOn. The CHAIRMAN : Have you anything to say, Mr. Darby- shire.—Mr. DARBTsHIRE said he did not understand that be- en distinctly promised to write that night. He did go to Mr. Wild as chairman of the meeting which nominated him, and also to Mr. Mason, and told them that he declined to serve as a guardian, and that they must take steps to ap- point someone else. He had no other motive than getting rid of the office, so that the township could appoint someone else as quickly as possible. He did not know the cot:Se- quences of not writing, or he should most certainly have written to Mr. Linker. He left himself in the hands of the Board.—The CHAIRMAN You distinctly understood that in consequence of your promise I said I should not bring it before the Board.—The VICE-CHAIRmAN :It was plain enounh.—Thepusiums.x: Will you retire Mr. Derbyshire.— The CLERK said all he knew was that he saw Mr. Darby- ' shire, the chairman, and Mr. Cliffe together, and the chair- man motioned for him and asked him if there was any ob- jection to the Surveyor serving as a guardian. He replied that there was no objection ; he had a perfect right legally. The CHAIRMAN then asked whether it was desirable or not,. and how could he get out of it. and he said by writing a letter to the Clerk of the Guardians refusing to serve. Mr. Derbyshire promised to write and said he would not serve. —Mr. MASON said Mr. Darbyshire did call upon Mr. Wild and himself and told them he declined to stand, and requested Mr. Wild to appoint someone !Ise. He had heard nothing more of it, but noticed Mr. Derbyshire had been acting as a guardian.— The CHAlRiaANiconsidered it right to bringthe matter before them, and the only question was what course would meet the case.—After some discussion in which the greater part of the members coincided with the chairman's objections. the Chairman suggested that Mr. Derbyshire be told they generally objected to his appointment as guardian, and that they insisted on his not attending as guardian for Stret- ton.—The CLERK: I think it will be better to say that the Board insists upon his devoting:Ahe whole of his time to the duties of his office.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE was then called into the room.—The CHAIRMAN said: Mr. Darbyshire, lam in- structed by the Boardj to express their disapproval of your accepting the office you have done. Having done that the matter ends, but with this addition that the Board ex- pent you to give the whole of your time to the duties of this Board.

DEATH PnoX SUNSTROKE AT APPLETON.—Mr. T. T. Ridgway, coroner, held an inquest at the Thorn Inn, Ap- pleton, on Thursday, on the body of Patrick Hannon, 34 years of age, an Irish farm laboureff. It appeared that de- ceased, who was a married man, bad been in England about fourteen weeks, and worked for Mr. Knowles, of Yew Tree Farm, Appleton. On .Thursday morning deceased and his fellow workmen, commenced work soon after five o'clock as they were busy in the bay. It was very hot where they were in the stack yard, but the deceased worked until about half past ten o'clock when he went to get his "bagging.' lie then complained of feeling ill and some brandy was aa- ministered to him, which he.„drank. Dr. Fox, of Warrington, was sent for but before he arrived deceased expired. The doctor was of opinion that deceased died from sunstroke, and was further of opinion that the death of the deceased was accelerated by his sleeping in a "paddy house which was overcrowded, there being nine persons sleeping in a loom having only the necessary space for three persons.--the jury returned a virdict that the deceased died from sun-. stroke.

div.p: Xttiers to tite editor.

STARR-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETIES. Sir,—My attertion has been called to a letter in your newspaper signed " Taylor and Longbottom." These worthies seem to think I have nothing better to do than to continually reply to their silly mis-statements ; they evidently supposing that if they continue throwing mud, some of it will stick. The woole matter arises from a false statement to the effect that three of rny London 'societies— the 175th, 177th, and 190th—were failures. This was an assertion made, without any proof; I have repeatedly denied it, and given proof establishing my statements. In the case of the 175th the action which resulted in its cessa- tion from business was brought about by the prime mover in the mischief, for base purposes, which were made manifest at the member's meeting, and he was treated with the con- tempt he so richly deserved for the part he had played, the work it had accomplished is still the matter for con- gratulation which the Board of Management thonght. The 177th did not make much progress until they got rid of this very man, who had contrived to get on the Board of manage- men t; but it is now doing well, has the full complemente members, and has a balance profit over and above its liability to the members of £B7. The 190th is full, (and a " second " society started at the same place, a very likely thing if the first had failed) is working well, and has a profit balance of £209. The orighaator of the mischief has been found out, proved the false man he is, and now is ignominiously silent; but why T. and L. are retailing these lies when they must know what they are, I cannot imagine, except it be that they think to get out of their liabilities. When I describe people guilty of such conduct as this as "Noodles" I am using the most charitable description possible to apply to tlaern. I have not evaded questions, but have replied with the facts quoted above; and if any of your readers seek to verify them the secretary of the Runcorn society has all the documents, and l am sure will produce them. Their sarcastic allusion to my "generous litudertakint; " to supply Printing, *c., at my risk is in bad taste when it is borne in mind they refused to take the risk, and their bland assurance that they did not know what benefit I should derive from it, will scarcely bear corn- ' parison with their own anxiety to know what they would get outsof it. But they have already began to shift their ground, but in attacking the principles of my societies they have fallen into an error which any ordinary business-man will see through.—Yours faithfully, R B. STARR. 35, Windmill-street, Finsbury, London, W.C., July 6,1881

HIGHWAYS, PUBLIC WORKS, AND f3ANITARE COMMITTEE.

A meeting of the committee was held on the 20th ult. The reconsideration of the Vista-road was ordered to stand over to next month. It was ordered that proceedings should be taken against John Gregg, of Warringten brownware ti dealer, for non-payment of toll on the 21st lt. It was ordered that subject to an arrangement being made with Mr. Legh's agent for a proper outfall at the rear of the Congre- gational Charch, Crow-lane, that the sewering of Crow-lane, from Fairbrotherßridge to the Oak Tree Inn, and from thence along High-street to Golborne-road, be proceeded with, and that tenders be advertised for accordingly. Plans for four houses in Park-road, for Mr. Geo. Lane; house and shop in Earle-street, for Mr. T. Sandereon - two cottages in Crown-street, for Mr. Wm. Marrow; and 11 cottages in Tamworth-street and Crown-street, for Mr. Geo. Bailey, were submitted and approved. On the motion of Mr. EMMETT, seconded by Mr. FousTER, the minutes were passed. The LAW CLERK said, according to the instructions of the Committee, a summons was taken out against John Gregg for non-payment of toll. Upon the summons being served upon him he called upon him (the law clerk), and after asking come questions Mr. Gregg said he did not under- stand the law before, and if the Commissioners would with- draw the summons upon his paying the expenses he would pay the toll in future. Thereupon the summons was with- drawn, and he paid the magistrates' clerk the eest of the summons.

GAS COMiareTEE. At a meeting of the Gas and Water Committee held on the 20th ult, it was ordered that the reduction made in the, price of gas at the last Board meeting commence from the end of the present month (June). Quotations for the sup- ply of gas coals for the ensuing year, together with the results of tests, were submitted to Mr. Brierley, when it was resolved to renew the contract with Messrs. R. Evans and Co. for twelve months. An application was read from Mr. E. Worthington, Sankey-street, to be authorised as a gas and water fitter for the distrtet, and the application was sanctioned. Mr. Brierley reported that the consumptien of water for the past year averaged abont nine gallons per day for all purposes. Mr. FORsTER proposed and Mr. Estragrr seconded the adoption of the minutes, which was carried. FINANCE COMMITTEE. At a meeting of the Finance Committee held on the 20th June, accounts amounting to 245 12s 541 were examined and cheques signed for payment. The minutes were passed, on the proposition of Mr. Emma. The School Attendance Committee's minutes, which con- tained nothing of importance, were confirmed. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD AND NEWTON BROOK. A letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated Bth June, advertin to the Commissioners' letter of the 15th March last, with reference to the pollution of Newton Brook in the Newton-in-Makerfield urban sanitary district, and stating that the subject would receive the attention of the Urban Sanitary Authority. The writer was directed by the Local Government Board to inquire what steps the Authority proposed to take in the matter. The CHAIRMAN suggested that the letter should be re- ferred to the Sanitary Committee. Mr. PENNINOTON said there was now no nuisance caused by the brook. The letter was referred to the committee A COMMUNICATION. The SußVEvort said he had received a letter from the Swinton and Pendlebury Local Board asking the Commis- sioners to co-operate with them in forwarding a petition to the Education Department with a view to removing the pay- ment of school fees from the Guardians to school atten- dance committees. The latter part of the letter asked the Commissioners to co-operate with them in forming an asso- ciation of local boards. In reference to the first part of the letter be might remind the Commissioners that some three ,or four years ago, when the committee was formed, they sent a petitien to the Education Department in similar terms to the one they were now asked to send, but nothing came of it. DEATH OF MR. THOMAS STONE, OF NEWTON.-Mr. Thomas Stone, a gentleman widely known and much respected in this district, died at his residence, Newton Park, early on Friday morning. The deceased gentleman had been on a visit to Campbilltown, Mull of Cantyre, Argyle- shire. While there he was taken ill, and after a stay of a few weeks was brought home to Newton, on Wednesday evening. After his return to Newton Park he became worse, .nd died, as already stated, about ten o'clock on Friday morning. Mr. Stone was known in various parts of the csuntry as a railway and public works contractor, and he was also the owner of collieries at Downhall Green, Ashton- in-Makerfield.

At Coventry, on Tuesday, a boot and shoe manufacturer, named Nathan Osborne, was committed for trial on the charge of having wilfully caused a fire on his preraises, with intent to defraud an insurance company. The fire occurred the day after the prisoner received from the company his policy of insurance.

, A speàial meeting of the Council was held on Tuesday evening, to take into consideration the making of a contri- bution toward the maintenance, in a certified industrial school, of several boys ordered by the magistrates to be sent to such school. 'The chair was occupied by Alderman Davies (in the absence of the Mayor), and there were also resent :—Alderinen Thewlis, Burgess, Holmes, Webster, present garrison, Chandlay ; Councillors Fairclough, Monks, Greening, Brown, Dixon, Woolfall; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), and T. Longdin (borough surveyor). Alderman Wmasrmi, in moving the usual resolutions, in respect to William Hackett, Thomas Cain, James Roach, Thomas Rouse, and Aaron Gristy, said it was a very re- markable circumstance that the Council should be called upon to sanction these amounts when in reality they had no ' power to make any alteration in them. This was one of ' those forms that had to be observed.
The resolutions were seconded and adopted.

At the monthly meeting of the Council, held immediately afterwards, the Mayor (Alderman Piekmere) presiding. Besides the members above mentioned there were present Councillors Milner, Barker, Broadbent, Burgess, Litton, Greaten, Francomb, tnd Mr. J. Paterson (gas mapaget).

THE LIVERPOOL NEW WATERWORKS. • -The MAYOR said it would be interesting to the Council to know that the Mayor and Corporation of Liverpool had been so courteous as to ask the Town Clerk and himself to the laying of the first stone of the new waterworks in Wales, and they had consented to go. • Alderman HARRISON: They might have invited the whole of the Council, sir.

THE MARKET COCOA MOOSE. At the request of the Mayor, the Town Clerk read the following memorial from stall holders and others engaged in the market: "To His Worship the Mayor and the members of the Warrington Town Council. The memorial of the following stallkeepvs and other persons who make use of the markets for business purposes showeth that your memorialists have heard with feelings of deep regret that the cocoa house situate in the new market, which was opened by His Worship the Mayor about twelve months ago, is shortly to be closed, owing to circumstances of which you will probably be aware. Your memorialists are of opinion that the said cocoa house was a great boon to a large number of persons who, until it was opened, had no facilities whatever of obtaining good food and drink of a non4ntoxicant character at moderate prices with conveni- ence to themselves. Your memorialists beg, therefore, to express their strong desire that it may yet be possible by some arrangements to prevent the loss of BO beneficial an institution. A letter dated July 4th from Mr. Thomas Morris, chair- man of the British Workman Cocoa Company, Was also read. It was as follows :—" Dear Mr. Mayor, I have received the enclosed petition, which I desire to convey to you for your kind consideration. Without any comment from me, I think the petition will speak for itself." Alderman CHANDLEY said that when the Market was altered it was considered desirable if possible to embody in the scheme a banditti; that would be suitable for the pur- poses of a cocoa house, and in deference to the wish of the Council or a large number of its members a shop Was let as a cocoa house at what was called at the time a suitable rent. Some time ago the Cocoa Company presented a memorial asking the committee to reduce the rent, for they found it Impossible to make the business pay at the rent they were Paying. The committee, whilst most wishful to further tine Interests of the company, felt compelled to treat them as other applicants for a reduction in rent had been treated,and subject the premises to public competition. This was ac- cordingly done, and the Cocoa Company not bidding suffi- ciently high, the reams were let to another party. The committee would be glad to receive any suggestions from the Council for their guidance in the matter. I Councillor Fan/el:omen : What rent did they pay before? Alderman CRANDLEY : £35 per year. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH,: What has it let for this time? Alderman CHANDLET said the premises now let for £35, and the Cocoa Company had the option of taking them at that sum, but they would not do so. The Towle CLERK said the premises now let for £36. • In reply to Councillor IFairclough, Alderman CHANDLEY said the premises were subject to three months' notice. Alderman WEBSTER said the Markets Committee had made a serious mistake in the matter. The premises, it ap- peared from the statement of Alderman Chandley, were built for the purpose of a cocoa room for the convenience of the market people, and when they were put up by auction it should have been with a reservation that they were to be- applied for that purpose. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR remarked that Alderman Webster was wrong about the intentions of the Markets Committee. The shop was not erected for any particular purpose, and was let to the highest bidder. Alderman CHANDLEY confirmed the latter statement, and said the Council had passed a resolution that all stalls should be let by public auction. Councillor BROADBENT observed that the premises had been 'specially arranged for cocoa rooms, and the company on first entering into them paid what they considered an exorbitant rent, with the assurance from the Markets Committee that if they found it too much they would reduce it. [Councillor Litton : I believe you are wrong.] As time went on it was found that there was a considerable lose on the business, partly owing to the fact that the market was only open two days a week; the company, however, understood that it would be open every day. Subsequently, Mr. Thomas Morris, on behalf of the company, waited upon the committee to ask for a reduction in rent, but this the committee refused to do. Notwith- standing that the company had paid this high rent, the committee allowed them to stand in the open auction for rooms which had been built specially for A cocoa house. He thought the directors might have received more generous treatment, and .he strongly regretted that the public and frequenters of the market should be deprived, by the action of the committee, of the great advantage of being able to obtain refreshments of this kind. He hoped the committee, under the guidance of the Mayor, would he soon able to assist the Cocoa Company in obtaining suitable premises for the frequenters of the market. COOOCMOT LITTON denied that any annugement RS to reducing the rent had been entered into,Pnd said the com- mittee had clone the best for the public and the market. If the Council chose to say that a shop should be appropriated for a cocoa house, that was,a different matter. , Alderman DAVIES related minutely the circumstances of the case, and remarked that the Council was under no &Ai- cation to provide a cocoa room in the interests of the market. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH thought it desirab'e there should he a cocoa house in the market, and he had no doubt the Markets Committee would be willing to do something in the matter if the Cocoa Company would make a proper application. Councillor GREENING observed that the Coeoa Company did not take the rooms because they could not afford to lose £3O a year: It was the people's own fault that the rooms bad been elnitl 43 they had not supported them as they ought

to have done. Councillor BROADBENT said the business had been in- creasing, and especially during the last week of the com- pany's occupation. The MAYOR had considered the cocoa house in the market a great boon, and he woo sorry that the contractors could not see their way to pay what lie considered a fair rent. He did not see that the Markets Committee could offer it to the Cocoa Company at a less rent than other people would pay. If application was made to the committee they might rind some place about the market for the erection of another cocoa house, not in quite so good a situation for business purposes, and let it at a less rent. The committee might then make it in a good paying concern. Alderman CrIANDLEy : I do not desire to offer any remarks doingan not egyoenud . Io u ra mw way in extenso, but I wish to say we regret the closing of the ainsstiatutcoionnuni committee, was „ , "Irto carry out the suggestion of the Mayor. We offer he stalls to the highest bidder. Alderman DAVIES: The Markets Committee, I take it, would be qnite prepared to give accomodation for a cocoa room if a recommendation to that effect came from the Council? Alderman CHANDLEY : Certainly. COUnCillOr BROADBENT : The Cocoa Company do not wish so much to fill their pozkets as to afford the greatest possible convenience to the frequenters of the markets. (Hear, hear.) The discussion then ceased. FINANCE COMMITTEE: AUDITORS' REPORT. THE LATCHFORD DRAINAGE SCHEME.—THE WORE OF THE BOROUGH SURVEYOR. [SPE.ctAL.] No. VI. • ALEXANDRIA (Con'minim). .To the European whose feet and eyes for the first time ' wander over the Oriental scenes, Egypt affords a succession of novel and interesting sights. The universal habit of squat- ting ie.a study in itself. The ease with which they gather . up their feet, and seem always at rest in that position, is very curious. And how essential it is in a chairless, nomadic life. What would not we have given in our camping tour I through Palestine if, at lunch time, we could have com- I fortably squatted around the border of the carpet spread for 1 our entertainment! There ware we, some kneeling and 1 sitting on our heels, some lying at full length, resting on one elbow sr on both; others sitting with their knees up to • their chins; while others were -seated on big stones which they had dragged in, in despair of finding any. ease on the ' ground. .1-40 not know what I mould have given for the ' ability to squat, if only for the honour of my country, and in the interests of European grace and ease of deportment! Tne Arabs seem as if they would not disgrace themselves by letting their feet hang down. I have seen them squatting on forms six inches wide rather than endure the degredation , or lend themselves to such a stiff and awkward arrangement : of the human body. Their mode of carrying children also interested us. Sometimes quite naked and sometimes I slightly clad, the children sit astride of their father or j ,mother's shoulders, with their faces towards the head. This mode, it seems .to me, has many advantages over- ours,' although our climate might not Admit of its adoption. They had been told that morning that the Board were in a position to save at least £l5O per annum by a re-arrangement.—Mr. MAR- SHALL: No, I never said so.—Mr. FRITH called Dr. McDougall' to order, and said the committee had not said so.—Dr. McDouRALL, addreseing the Chairman, said be would like to know whether Mr.,Handley, who was speaking to the reporter for a contemporary, was prompting him not to report what he (Dr. McDougall) was saying.
