Ido not think that Mr. Handley ever made a proposition that the reporters should not report in his life.— The CHAIRMAN: As regards that I think the reporters could not very well report it. (Hear, bear, and' laughter.) —Dr. McDonciALL said be had strong reasons for objecting to the appointment of the committee. On the approach of the "silly season" they invariably had something new brought forward which did not recommend itself to any- body but the imaginative brains of certain members of the Board. It was perfectly evident to any unbiassed mind that unless they were going to " clip" their officers or abolish one altogether no such reduction as had been suggested could be made. Not a syllable had been vouchsafed to them as to why the recommendation had been made, and they were entirely left in the dark upon this part of the question' ' It would, be amusing to the public perhaps to know that they had exactly four officials in the public service of the Board and actually it took nine members to reform their . duties. They were about to attempt mending the "official pot " and it took "nine tinkers "to accomplish this object. ("Oh, oh.") Could anyone conceive of a more ludicrous recommendation than that one-half of the members of the Board should form a committee? (Laughter.)—Mr. LYON: May I ask whether it is Parliamentary for the doctor to refer to nine Other members of the Board as tinkers? (Loud laughter.)—Mr. MARSHALL (satirically): Oh, he is dignify- ing the Board now in his usual way.—Mr. WILLIAMS: lam glad I am not. a member of the "tinkering committee." (Laughter).—Dr. MCDOUGALL (laughing) : I will withdraw the word if you like.—Mr. SPEAKMAN: Which-half of the members does Dr. McDougall allude to 7—Dr. MRDouRALL expressed his opinion that they should not make com- mittees too large. They might just as well constitute the whole Board into a committee straight away. Referring to other matters he said the .Board bad been penny wise and pound foolish, and that was the reason why they were now supplicants at the feet of the Local Governmentßoard asking ' them to remit the surcharge of £l,lOO. Their officers had I been kicked about a good deal during the past seven or eight years, and he did not see any terrible objection to a corn- mittee being appointed, but he objected to so large a com- mittee as proposed, and therefore begged to move that it be , expunged.—Mr. Donsotr seconded the amendment.—Mr. LYON said Dr. McDougall had been speaking of the assump- tion that all the members of the committee would vote one way. He wished to know why the appointment of such a committee had been moved. —Mr. MARSHALL said in replying to Mr. Lyon's question be might at the same time answer a remark made by Dr. McDougall and say that as regarded imaginative minds, he (Dr. McDougall) would receive the prize for imagination if one were given. (Laughter.)—The CHAIRMAN: Come now, that is personal.—Mr. MARSHALL: It is, sir, and I know it. I am expressing my opinion of the doctor, and I have a right to do so.—The CHAIRMAN: You have no right what- ever.—Mr. MARSHALL: I don't like to make a statement and afterwards have to withdraw it. I would sooner not make any statement. (Laughter.) Mr. Marshall then explained that in letting off the contract to Mr. Cliff it had released one of their officers from a large share of his duties. There- fore it would be a waste of money to retain his services when they might possibly save £lOO to £l5O per annum. Mr. DOBSON thought the re-arrangement a very important matter, and that being near the annual election it would be well to leave the question for the consideration of the new Board.—Dr. McDougall's amendment was bet, and the original motion was carried. CANAL BOATS AND BOSEITAL COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee, which were passed on the motion of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. LYON, stated that a draft of the grant of land on the Weston-road, ant that a tracing of the proposed hospital had been considered.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated the 2nd inst., adverting to the Commissioners' letter of the 10th April, and enquiring whether they were now in a position to sabmit to them plans of the hospital which they proposed to erect for the treatment ef cases of infectious disease occurring within the district.—lt was decided that a letter be sent to the Local Government Board, stating that plans of the proposed hospital had been approved of by the Board and would be forwarded in the coarse of a few days.—The offer of Mr. G. Clarke as to the roller was accepted. THE LODGING-HOUSE BYE-LAWS. It was resolved on the proposition of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. LIMN. that the usual course te adopted under the 184 section of the Public Health Act, to make the hytslaws adopted by the Commissioners as to common lodgings, legal. THE NEW CANAL BOATS' ACT. Dr. MCDOUGALL referred to the importance of something being done by the Board as to watching the progress of the Amended Canal Boats' Act. The old act had caused the ratepayers to provide education facilities for a great number ' of children, and he hoped the new measure would not further increase their responsibilities in this respect.—Mr. HANDLEY offered the Board a brief explanation of the provisions of the new measure. It provided for an annual -inspection of the boats; that each vessel's certificate should be produced once a year and endorsed,; and that the in- spector should have the power to enter boats at any reason- able time during the night; and be believed the provision as to the education of boat children, would relieve the Board to a considerable extent as to their present obligations. Boat people would have to produce to the inspector the child's pass-book, showing what standard it had passed, and until it had passed a certain standard, it would not he permitted to lice on a vessel—lt was agreed that the Bill should be fully considered at an early meeting. DR. MCDOUGALL AND THE FIRE BRIGADE stratum-ern:tarn The General Purposes Committee's minutes were passed, on the proposition of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. J. J. SpEARMAN.—Dr. McDoroALL complained that an account of 9s. 6d, for services said to have been rendered by the Fire Brigade at Whitsuntide, in watering the fair ground, was not in the accounts recommended for payment by the committee. He wished for information on this as the Superintendent of the Fire Brigade had resigned in conse- quence-of it not having been forwarded for payment.—Mr. NORMAN said the committee thought it hardly fair th .t the superintendent should make a special charge for such work. Other members considered the action of the superin- tendent marked by much precipitancy, unless it was under- stood that he was not a servant of the Board. THE FINANCES: THE RESIGNATIONS. The minutes of the Finance committee reported that Mr. J. J.Speakman had been appointed chairman. The total receipts for June had been £232 39. Pd.—Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said he was glad the Board was in its old financial position.—Mr. MARSHALL: What is the balance in the bank ?—Mr. SHAW: Don't ask that. (Laughter.)—Mr. NORMAN seconded the motion.—Mr. HANDLEY said if the Board had resumed its old and good financial position he should like to know when the change took place. He believed it was a fact that in order to work the business a bill amounting to something like £350 had been withheld; and also that there was another for 9s. ed. which had not been paid. (Laughter.)—Mr. NORMAN said he had not heard of any such bill.—Mr. HANDLEY: I did not ask Mr. Norman, but the Chairman of the committee.-- Mr. SHAW : The question will not bear investigation from beginning to end. I don't like to discuss it. (Loud Laughter) The minutes were then adopted. Mr. NORMAN moved that as Messrs. Frith, Handley, Mar- shall and Meadowcroft had resigned their position as mem- bers of the Finance Committee, Messrs. P. Speakman, G. S. Hazleburst and J. Dobson be added to the committee. The motion was seconded by Mr. J.. 1, SPEAKMAN and carried.— , Mr. HANDLEY: Of course we are to understand that the secretary will seed us the usual notices of meetings, for I have been informed that I have not resigned 7—The CHAIR. MAN: You have resignecl.—Mr. HANDLEY: I am informed not, therefore I am entitled to the usual notices.—Mr. MAR.- SHALL: Has the secretary got the written resignations? (Laughter.)—Mr. NORMAN: You are not on the committee

at all, whether or not.—(Latighter)—Mr. Meruomur, That is too personal. (Loud Laughter.) I am asking a question and what &f r. Norman says has nothing to do with my ques- tion.—The CHAIRMAN:. We must really get on with the business. We are wastingthe whole morning.—Mr. Man- suata. : I have asked for copies of the resignations.—The CHAIRMAN : Give notice for them.—Mr. SHAW: There can be no such resignations as the members ef the Finance Com- mittee gave at this Board. They know themselves who have resigned. . . _

• Mr. MARSHALL (very excitedly): You are ambitious enough for the ticket. You want it, do you. I have As much right to it as you have. (Sensation.) • Dr. McDorroarz (warmly): You have insulted the chair, sir.

MR. a. I. SPEAKMAN ON THE OAS QUESTION. Mr. .1. SPEAKMA.N moved, in accordance with previous notice, that :Messrs. T. Norman, James Dobson, S. Taylor, P. Speakman, J. J. Speakman and the Chairman be ap- pointed a committee to take into consideration the question of the price of gas charged by the Runcorn .Gas Company to the I3oard.—Mr. HANDLEY thought the reasons for appoint- ing such a committee ought to be given before the constitu- tion of it was proceded with.—Mr. SHAW was of the same opinion. He added that if the Gas Company liked, they might put Is. per 1,000 feet on the price of the gas.—Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN said it was a well known fact that the Gas Company oculd not pay a dividend of more than ten per cent, and it was for the committee to look into the matter and see if the dividend was really paid as it ought to be. (A laugh.) He found that Runcorn was in a pretty good position as to the price of gas, though there were other towns which were lower.—Mr. Darn : Will you kindly name them ?—Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN : Not at present.—Mr. FRITH said it was hardly fair to make such an assertion without naming the towns.— Mr. SHAW was of opinion that the ground mentioned by Mr. Speakman was a good one. If the company were making more than the ten per cent., the Commissioners had a right to a reduction.—Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN thought the proposed committee would in course of time bring something before the Board which would be worth recording on the minutes.— Mr. MARSHALL, during the number of years he had been a memoer of the Board, had always thought the Commis- sioners paid a high price for gas. However, he might state —if he might be allowed to make a remark in the nature ef a quotation—that be had no desire to be one of the a tinkerers" on the committee.—Mr. FRITH said that if there was one thing which he valued more than another it was consistency, either in a man or a public body. Now, at the last meeting of the Commissioners, at which Mr. J. J. Speakman was presetrt, they passed a resolution thanking the Gas Company for reducing the price of gas. Mr. Speak- man was one of the Commissioners present at that meeting, and the motion was paseed unanimously, and that gentleman must have voted for it. The Commissioners knew very well I that the reduction was granted by the company without application having been made for it by the Board. Since he first came to Runcorn—now geeting on for twenty years— the Gas Company had endeavoured to do the best they could not only for themselves but for the consumers generally.. As a very old member of the Gas Association, he could confidently say that he looked with pride upon the price which had been charged for the ghs supplied to the town. The Gas Company had never paid more than ten per cent.—Mr. SPEAKMAN withdrew his motion, and inti- mated that he would bring forward a somewhat more com- prehensive one in regard to the question at the adjourned meeting.

Mr.lVassiteLL: Yes, I know I have, because I have been insulted. But don't you say anything, because I shall deal with you. Dr. McDouGALL (defiantly, and leaning over the table to the speaker in a rather threatening attitude) : What! you will deal with mei Do you think lam going to be— Mr. MARSHALL: Yes, I will make you answer some day. Dr. McDotromm moved that the ex-Chairman do not re- present the Board at the gaming ceremony of laying the foundation stone of the Vrynwy embankment. , Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN seconded the motion.

This motion was allowed to drop, and a further resolution that the Secretary be allowed a day's absence to attend the ceremony, was carried on the proposition of Mr. FRITH, seconded by Mr. MARSHALL. This concluded the proceedings, which lasted about three hours and a half.
Mr. W. H. LimaitEn, clerk to the Board, has received the following (copy) letter:—

"Town Clerk's Office, Dale-street, Liverpool, sth July, 1881 I Dear consequence of a cometumoation from your Chairman, I beg to inform you that thb invitations to Chairmen of Commissioners and other pubic bodies for th• 14th inst., were issued to them in their official capaolty. and were regarded as beirig accepted by them in that capacity: so that, in the event of a change in that office, the invitation would pass on to his successor. The invitations to the ' cl.rks ' were intended for the Law Clerks, and not fos the secretary, in 'Cases where there is a Law Clerk.—Yours truly, _ _
J. RIMIER. W. IL Musket., Eq., solicitor, Law Clerk to the Runcorn Improvement Commisskners, Runcorn."

div.head: NUISANCE.
div.p: A NUISANCE.

Mr. DOBSON drew attention to a nuisance caused by a de- fective sewer in Pcnnington's-row.—Mr. NORMAN was of opinion that such matters should be attended to by the In- spector of Nuisances. It was a very unpleasant thing for members of the Board to have to bring forward reports of nuisances.'

div.head: ADJOURNED I%SEETING.
div.p: ADJOURNED I%SEETING.
On the motion of Mr. HALEY, seconded by Mr. MAR- KT/am, it jives decided that an adjourned meeting of the 'Board be held pn the 11th inst., to consider .the position of _ .
, the Board in reference to Mr. Beasley and Waterloo House.

div.head: TEE NEXT MONTHLY MEETING.
div.p: TEE NEXT MONTHLY MEETING.

WHS decided that the next monthly meeting be held on Wednesday, the 3rd August, in consequence of the Board day being a Bank Holiday. WHO SHALL HAVE THE SPOILS ?-A LIVELY SCENE. Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN said he understood that two tickets had been sent by the Mayor and Corporation of Liver- pool inviting the Chairman and Clerk to the laying of the foundation stone of the Vrynwy works on the 14th inst., and be wished to kaow in whose bands they now were. The CHAtaistax : I heard on Friday night that the tickets

had been sect. Mr. MARSHALL : I rise to order. Is this extraordinary business ? It is not ordinary business, and it must, there- fore, be extraordinary. Mr. Speakman ought to give notice of motion before being permitted to enter upon such a question. The CHAIRMAN: I heard on Friday that an invitation had been given, and I certainly took it to mean the Chairman and the Law-Clerk, whoever they might be at the time the ceremony of stone laying took place. The ipvitation does not say Mr. Marshall or Mr. Steele, but the Chairman and Clerk of the Board. Mr. MARSHALL remarked that he was prepared to answer for anything he had done in the matter. Dr. McDorcau. considered that they were. fully entitled

to have information upon such a matter. All communica- tions ought to come before the Board. In the case then being discussed, the invitation from the Corporation of Liverpool had not been submitted to the Board. Of course if the tickets had been sent to the individuals who held them, in their private capacity, then tile question was alto- gether altered. Undoubtedly the invitations were meant for the gentleman who might be chairman of the Board at the time the foundation stone laying took place, and the one who was acting as clerk. He should like to know whether the invitations had been accepted, and if so, whether on official note paper. The SECRETARY said he had received a circular signed by the Mayor of Liverpool, which he had accepted en his own behalf. The Secretary-produced the circular, which the Chairman proceeded to read. Before he had finished Mr. MARSHALL rose to order, and said that according to the 3rd standing order of the Board they had no power to discuss the question at that meeting. He was sorry to dis- pute the ruling of the Chairman, but it' was extraordinary business. He really must ask the Chairman to abide by the standing orders. The CHAIRMAN proceeded with the reading of the letter of invitation, which in effect invited the "Clerk of the Lc cal Board of Runcorn" to attend the ceremony of laying the foundation stone. Dr. McDotroact : Is ther%any reply to that? The SECRETARY : I accepted the invitation en my own behalf. Dr.McDoccau:: You were quite out of order in doing so. Mr. HANDLEY quothfg from the Act of Parliament, said, 'the expression Clerk shall mean the Clerk to the Commis- sioners, and shall include the word Secretary." The LAW CLERK: That is where there is simply a sec- retary. Mr. HANDLEY : Mr. Linaker is not clerk to the Commis-

-- goners, but the Law Clerk. Dr, MCDOUGALL said the time of the secretary was the lb od'' s and in accepting the invitation without their sanc- tion he had done wrong. Mr.!Furrit rose to order, and said it was undignified on tilt part of the Board to discuss the question' because it would be sure to get to the ears of the Liverpool Corporation. D. McDounett said if the thing had been done in a straightforward manner he should not have said a syllable about it. It was clearly the duty of the secretary to have brought the letter before the Board. With respect to the in- vitation now in the hands of the late Chairman, it was a question of honour. The ex-Chairman must have known when he received the letter that his office would expire within a few days after he received it. Mr. P. SPEARMAN rose to order, and said bethought the whole discussion was proceeding irregularly. Dr. McDoroart, : We are not. It is an official communi- cation. The LAW CLERK stated that although he did not care two straws about the tickets they were no doubt intended for himself and the present chairman. At this point the Board room was a scene of great dis- order, as many as six members being on their feet together. When the uproar had somewhat subsided, Mr. MARSHALL moved that the standing orders of the Board he abided by. Mr. SPEAKMAN seconded the motion. The CHAIRMAN remarked that there was no proposi- tion before the Board, as Dr. McDougall had possegsion of the floor. Mr. MARSHAL (excitedly): If that is the case any one can rule as he likes. Dr. McDOuOILL would not move a vote of censure on the secretary, but he hoped it would be a warning to him in the future to submit all communications to the Board. He should conclude his remarks with a motion that unless the ex- chairman handed the ticket to his successor— Mr. MARSHALL (warmly): It is not within your province to interfere in the matter. , Dr. MCDOTGALL : But it is. Mr. MARSHALL: I ant not going to be insulted by either , Dr. McDougall or yourself, Mr. Chairman, in this matter. We have had too much of that sort of work. If you had come to me fairly and honourably, then I would have answered all questions, but I shall not after this skulking hole-and-corner work. The LAW CLERK said he matter was one easily to be settled. They had to consider what was the wish of the . Corporation of Liverpool. 3 Dr. MCDOUGALL: They mean the Chairman for the time being and the Clerk. Mr. MARSHALL: lam not going to be insulted, and then : be forced to knuckle under. We have had too much of that . during the past year from members of the Board. . Mr. HANDLF,I: I submit that with regard to the invita- tion addressed to the " Clerk " it was intended for the • secretary. . Mr. P. SPEAKMAN: Mr. Linaker says it was for him. 1 The Lim CLERIC: No. I don't; and I tell you distinctly . that I don't care to go. Mr. HANDLEY: It is a personal matter whether Mr. Mar- shall gives up the ticket to his successor. The CHAIRMAN (excitedly) : I object to that remark very strongly. It is not a personal matter, and this is a libel on the whole Board. Mr. HANDLEY: You mistake my meaning, Dr. Steele. The CHAIRMAN: I hope I do. Mr. HANDLEY explained that his meaning was that whether Mr. Marshall gave up or retained the ticket was a matter concerning only himself. „ Mr. MARSHALL, addressing the chair, asked why Dr. Steele had sant a message to him through the Clerk from a caucus meeting. Was there anything honourable or dignified in a course like that? No doubt there had been an intention to insult him, but he was not there to be insulted or to Embmit to such hole-and-corner and selfish work. The CHAIRMAN : You are perfectly right. It is selfish I work, no doubt. Did you behave as a gentleman ?

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
Moikmay.—Before Mr: S. B. Chadwick (chairman) and Mr.
C. W. Hazlehurst.

THE YOUNG HUSBAND AND HIS FATHER-IN-LAW.—Geo Gandy. a respectable-hsoking elderly man, was summoned for having, on the 30th ult., assaulted George Betley Shaw, a young man, formerly assistant clerk to Mr. Danby, clerk to the Widnes School Board.—Complainant said defendant was his father-in-law. On the 30th ult. he was in the Bridge Hotel, Ashridge-street, talking to the barmaid, when defen- dant entered the house, seized him by the throat, pulled him away from the young lady, and swore what he would do to him. Defendant acted so roughly that he caused him to be- come black in the face, and unable to speak for a few minutes. His (Shaw's) wife followed her father into the house, and had it not been for her interference Gandy would have proceeded to further extremities.—ln cross-examina- tion, complainant said he should have been married to defendant's daughter three years on the sth August. He was now living with his mother, and out of work. He did not know where his wife was living: Her father had taken her away from him four or five times. He had no house of his own. He could not answer a question as to where he spent most of his time. He certainly went to the Bridge Inn occasionally, but he denied that he spent the greater part of his time there. 'Whilst he 'had been out of work he had, fond his wife and family food and shelter. He would swear he had never as- saulted his wife.—Sambel Tomlinson, Duke's Field, gave corroborative evidence.—Mr. Linaker, for the defence, ex- pressed his regret that he could not call his client. Defen- dant had during the whole of his married life ill-treated and abused hia wife. On the Thursday named, defendant met his daughter walking on Portland-street, and he aaked her where she was going. She said she did not know. Her bus- hand had abused her, and she had no home for herself or , children. He retnarlced to her, "I wonder whether he's at Heye's public-house ?" He then went to Heyes's, and SAW complainant there. Defendant admitted that he took hold of Shaw, shook him, and told him that if it were not for the law he would do something for him. Complainant. had brought this on by the manner in which he had treated his wife; and he appealed to the Bench as to whether they did not consider that, under the circumstances, the old man was not justified in interfering. He proposed to call his daughter, to prove that she had been ill-treated, but the magistrates ruled that she could not give evidence against her husband.—The Chairman said the magistrates felt that there was no doubt that defendant had been provoked, but they could not shut their eyes to the fact that an assault had been committed. Defendant would be bound over, him- self in £lO and two in £5 to keep the peace for six months. Complainant asked that he might be allowed the costs of his witnesses, but the Bench declined to grant them. After the proceedings had terminated, complainant returned into court and said the defendant's family were doing all they could to damage his character, and their conduct rendered it almost impossible for him to get another situation. The other day one of the defendant's relatives told him to his face that he was a thief and a robber, and when they would say such things to him, he was at a loss to know what they would say of him behind his back.—The magistrates advised him to consult a solicitor. NEGLECTING TO MAINTAIN A MOTHER.—WOL Stanley, whose wife appeared for him, *as summoned, at the in- stance of Mr. Houghton, collector to the Runcorn Board of Guatdians, for neglecting to contribute to the support of his mother.—Mr. Houghton said that on the 17th January defen- dant was ordered by the Bench to contribute Is. per week, and to pay 13s. 61. costs. He had not paid a penny, and now there was £1 16s. 6d. owing.—Defendant's wife said he WAS out of work, and had 'no home.—A distress warrant was ordered to be issued for the amount owing and the costs. A Womatior's QUARREL.—A young, man named Enoch Sefton was charged with a violent assault on a well-dressed man named Edward Creaney,Complainant said at half- past six o'clock on the morning of the 27th ult., as he was at work, defendant, who was employed at the same place, came up to him and asked him about some money which he alleged complainant owed him. He told him the cash was not due to him, on which defendant called him several bad names, ran at him, and gave him a violent blow in the face, kaock- ing him down. Whilst on the ground defendant struck him several times, and he was only rescued by several of the workmen. Defendant then pursued him again, and during the row which followed complainant was rather badly hurt by some timber. Defendant throttled him so savagely that for some days he had not been able to swallow any solid food. or to work.—ln cross-examination, complainant said defen- dant asked him what he had done with the 15s. he had received on his account frorri Astmoor tanyard, as he had only had 10s. of it. He told defendant that he did not owe him 15s.—In defence, Sefton said complainant rally owed him the money, and he went to him about it, and told him that though he had got £5 15s. subscribed to send to the Land League, be was not going to make it £6 with his ss. Complainant then hit him in the face with his fist, and fol- lowed him some distance, after which a fight took place. He (defendant) only acted in self-defence; and he really ought to have summoned complainant.—The case was ad- journed for a fortnight in order that witnesses might be called OR each side. •

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. IV. N. Heald, and Mr. H. S. Hall.

LIVELY FEMALES. - Margaret Taylor. and Mary Ann Kegan were summoned for fighting in Walter-street, on the Sth inst. P.C. Stott proved the case, and each defendant was ordered to find sureties to keep the peace for six months. —Mrs. Kogan then charged Mrs. Taylor with assaulting her. She stated that the defendant struck her several times without any provocation.—The summons was dismissed. t.-;

AN UNHAPPY MARRIAGE. James Houghton was sum- moned for 'assaulting his wife Harriet. Mr. Swift, senior, appeared on behalf of complainant, and said that the per- sons in the case bad been married about thirteen months. I Mrs.Houcthtou made the acquaintance of her present husband whilst he lodged at her house. At that time he conducted himself very well, and on Sunday invariably went to church in the morning, and spent the rest of the ilayln reading the British Workman, and books of an edifying character. Probably he was induced to propose marriage to her owing to his knowledge that she had some furniture. During the year and ten months they had been married, defendant had rendered the life of his wife perfectly miserable and intoler- able by his threats and violence. In October last she parted from him fora brief time. On the sth ult., defendant was drinking all day, and when he got up on the following morning he asked her to find him some money for drink, but she refused. He abused her and then went out and took a considerable quantity of liquor. On his return in the afternoon, he struck her and caused her to fall. Defendant had rendered it nearly impossible for his wife to go back to him. Since the quarrel he had tried to dis- pose of some of the furniture. Complainant and her wit- nesses gave evidenee in support of 'this statement.—Mr. Husband, who defended, said the complainant had irritated the defendant to strike her, so that she might get a judicial separation. In support of this he called a woman named Charlotte Hodgkins, who said that immediately after the assault complainant came up to her and said, "He has just done what I wanted him to do."—The magistrates were of opinion that an assault had been committed, and ordered defendant to be bound, himself in £5O and two other sure- ties, to keep the peace six months. THE DRINK AGAIN.--Mary Ann Foy, a young married woman, was charged, on remand, with stealing lilbs. of bacon and a pillowslip, the property a Henry Reading, of 59, James-street. On the 29th ult. there was a child's funeral at prosecutor's house, and prisoner was called in to render assistance,. After she had gone the things were missed. Prosecutor's wife went to the prisoner's house, and charged her with stealing the things, and she admitted the theft. In defence, she said she "had had a drop of drink." It was stated that the woman had previously borne a good character.—The,,Bench said they would take this into con- sideration, and as the prisoner had already been in custody a week, would only sentence her to pay one guinea, includ- ing costs, in default of which she would be sent to gaol 14 days. THE CHARGE OF UNLAWFULLY WOUNDING. Kate Dogherty was brought up on remand, charged with unlaw- fully wounding Margaret Bell, widow, of Grenfel-street, under circumstances which have been fully reported io the Examiner. The charge was now altered to one 6! common assault, as Dr. Cooper had been unable-1., find any marks of violence upon complainant, such as was supposed she would have had if the injuries she had received had been of 80 violent a nature as she represented. Ellen Whitfield, and a neighbour named Ann Murphy gave evidence in support of complainant's statement up to a certain point, br,t they were unable to speak to seeing the prisoner kick her --On being ; charged, Dogherty admitted striking Bell, but d. uied kick-

lag her.—Fined 20s. and costs, and, in default of payment, to be sent to gaol 14 days. ALLEGED SERIOUS ASSAULT BY Two BROTHERS.—John Grady, and Thomas Grady, two brothers, Irishmen were charged with unlawfully wounding John Doyle, who had surrendered on a, warrant which had been taken out against them. Complainant, who lives at Simm's Cross, appeared with his head bandaged, and said that on Saturday night, , about twenty minutes past eleven o'clock, he was standing ' at his own door in Wareing-street, talking with a young I woman, when the two prisoners and another brother came up. They asked hi ni if a man named Kearns lived there, but before he could reply they said "I believe you are the one that we want." They knocked him down, kicked him whilst he was upon the pound, and "dropped a brick on him." He was so badly hurt that he had since been attended , by a doctor and been unable to follow his work. Prisoners were remanded until Friday, in order that an effort might be made to apprehend the third man.

div.head: /VIDNES WAT kRWORKS OFFICIAL INSPECTION.
div.p: /VIDNES WAT kRWORKS OFFICIAL INSPECTION.

On Tuesday, the members of the Widnes Local Board paid a visit to the various waterworks in their possession. The weather was of a very sultry characteri the thermometer being about 100 degrees in the sun. The gentlemen who formed the party mustered at the Board-room, at two o'clock, and took tfleir seats in a first-class wagonnette, drawn by a splendid four-horse-team, under the personal superintendence of Mr. James W. R. Fowler, of the Central Hotel, Widnes. The gentlemen present were Messrs. Eustace Carey, chair- man of the General Purposes and Parliamentary Committee; Holbrook Gaskell, Junr., J.P., Thomas Handley, Benjamin Brown, Dr. O'Keeffe, W. H. Kershaw, S. Sadler, D. Foster, Thomas Beasley (law . clerk), T. Higginson (surveyor), R. Roberts (engineer), E. Timmins (contractor), Dr. Cooper (medical officer of health), J. Dickson (inspector of nuisances), and the representatives of the press. The party proceeded through Appleton, Hough Green, and Upton, to Stock's-well. The scenery along the route was of a beautiful description, and a stranger would never imagine that within such a comparatively short distance of the smoky and chemically polluted atmosphere of Widnes there were so many pleasant lanes and nooks "With seats beneath the shade, >l' talking age and whispering lovers made."
Hand

The scent of the newly mown hay came fragrantly upon the breeze, which was a pleasant relief to the great heat. At Stocks Well the company left the conveyance, and inspected the two massive engines, named the " Virginia " and ths "Mary," eachoof 50 horse power. The former was named i after the wife of Mr. John Knight, who was chairman of _ .

the Gas and Water Committee a—t the time the waterworks were opened. The " Mary " was so calltd after the wife of Mr. McClellan, who was at the time chairman of the Board. The locality took its name from a spring which used to flow naturally on the surface, and ran through a small bleachworks erected on the adjoining land. The liquid was'a magnificent stream of pure water, which was always at the same temperature, showing it came from a great depth. The Board purchased the adjoining land, and constructed a well which•drained the natural spring. One evening, when they bad reached the depth of 60 feet, the workmen left their barrows and implements at the spot, and on coming to their labour in the morning they found the force of water had sent out "the bottom of the well," and their barrows were seen floatiug on the water which was level with the surface, and running away at the rate of a thou- sand gallons per day. Up to the end of August, 1808, the well constructed under such difficulties continued to be the source of the water supply of Widnes. A shaft is now be- ing sunk to 350 feet, and a depth of about 200 feet has been already reached. The party next drove on to the magnificent works at Netherley, where there are three wells, two of which are a hundred feet deep and one of thirty feet. Pumping is going on night and day at the intermediate well, with a very powerful pump, which lifts about 1,000,000 gallons in 24 hours. During the time,the members of the Board were on the spot, the pump was going at a speed calculated to raise 750,000 gallons in a day. Tbe chief well has a 24 inch boring, down to a depth of 300 feet. The shallow well has a small ex- perimental boring with a depth of nearly 600 feet. The whole of these borings and wells, yield water to the amount of 1,500,000 gallons per day. The engine over the in- termediate well is of 100 horse-power, with 14 inch open-

..-...- - . , pumps ; and there is also a horizontal force-pump dis- charging to the main reservoir at Pe x Hill. The new buildings at these works are approaching completion, and new machinery and boilers are being put down, which will be in working order in the course of a few months. The architectural style of the buildings is semi-gothic. The main building consists of an engine and boiler-house, and eoal stores. There are also some very pretty and com- modious cottages, the architecture of which harminses with the rest of the main structure. One of the conditions on which the Local Board bought the land was that the buildings they erected should be of such a kind that they would be in keeping with the resi- dential property in the surrounding neighbourhood, which accounts for the exceedingly ornamental appearance of the fabric which would not appear greatly out of place even in Queen's-road, Liverpool. A good effect is given by the use of grey bricks and red brick terra-cotta dressings, wkich are of excellent quality, and supplied by Edwards, of Buabon. The pumping machinery has been made by Messrs. Rebert Daglish and Co., of St. Helens, and is of a very powerful character. Messrs. Collins and Sons are the contractors for the buildings, and Mr. C. 0. Ellison, of Liverpool, the architect. The clerk of works is Mr. Wm Hodgkinson. All the wells belonging to the Widnes Board have been sunk by Mr. Timmins, whose work is so well known throughout the district. The chimney of the engine hours is 120 feet high, and is finished in the style of a campanile, so that it has a very striking appearance, and is a conspicuous object for miles around. At the time of the visit two flags floated from the lattice work. The total cost of the buildings and taachinery is about £lO,OOO. The four cottages which adjoin the .main buildings are occupied by the engine drivers and stokers. The company next drove on to Little Woolton, where a capital knife and fork tea was provided at the Bowling Green Hotel, by thief Misses Roberts. The members after- wards visited the Belle Vale-artesian well, which is about 35 feet deep, with a trial boring down to 500 feet. The overflow water runs down to the Netherley pumping station at the rate of 50,000 gallons per day; and we understand that even five times a greater yield can bo. obtained. The ride home was anything but a pleasant affair, as it took place in the midst of one of the severest thunderstorms which has visited the district for years. The company reached Widnes about a quarter-past nine, heartily thankful that they had managed to escape a thorough drenching owing to the wagonnette being covered. A multitude of sad , experiences are conveyed in the simple statement that it was not enclosed at the sides.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly-meeting was held on Thursday. Mr. T. Sutton-Timmis presided, and there were also present—the Revs. G. Holloway, James Clarke, Messrs. John Brock, R. Holden Davis, H. Wade Deacon, Dr. O'Keeffe, and Robert Shaw.—The report of the District Education Committee showed that during June the number of cases summoned before them had been 73, of whom 66 were for contraven- tion of the Education Act, and seven applications for pay- ment of fees. Fees were recommended to be paid in seven cases. There had been eight prosecutions, an equal nuntber of convictions, and one had been sent to an industrial school. It was recommended that Mr. William Hartland be appointed a member of the District Education Committee, in the place of Mr. R. Holden Davis, resigned. The report was adopted, —The report of the School Management Committee recom- mended that Mr. Holden Davis be appointed a member of the committee in place of Mr. Martin Taylor ; that schedule C, regulating the salaries of teachers, be rescinded, and one which was submitted substituted. A discussion took place upon the table, after 'which Mr. Holloway adopted the suggestion of the Chairman, that it be re- ferred back to the committee for re-consideration.— The Sites and Building Committee reported that the floor lof the infants' class room at West Bank had taken fire through an accident, and damage to the extent of £3O 10s. had been done. The agent of the insurance company visited the school, and gave instructions for the damage to be repaired at once. The Committee obtained an estimate, and recommended that the tender of Messrs. Roberts Bros., dated June 28th, he accepted for completing the work for the sum of £3O 10s.—The CHAIRMAN said it must be very eatisfactory to the Board to know that the school was Insured with a liberal office, who made no hesitation about paying the claimwhich had had to be made upon them.— The Crontx read the 011 owing communication addressed to the Chairman:—" Property Owners' and Ratepayers' Asso- ciation, Widnes, June 25th, 1881. , Sir,—At a meeting of I this association, held on the 22nd inst., it was unanimously I resolved that a letter be sent to you asking your serious ! consideration (considering the present state of trade in , Widnes, and the School Board rates'; beimr so high) ' as to the possibility of reducing the salary of Mr. Danbn the clerk, from £3OO to £2OO per year.—Yours truly, GEORGIA ATKIN FORSTER, secretary."—The CRAIrtsfAN said the letter had been addressed to him as chaitman, and, as a matter of coarse, he had laid it before the Board.—Mr I . SHAw moved that the writer of the letter be asked to IsY before the Board the particulars upon which the statements in the letter were based.—The CHAIRMAN asked Mr. Shaw I if he thought it was worth while to get into a controversy iwith the writer of the letter. He (the speaker) did not think it was desirable. The letter all pointed to Mr. Denby. —Mr. BROCK said that, if necessary, he would propose en amendment to the effect that the letter lie upon the table.— The CHAIRMAN: The motion has not been seconded (Laughter.) Mr. TIMMIS went on to say that he considered the gentlemen constituting the Ratepayers' Association I should bear in mind what the Board had done, and that the , expenses had to be divided over the various schools of the district.—The matter dropped, and the proceedings termi- nated.

Out, readers will be glad to hear that these are the largest returns for several years. The trade of the port is evidently in a prosperous condition.

This Company has been formed for, amongst other purposes, the purpose of working, letting on hire, and selling telephones. and also of acquiring and taking over the business, assets, plant, sto.ik-in-traie, goodwill, and liabilities of the Lancashire Tele- phonic ExChange, Limited. The terms of purchase have been arranged, and are embodied in an agreement dated the 25th day of May, 1881, as varied by an agreement dated the 23rd day of June. 1881, the consideration for such purchase being £lO,OOO in cash, £50,000 in fully paid-up shares, and a further £50,000 either in cash or in fully paid-up shares; at the option of this Company. This Company has been promoted and established by shareholders in the Lancashire Telephonic Exchange Limited, representing substantially all the shareholders in that Company, and the promoters themselves fixed the terms of the purchase before the present Company was incorporated. The liabilities of the Lancashire Telephonic Exchange Limited do not exceed £lO,OOO. The United Telephone Company has granted to this Com- pany a license for the use of all its patents in the counties of Lancashire and Cheshire, the south-east part of Westmorland, the six northern counties-of Wales, and the Isle of Man, in con- sideration of £50,000 in cash and £5O 000 in fully paid up shares, and an- annual royalty of £2 per instrument. The conditions upon which such license has been granted are embodied in the before-men- tioned agreement, dated the 25th day of May, 1881, and under such agreement this Company has become the sole licensee for the Bell, Edison, Crossley, and othor patents, the property of the United Company, and-also foi all other patents which the United Company shall hereafter acquire. The formation of the Consolidated Telephone Construction •and Maintenance Company, Limited, has practically placed all telephone interests and patents under the control of the United Telephone Company, Limited. . The Lancashire Telephone T. --bane, Limited, was inc .1110- rated in August, Ism and ha on worked as a private Corn- pany by a few individuals for i., at twenty months. In the ! face of many difficulties incidet- to a new undertaking, it has created a business with a gross , ontal (including contracts in hand) of £22,000 per annum, and is is now thought that the , business can be much better develops. hy extending its pro- prietary, and more especially loy inviting the subscribers to the Company's Exchanges and renters of private wires and instru- ments to become intertsted in the success of the undertaking. The number of subscribers to the Manchester and Liverpool Exchanges already exceeds 880, and is increasing weekly. Exchanges are being established in Barrow, Preston, Black- burn, Bolton, Oldham, and other towns. Toe Postmaster-General has offered this Company licenses for the working of Exchanges in all the -important towns in the above-mentioned districts, upon terms identical with those agreed to by the National Telephone Cempany, Limited, and which terms fully appear in a letter dated the 4th June, 1881, written on behalf of the Postmaster-General to Ur. G. B. Dew- hurst, the Chairman of this Company. and in the print of the agreement between the Postmaster-General and the National Telephone Company, Limited, referred to in such letter. 1 Applications tor shares should be made upon the form which can be obtained from the Company's secretary or bankers, and: forwarded to the bankers of the Company, together with the amount payable on application. If no allotment is made, the deposit will be returned without deduction, and, where the number of shares allotted is less than the number applied for, the surplus will be credited in reduction of the amount payable on allotment. • The agt cements above referred to, as dated the 25th day of May, 1881, and the 23r3 day of June, 1881, are made between the United Telephone Company, Limited, of the first part, the Lancashire Telephonic. Exchange; Limited, of the second part, arid this Company of the third part; and such agreemeria, and the said letter of the 4th June,llBBl, from the Post- master-General to Mr. G. B. Dewhurst, and the print of the agreement between the -Postmaster-General and tne National Telephone Company Limited, referred to in such latter, and also the memorandum and articles of association, may be in- spected at the offices of the Comapny's solicitors. The Directors are advised that the before-mentioned agree- ments are the only contracts; the date and parties to which , are required by section 38 of the Company's Act, 1867, to be specified; but, to prevent any question, they draw special attention to the fact that all current contracts entered into by the Lancashire Telephonic Exchange Limited, whether with customers, manufacturers, or employes of that Company, or with property owners and 'others, relative to the premises occupied. and the way leaves and easements acquired or exercised by that Company, or otherwise howsoever, have been taken over by this Company. All anon, ations for shares will be received and allotments made on the footing of no future question being raised by reason of the omission to sp-cify in this prospectus the dates • and names of the parties to such contracts. Dated the Ist day of July, 1881.

TELEPHONE INFRINOEMENTS.—The DIRECTORS of the UNITED TAILEPHONE COMPANY (LIMITED) have requested their licensees and Representatives, The Direc- tors of the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephonic Exchange Com- pany (Limited) to give the following otioe ' TUE UNITED TELEPHONE COMPANY are the Owners of all the patent rights in this country granted to Professor Alex- ander (*reliant Bell and Mr. Thomas Alva Edison. relating to the original Magneto Telephone and the Carbon Transmitter. All persons are CAUTIONED against manufacturing; ielling, supplying, or using any of these lash uments, except under the license of the CI impany. THE UNITED TELEPHONE COMPANY have been advised by eminent counsel that all forms of transmitter in which carbon is used in a free or powdered form, as for instance in the transmitters usually known as Moseley or Runnings, and that all the so-called microphone transmitters, including those known as the Crossley and the Gower Bell, are infringements of Mr. Edison's patent sof 30th July, 1871, No. 2,909, as amended by disclaimer. VIE UNIT nD TELEPHONE COMPANY have acquired the patent rights granted to Louis John Crossley under the letters patent, dated let February, 1879, No. 412, and all rights to make, use, or sell the Crossley modification of the carbon trans- mitter, are now vested in the Company. Further, by Arrange- ment with the Consolidated Telephone Construction and main- tenance Company, Limited (the owners of the Gower Bell Patents) the United Telephone Company have the sole right of supplying for use in this country the fkower Bell modification of the carbon transmitter, constructed under the patents dated 3rd Octobe 1878 (No. 3,892), 25th January, .1879 (No. 315), 30th January, 1879 (No. 394), 24th February., 1880 (No. 814), 26th June, 1880 (No. 2,810), and 10th December, 1880 No. 5,482) and no other persons or companies are entitled to supply the same for use in this country. No form of Magneto Telephone, and no form of Transmitter in which arlion ar any other equivalent substance is employed, whether known as Edison's, Moseley's, Runnings', Crossley's, Gower's, or by any other name, can be manufactured, sold, supplied, or used in this country, except under license from the UNITED TELEPtiONE COMPANY (LIMITED). Proceed- ings will be taken against persons infringing the.Campany's Patent and other rights as aboveset forth. • The public are CAUTIONED against using any of these in- struments, except such as are obtained from the United Tele- phone Company, or their licensees, save and except any of 5,000 transmitters, made for Her Majesty's Postmaster-General, and which bear special marks of identification, whieh are pro- tected under the fiat of Her Majesty's Attorney-General, dated the 4th day of June, 1881. By order of the. Board, 6th July, 1881. JAMAS BRAND, Chairman.

This Company is formed for the purpose of erecting works, I and carrying on the business of Salt and Chemical Manufac- turers, on a very extensive scale, at Middlewich, In the County of Chester. and generally for the pnrpo.-rs specified in the Memorandum of Association. ' Great Salt deposits exist at Middlewich and other places in , the County of Chester. and brie is raised or pumped from these deposits, and manufactured by evaporation into salt for . home and foreige consumption. In addition to over half a million tons used at home over one million tans were exported last year. The Cheshire salt district yields by far the greate t portio 1 of the supply; in fact, it has practically the monopoly of supplying the world with salt, furnishing, as it does, 1 000,900 tons per annum for expert from Liverpool, and up. wards of 400,000 tons to the chemical works of Widnes and ot. ser towns. There can be no doubt that the' stilt trade is one of the most important mineral industries of the -kingdom. The trade is also a most proitabie one. The manufacture of chemicals, in which salt is most eaten. sively used, is also a very profitable business. For the commencement of operations an eligible site, con- taining about five a half acres, on which valuable brine springs or runs exist, situate at Kinderton, Middlewich, in the County of Chester, and adjacent both to canal and railway, has been secured nir the first works of the Company on advantageous terms, the pus chase money for which (Z20.0Q0) will be paid by the allotment to the Vendors of 1.400 fully paid-up Ordinary Shares, and the balance (213,000) in cash. The estate is freehold, and beneath the sart:ce of the sell is a very fine bed of clay, irom which all the bricks for the erection of the necessary works and buildings can be made. This will save a considerable outlay In the cost of the works, On one portion of the estate there is a valuable bed of sand, which can be used in the building of the proposed works of the Company. There is also a large mansion and outbuildings, suitable for the residence of a Managerand for the Company's offices on the estate. The Company wild be prepared to adopt the best machinery, methods, and pcLents which may be invented from time to time for the manufacture of both : alt and chemicals. This Company will raise the brine for salt making from its own land, and will thus save the royalty or rate of 6d. per ton I of salt ordinarily paid by salt makers in the district for brine. I pais alone will effect a great saving in the manufacture of salt of this Company; and, in addition to this, the saving in the price of the cost and carriage of salt to be used in the manufac- ture of chemicals by this Company (salt hiving to be purchased by other chemical manufactures) will be very great. The Salt Works at both Northwicti and Winsford are subject to occasional stoppages and to great da age and disablement, caused by subsidences of the laud, in c isequence of the large and contmual extraction of salt-rock andbrine therefrom. The Works of this Company will be &Wild upon solid virgin ground. some miles distant from these sinking places. The brine at Middlewich is also of Ja4etter class and of greater strength for salt making purpos4Apan that got either at Northwich or Winsford, and a nese source of supply suet as the one DOW proposed to be worked will be of Incalcu- lable value. The site ~.f the proposed Works. being In close proximity to to the Trent and Mersey Canal, and abutting on the London and North-Western Railway, this Company can lead its manu- factures direct into railway wagons at the Works, and will consequently be able to save a considerable amount paid by other manufacturers at Middlewich for c artage to the rail- way. The subsequent erection or purchase of other works at suit- able places in the district is also contemplated. The existing salt and chemical works in the Cheshire districts are doing prosperous and increasing trades, and from the known remunerative character of both businesses the Directors are of opinion that the Share Capital of this Company will even in times of depression in trade earn a minimum profit of 15 per cent, per annum, and that these dividends in active seasons will be largely Increased, and they are satisfied that the shares of this Company will be a sound and lucrative investment. It is estimated that the pr-sent issue of capital will be amply sufficient to enable the Directors to complete the pur- chase of the estate named, and to erect and finish works thereon to a large and paying extent, as well as provide a suffilent surplus with which to commence business. The vendors of the site aud brink springs already selected for the first works of the Company are ,o satisfied with the pros • peas of the undertaking that they haVe agreed to depmit ordi- nary fully paid up shares of the Company to the value of £7,000 with she JD rectors for two years, as a security for tbe payment of a dividend of 7f per cent. ppr annuca on the pre- ference shares of the Company. Application will be made in due course to the Stock Ex, change for an official quotation of the shares of the Company. The only agreements entered into are one for the purchase of the freehold site and brine springs at Rinderton. Middlewich, dated the 20th day of May, 1881, made between Joseph Jack- son and Thomas Capper of the one part, and Thomas Bost: cit for and on behalf of the Company of the other part, and another made between the said Thomas Rostock on behalf of the C m- pany of the one part and William Poole of the alter part as to the charges and expenses incidental to the formation and organisation of the Coo pany. Copies of the kiernorandurn of Association and of the above- mentioned agreements may be inspected at the registered offices of the Company In case of no allotment being made the deposit will be returned in full without any deduction whatever. THOMAS CAPPER, at the ROYAL HOTEL, 'RUNCORN, on MONDAY, the 18th JULY, 1881, at the hour of Four for Five o'clock in the afternoon punctually, subject to the conditions to be then produced, in one or more lots as may be agreed upon at the time of sale. All those Seven well-built. MESSUAGES or Dwelling- houses, with the gardens and appurtenances thereto belong- ing, situate at Weston Point, near Runcorn, in the county of Chester. The site of the houses and gardens attached to each contains In the whole 26 perches of land, of eight yards to the perch, or thereabouts. The-whole are held under a lease bearing date the 3rd day of May, 1824, for a term of 100 years, 43 years of which are unex- pired. The ground rent is £3 ss. per annum, which will be apportioned if offered in more than one lot, payable on the let January in each year, and they will be sold subject to the con- ditions and reservations contained in the said lease. The purchaser will have to pay one-hal? of the expense of keeping Ia repair the road or street, 12 yards wide, on the south side or so much thereof as adjoins and lies near to the plot of land demised by the said lease. The houses are contiguous to the extensive docks of the River Weaver Navigation, and also to the site of the new salt works proposed to be built and carried on by the Mersey Salt and Brine Company, Limited, at Weston Point. Mr. Richard Rhodes, one of the tenants, will show the property, and further particulars may be had by applying to the AUCTIONEER, Northwich, or at the office of Mr. BRAD- AMINE. solicitor, Northwich.

Valuable FREEHOLD RESIDENCES, FARMS, and Small Holdings at MOBBERLEY, NEAR KNUTSFORD, in the County of Chester, within 12 miles from Manchester.—TO BE SOLD BY AUCTION by order of the Executors of the late F. O. Watkinson, Esq., by MR. THOMAS CAPPER, at the UNICORN HOTEL, ALTRINCHAM, on TUESDAY NEXT, the 12th day Of JULY, 1881, at half-past four for five o'clock, p.m., subject to conditions to be then produced, in the following or in such lots as may be determined upona t the time of Sala. LOT 1.-A. RESIDENCE known as "Grove House," situate on the high road between Alderley and Enutsford. Cheshire, about one and a half miles from Mobberley Station, and half a mile from Mobberley Church and Post Office. The house contains 3 entertaining-rooms, 8 bedrooms, dressing-room, laundry, and every modern convenience, with stabling for 6 horses, loose box and carriage-house, shippon, barn, aid capital farm buildings. and splendid orchard and garden, together with several fields adjoining. The whole containing 19 acres 2 roods 13 perches, or thereabouts. LOT 2.-A Plot of eligible BUILDING LAND known as "New Croft," containing 3 acres 16 perches, adjoining Lot 1, at present under cultivation and occupied therewith. LOT 3.—A Plot of eligible BUILDING LAND known as "Near and Far Four Acres," containing 11 acres 2 roods and 20 perches, situate near Lot 1, at present under cultivation and occupied therewith. LOT 4.—A Plot of LAND called "The Sand Croft," contain- ing 2 roods 26 perches, situate near Lot 1. Two cottages adjoining and two chief rents arising out of three other cottages adjoining amounting to £2 161 Bd. per annum. 1 LOT 5.—A FARM known as "Grange House," situate on the high road between A lderley and Knutsford, distant one mile from Mobberley Church and Post Office. The house is sub- stantially built and very finely situated and could readily be adapted for a gentleman's residence. The house and farm com- prise 35 acres 37 perches. LOT 6.—A FARM known as "Barlow House," situate in Mobberley, two and a half miles from Wilmslow Station. The house stands well and ltommands a fine view of the adjoining country. The farm comprises 44 acres 1 rood 2 perches, and the buildings are most complete. LOT 7.—A Plot of Arable LAND, situate near Lot 6, known as Old Meadows," and containing 11 acres 1 rood 4 perches. Lox B.—A FIRM known as "Paddock Hill," situate about one and a half miles from Mobberley Church and Station, con- taining 7 acres 33 perches of land with complete farm buildings. LOT 9.—Six Closes of LAND adjoining. Lot 8, and containing 13 acres 0 roods 37 perches, now occupied as part of Paddock Hill Farm, and known by the names of "Half-acre," "Near Knoll," "Near Moss Croft," "Lee Meadow," " Further Knoll," and "Further Moss Croft." LOT 10.—A Piece of Arable LAND situate near Lot 8, and occupied therewith, and containing 1 acre 3 roods and 14 perches, known as " Kellicks." LOT 11.—A Piece of LAND near Lot 8, and occupied there- with, containing 2 acres 2 roods 17 perches, known as "Green- lane Field." LOT 12.—A FARM known as "Mount Pleasant," situate about one and a quarter miles from Mobberley Church, con- taining 21 acres 26 perches of Land. Good House and most complete Farm Buildings. The above properties are all well let. The land is in a most excellent state of cultivation, and the buildings are in good repair. The lots have been arranged with a view to meet the demand for small freehold holdings, and two-thirds of the pur- chase money can remain on mortgage at £4 10s. percent. The various lots will be shown on application to Mr. Ilottershead, Grovd House, Mobberley, who will send a conveyance to Mob- berley Station to meet any persons desiring it. Conveyances can also be obtained at llnutsford, Alderley, or Wilmslow Stations. Plans and conditions of sale may be had ten days before the day of sale on application to any of the under- mentioned. For further particulars apply to the AUCTIONEER, North- wich ; to ROBERT HOLLAND, Esq., Norton, near Runcorn; or to Messrs. BANKS & KENDALL, Solicitors, 26, North John-street, Liverpool.

MAKINSON AND WILCOCK, in returning their sincere thanks to their numerous patrons and the public generally for the very kind and liberal support they have hitherto received, hope, by strict attention to the interests of their clients, and the prompt, and faithful discharge of their duties, to continue to merit the same; the more so, as they are able to offer ad- vantages not generally enjoyed by those engaged in the same business, Mr. Makinson having had from early youth practieal experience of the English Timber, Stone and Building Trades, and of Farming in all its branches, being at the present time a farmer himself on a large scale; and,in addition, having served his apprenticeship to the ENGINEERING and MILLWRIGHT busi- ness, besides having had, during the last TEN years, consider- able practice in Valuing and Selling Colliery, Quarry, and other Machinery and Working Plant, Growing nd Fallen Timber, Farming Stocks, Growing and Gathered Produce, Stocks-In- Trade, Household Furniture Innkeepers' Effects, Houses, Buildings, Landed Estates and Property generally, and also in cases involving Damage and Trespass.
